reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: Solemn and aching with experience, tenderness—solemn, because it is so damn funny. We could spend whole evenings discussing the endless contours of the Dee Wallace character; I could spend the night on that Altmanesque zoom into her face in the mirror, after he fails to get it up, when she thinks, It's me again. Edwards' gift is to make you laugh and wince at the same time; the darkness of a theater is needed to work through these private misgivings in peace, and the largeness of a wide screen is needed to fully get its gag-littered profundity, as I didn't the first time I saw this on a Blu-Ray.

reviews.text: There are a couple of ways of reading 10. First, you can interpret it as a very 1970s tragicomedy about a successful songwriter (Dudley Moore) who responds to a midlife crisis by pursuing a young, beautiful, and newly married woman (Bo Derek) who’s way out of his league. Second, you can enjoy it as a brutal satire of middle-aged men’s propensity to feel anxiety over their physical and sexual decline once they reach an age when they realize they are no longer ideal sexual mates for sexy young women.

As far as the actual content of its wartime satire goes this ranges from passively amusing "what a mess!" mayhem to pure conservative boomer fantasy nonsense (something he has in his own movies sometimes but so pronounced here I have to imagine that's some Milius' music I'm hearing), and Spielberg has a machinelike approach to gags that kinda prevents this from having the fully spontaneous freewheeling chaos it thinks it has. So I completely get anyone just stone-faced checking out but still... What a mess! You know? And the sheer technical commitment to it. reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Drawing influence from disaster movies, ensemble epics, and any number of WWII pictures, 1941 is more ambitious in scope and scale than most films ever dare to be. I would not call it a success—maybe 20% of its anarchic antics elicited laughter from me, and that’s a pretty low batting average for what is ostensibly a comedy—but in spite of that, I spent much of its bloated running time with a different kind of smile on my face, gazing upon one of Hollywood’s ultimate “blank check” projects, admiring how fully Spielberg committed to the grandeur of its Panavision photography and to the chaos of its practical effects. It’s a mad, mad, mad, mad war, and if nothing else, the production captures that spirit.

For all the guy gets blamed for Hollywood's addiction to event-movie excess, this might be the only truly bloated blockbuster he's ever made; it's like an accidental critique of the military industrial complex, trying to win its own little war for audience affection by throwing obscene resources at it. reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: I like slow movies (The Turin Horse, 2001: A Space Odyssey). I like romance movies (Carol, Chungking Express). I like movies dominated by stunning visuals and voiceover (The Tree of Life, Apocalypse Now). I like slow, visually stunning, romance movies split into three sections (The Handmaiden, Moonlight). Yet 5 Centimetres Per Second is slow, visually stunning, somewhat romantic, split into three sections and a complete failure. It's boring and uninteresting. This is a film where nothing happens, and not in a way that the some of the greatest filmmakers (e.g. Tarr, Tarkovsky) manage to make work. Instead, Shinkai fills his film with cheesy moments, pseudo-intellectual voiceover and pointless shot after pointless shot. If not for the photorealistic animation and cleverly conceived structure (which is still poorly executed), this would be an unwatchable mess. As it stands, it's merely a boring, useless film with some redeemable features. Very disappointing.

reviews.text: Told over the span of, you guessed it, 52 Tuesdays, this movie documents the relationship of a teenage girl with her mother, who's currently undergoing a sex change. Though I wasn't blown away by it to any striking regard, I did appreciate the artistic approach it takes to its narrative. The effectively sad story it tells was a great bonus as well. Although I found it hard to really like many of the characters, I did at least feel for them, as the well written script allows the room needed to connect with them at a very basic degree. All in all, this is an Australian indie worth your time, just so long as you go into it without expectation. It also helps if you let yourself lose count of how many Tuesdays are left at any given point of the film.

reviews.text: 52 Tuesdays covers one year in the life of sixteen-year-old Billie as her mother goes through gender reassignment to become a man - and the effect it has on her own sexual awakening. At the beginning of the film her mother asks Billie to move out for one year. She says that living alone is a necessary part of her transition. Billie doesn't hide her hurt and they make a deal: she can come and visit her mother every Tuesday. What follows are a series of titles that track the next 52 Tuesdays - and the mounting strain between mother and daughter, who are both in a state of transition. Interestingly, this film was shot every Tuesday over one year.…

reviews.author: LEATH3RFACE
reviews.text: Found footage Vietnam war movie? Yes, please. Why aren't there more war found footage films? Seems like some untapped potential there. Anyway, this is one of those early found footage style films that feels way ahead of its time, even if it takes a bit to get going. The first stretch is pretty slow, mostly following a military cameraman embedded with a platoon during the Vietnam War. It opens with interviews and casual interactions between the soldiers, giving you a feel for who they are before anything really kicks off. At first it almost feels like a slice of life documentary more than a war movie.

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: Horror has long been the default domain of found footage, so I always enjoy discovering unsung gems that branch into other genres like Snow on tha Bluff and Punishment Park. 84 Charlie MoPic isn’t just an excellent indie Vietnam war film whose grunts-in-the-shit focus would make Fuller and Mann proud. It’s also one of found footage’s earliest examples, released the same year as The McPherson Tape.

reviews.author: doppelgangerdev
reviews.text: Nam' found footage drama that's actually a bit heavier than it originally let on. Clearly a small production, but it still provides enough to fit it's gritty frame. It clearly defines the varied members of the platoon. There's a solid mix of character irreverence, some confrontation with the war itself (common in later 80s Vietnam films) and sparse shootouts with unseen VC.

reviews.author: Cusack-edev
reviews.text: This is often heralded as one of the best found footage films out there. "MoPic" is short for "motion picture" and 84C is the grouping under which combat cinematographer lies. So basically this is the footage of that job title. Unfortunately this is insanely boring and focuses way to much on war cliches which made me roll my eyes numerous times. The cinematography is also barely found footage as it's much too good to be. It's basically shot like a movie without amateurish angles and shaky movement and for that reason it's less found footage and more a regular film. Overall, it's alright I guess. Some people obviously like it but I can't recommend it.

reviews.text: Seventies WWII movies are a strange beast. There’s a bit of that gritty realism creeping in on films that at their core, still want to be triumphant feel-gooders. Rather than a battle between the Nazis and the allies, this production feels like a struggle between new American and classic British cinema. It’s James Caan and Elliot Gould vs. Edward Fox and Dirk Bogarde, Redford and Hackman vs. Olivier and Hopkins, stark seventies ADR vs. gorgeous diffused cinematography. The scale of this film is truly incredible and so strange to see a practical match for the limitless production values of modern war movie CGI. Boy, this is beginning to sound like I know what I’m talking about. Better comment on something trivial…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Lord Attenborough may have garnered a Best Director Oscar for Gandhi, but this 1977 film is the most entertaining film he ever directed. A talented actor himself, he brought together the greatest cast ever assembled for a seventies production and gave us a thrilling account of The Allies' most ambitious failure during September of 1944. Attenborough's film is epic in every way, from the spectacular set pieces, the incredible number of extras, and that cast of superstars. Connery, Caine, Bogarde, Caan, Fox, Gould, Hackman, O'Neal, Hopkins, and Robert Redford just on the allied side of things. By the time we added Schnell and Kruger on the German side and Laurence Olivier and Liv Ullman as Dutch civilians, this film had…

reviews.author: Adam Nayman
reviews.text: So many angles of attack in this one: it’s simple; it’s sophisticated; it’s Spartan; it’s double-edged; it’s familiar; it’s startling; it’s goofy; it’s nightmarish. And it’s all held together by probably the richest pair of lead performances in any Cronenberg movie since THE FLY, a husband and wife with different yet finally convergent fetishes for role playing, Viggo hilarious as a man carefully measuring his every move until the jig is up and Maria Bello wringing consistently interesting variations on the idea of commitment. Great fun, including some slapstick gunplay that signals our hero’s awareness of the kind of movie his financiers wanted him to make, and which he has, but only in a fashion, and, as ever, on his own terms

reviews.text: Unforgiven for plaid shirt and jeans Southwestern Ontario farm dads. Economical old-fashioned neo-western crime pulp material with pretty broad ideas regarding identity construction and the corrosive effects of violence and the protection/performance of The Family Unit layered into a narrative that traffics in cliché macho mob revenge fantasy-isms, but very effectively realized with a freshly bruised, existential feeling riding underneath it; an open-wound stickiness, brutality, sexuality and moral weight that only Cronenberg approaching the familiar with the somber and intellectual engagement of an art film could pack it with. Even when tasked with giving us the sex and violence required of the genre he's operating in, I've always appreciated how awkward, gruesome and unheroic the moments of action are staged to…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Ford updated to the 21st century. History as a series of self-deceptions as myth gets subdued into role playing. Cronenberg clear direction blows everything wide open. As the title, perhaps the most wry joke in a pretty funny movie, promises, it is very surgical handled. It is a neowestern that, like most post bicentennial westerns, barely bothers to disguise that it is a mainstream art movie, but there's hardly a ponderous note and while Cronenberg finds an impressive double balance between delivering the goods (meaning blowing heads up) and implicating the audience (meaning keeping critics happy), it has an impressive propulsive quality. A self-annihilating journey that follows as impeccable as it is inevitable towards a release. The blocking is so…

reviews.author: clare
reviews.text: Beautifully fractured editing. I love the streams of jump cuts and outre psycho-sexual tableau in the dream sequences. I think they may be among the most captivating images Fulci has captured. And I've been so impressed by the tautness (questionable police procedures aside) of his scripts. It stacks the twists, while also managing to orbit that Argento theme: unreliable memory, objective reality vs. the subjective experience. I love that to dramatize this conflict, it weaves the "hard" facts of the detective genre to the surreal abstraction of art-house experimentalism. It puts us right in the thick of it. We can't be sure of the facts. We can't be sure what's a dream. And it ebbs and flows between those poles…

reviews.text: This is such a different beast from the Tobe Hooper miniseries that it defies any attempt at comparison. I had a teacher once, in like seventh grade, that considered Salem's Lot to be the scariest film he'd ever seen, and I know it traumatized its share of kids back in the day. This, however, is more spoopy than spooky. It's a very silly vampire adventure with some very silly vampire makeup effects and a story that's fun but hard to take too seriously. This is the kind of thing I would have loved as a kid, and which I find soothingly nostalgic now. It reminds me of things like Monster Squad and the sillier Corey Haim and Frog Bros moments…

reviews.text: This is a surprisingly solid second splatter effort from D’amato and Eastman. It’s not really a sequel to Antropophagus, but it’s often billed as such because of that pairing. There’s lots of blood all over the place and a couple of really tense and squeamy scenes like a bandsaw to the cranium and a head shoved in an oven and slowly cooked alive. This is one case where it’s not hard to see how this made its way to the Video Nasties list. There are a couple of parts that are too talky, but the third act is all-in so it balances out.

reviews.text: A spiritual sequel to Joe D'Amato and George Eastman's previous collaboration Antropophagus. Absurd is an absurd take on Halloween, with Eastman once again cast as the seemingly unstoppable killer - this time literally immortal thanks to some kind of church experiment (?) and let loose on small town USA (which obviously isn't in the USA.) The film really forsakes the atmosphere, which was key to Antropophagus, but makes up for it by really ramping up the gore. Eastman is ever the imposing presence when he's on screen and really notches up the kills here with an array of power tools, garden tools, his bare hands and even an oven. reviews.text: A critical examination of media manipulation, as well as one man's corrupt, selfish actions. Wrapped in the traditional Billy Wilder social-satirical manner, with Kirk Douglas being simply great in every single way—flawlessly showing a man so consumed by selfish gain and greed that he ignores all else around him. How far is someone prepared to go to get the attention they so much want? A film that is continuing to be relevant now and will be for some time to come.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: People often talk about media and cultural critiques in films being ahead of their time or somehow still relevant even after so long. The point of view is often (but not always) a certain amount of awe or wonder at how the film could manage this timelessness, but in this case, and ones like it, I often just feel sad. I've made a similar point before, but this film, and others like it, are failures. The media circus has only gotten grosser, more callous, and protracted. There is no Mr. Boot now, though. Every little paper, major news network, and blog site is full of Charles Tatums instead. The lesson they took from this film wasn't to respect human life…

reviews.text: Six years on from Kidulthood, and writer and actor Noel Clarke also takes on directorial duties, as well as main star status, in this sequel. Adulthood lacks any real character development, which makes it difficult to invest in the plight of Sam and his various friends and (mostly) foes. The film-making is cheaply flashy, Clarke too pre-occupied with what he could do rather than whether or not he should. The quality of film-making is an unfortunate step-down from the below-par standard set by the first film. On a positive note, Danny Dwyer is great in the minute or so he’s on screen, and UK rapper Plan B does decent work with the lacklustre material he’s provided.

reviews.text: A close-proximity, stylized documentary depiction of colonial cruelty and arrogance entering a feverish, bleakly slapstick jungle dreamscape and getting violently swallowed by the earth. Ants "conquering" a hill and calling themselves gods even while they slowly kill each other, starve to death and deliver rousing speeches to literal monkeys. Feels like a pretty clear precursor to the indifference of nature and sensory madness we'd eventually see in things like Sorcerer and Apocalypse Now, and between this and The Great Silence you could have one hell of a double feature of Klaus Kinski as an eerily quiet psychopath who reveals his aspirations of grandeur and unhinged, violent impulses when granted political power. "The earth I walk upon sees me and quakes."

reviews.text: A slow, transgressive, desperate plunge into hell and disarray with a standout performance from Klaus Kinski, who masterfully conveys the self-destructive nature of greed and power. A film fundamentally concerned with the essence of social structures and hierarchies that maintains a documentary-style low-budget approach filmed on location, making you feel like an innocent subject amidst not just the mayhem but also the stunning, seemingly eternal landscapes. Surprisingly only my fourth Herzog but this was just the kind of film I was on the hunt for tonight, and one I'm definitely looking forward to delving deeper into and recommending to others.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Anything with as many directors and as many disparate segments as this is bound to be a hit-or-miss affair, but the overall experience has a certain cumulative effect that it couldn't have had upon original release. Steeped in relics of the videotape era, its recreation of late-night cable works now as a nostalgia piece, arguably better than it does as a comedy. Still, there are certainly laughs. The John Landis segments are uniformly consistent—his Arsenio Hall-starring opener "Mondo Condo" had me rolling—and Joe Dante's brilliant "Critics' Corner" rockets past humor to thrive on sad existentialism.

It has so much going for it - leaning into baroque camp with that title, shepherded by fun-loving filmmakers Joe Dante, John Landis and Carl Gottleib, featuring a hundred familiar faces from popular movies and shows you've seen, using the anthology style to cram in your money's worth of little "SNL"-style joke ideas, lampooning an assortment of pop culture fads like sci-fi B-movies, "Siskel & Ebert", "Unsolved Mysteries", TV commercials, comedy roasts, erotica, reactionary educational videos like…

reviews.text: Pretty good documentary. It covers the history of American exploitation cinema that opens with the origin of filmmaking at the hands of Thomas Edison in the late 1800s and closes with the release of current faux-exploitation movies such as Grindhouse. In between, virtually every kind of low-budget fringe film gets a shout-out: the pre-Code films of the 1920s-1930s, the birthing docs of the 1940s, the drive-in biker movies and teenage monster movies of the 1950s, the nudist colony films, the crueler bondage films, Nazi fetish films, blaxsploitation, and of course sex, porn and gore.

reviews.author: dantesring
reviews.text: This film falls into that variety of documentaries that are designed as a primer to a larger topic. The history of the grindhouse films and its many forms is just too ungainly to capture in a single film and invariably it would be impossible to cover it all in a meaningful way. What AMERICAN GRINDHOUSE does is give us the highlights and encourages us to dig deeper.It does have a style that is a little too on the nose and sanitized for the material, but we do get a lot of knowledgeable talking heads (but please, enough of John Landis. He seems to be in every film documentary), and most importantly we get a ton of footage from the…

reviews.text: It may be surface level, but that makes it a perfect educational piece for those new to exploitation. With direct recollection from John Landon’s, HGL, Joe Dante, Bill Lustig, and a myriad of film historians, it is a wonderful summation of all things sleaze, porn, blacksploitation, and everything else that has pushed the buttons of morality starting all the way back in 1914. Drenner creates a wonderful chronological narrative that holds the hand of the newbie as they traverse Russ Meyer and Fred Williamson after braving Tod Browning. The documentary is masterfully narrated by Robert Forster (RIP) when not being coached by Larry Cohen or Ted V Mikels or so many other brilliant names in cinematic history.

But more so because it’s the antithesis of Late Cruise’s brand: it’s narratively baggy, he’s mortal and morally compromised, and when it ends you don’t think he’s the most impressive man alive. There’s something amusing about Maverick landing on dirt runways in Central America and hustling the CIA, but why was it shot on an iPhone with the Studio Light filter slid to 100? If this had marked a transition to gruff, exasperated leading roles — like Newman’s Nobody’s Fool and Twilight period — it might have been more coherent with his story. But Cruise was right back to Ethan Hunt after this. I hope he does eventually get to that period.

reviews.text: As a cartoon musical, it's decent; as a story of cat/mouse hegemony and subjugation, it's fascinating. But as a period piece? Jaw-dropping. An American Tail's New York City c. 1885 is bustling, feculent, corrupt, and candlelit, with poor little Fievel tossed this way and that around the Lower East Side. Sewers, piers, shoeboxes... everywhere's strewn with trash and fraught with danger for an immigrant mouse in an oversized cap. I was also impressed by the movie's literary points of reference: Julius Caesar, The Pirates of Penzance, The Brothers Karamazov. This movie's narrative curvature may be familiar, but its writing is agreeably sophisticated and its milieu dense with detail.

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: Cheap, DTV kiddie-krap that continues the franchise after the first sequel had effectively killed it. The first thing they do is have Fievel reveal that the second film's western adventure was only a dream, just so they can go back to Manhattan for an even more poorly-written one that involves Indians anyway! The animation is pretty dreadful, the musical score is wholesale stolen from the first film, the gags are unfunny and unearned, and the story is dumb. The only good things about it are its messages about North America being stolen from the natives and that the rich and powerful manipulate and divide the masses through fear, but even I am weary of seeing that in children's films anymore because it just doesn't seem to sink in. Enough of those kids still grow up and elect those same villains into positions of power anyway. So, what's the point?

reviews.text: Do you ever have the feeling where a movie was actually made for you? Where every character reminds you of either yourself or someone you know well? Where every time you hear the (perfect) score you feel energized and happy? Where every scene is so entertaining but also memorable and smart? Where the time period in which the movie takes place is the time you wish you could time travel back to? Where you know the location of the movie so well that you feel like you're there? Where the long takes are so good that you feel embraced with the characters? Where the dialogue is so natural and you feel as if you've said or could say lines that these characters say? Where you are comfortable with yet completely blown away by every scene? Yeah, that's what An Unmarried Woman is for me.

reviews.text: A subtly natural yet chaotically impressive amalgamation of the expressive nature and underlying perplexities of relationships, mental health and sexuality. It’s a metaphor that swirls around a character and inspects her in a simultaneously euphoric yet depressing way that exemplifies and understands what solitude truthfully means. It doesn’t view loneliness as a complete negative, in fact, it views it as a progressively difficult yet rewarding idea that brings out strength and compassion in human beings. Erica goes from lost, to troubled, to angry, to confused, to bold, to disgusted and a plethora of other continuous and challenging emotions until she has found herself again. Due to the trickery and confusion of her entity as a whole throughout this time -…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: As the rights of women (and the rest of us) are actively being stripped away, it's probably a good idea to remember that the idea of a woman choosing not to define herself via her relationship with men is still such an exceedingly rare thing in film even today that it feels fresh and even politically progressive. Carried by Jill Clayburgh's performance, this film slowly builds from her apologism for the men in her life to a satisfying series of expressions of independence. Meanwhile, it lets both Clayburgh's character and the men in her life being flawed and complicated without endorsing any of the toxic behavior.

Co-written by Jonathan Demme, Angels Hard As They Come, featuring a young Gary Busey as a fellow hippie trying to aide Glenn’s Angels, is reasonably entertaining even if its finale is anticlimactic and has little bearing on Glenn himself actually saving the day. reviews.text: Who would've thought that Mel Gibson, with all his issues, could create such a rich tapestry of an ancient culture without resorting to cheap cliches and stereotypes? "Apocalypto" is two straight hours of the most intense, nail-biting, ferocious, balls-to-the-wall cinema I have seen so far this year. Mel Gibson might just be the best director of all time when it comes to visceral, bone-crunching cinema. For the duration of the runtime, I was tense, thrilled, sickened, and completely blown away by how well-made this film was. I can't believe I put this film off for so long. It's a masterpiece!

reviews.text: It’s difficult not to be impressed by the magnitude of what unfolds here. The film is one of those rare works that seems to contradict the very idea of conventional war cinema. Instead of celebrating victory, it strips war down to its naked essence, fear, betrayal, endurance, and the slow death of hope. It’s, in its way, the antithesis of triumphal narratives, refusing the easy consolations of Hollywood-style heroism, but still, there is a certain pleasure in the camera, a hidden heroism in fact, that of “fighting and dying for a greater cause.”

Britt Robertson stars as Katie, a confused young woman who takes a year off before going to college, blogs anonymously about her promiscuity leading to shame and self-deception. Acting was great, with help from Christian Slater, Martin Sheen, Robert Patrick, and Justin Long (liked him Literally, Right Before Aaron and Tusk), all playing pretty flawed characters. It has a long way of telling the story but it all eventually comes together, effectively building empathy with the main character. The film was not extremely heavy but does deal with mature themes. I didn't care for the self-referential ending. Not a perfect film but it evokes interest, it’s watchable.

reviews.author: Daniel Shillito
reviews.text: At the Earth's Core is utterly joyous nonsense, extravagant, colourful and thoroughly preposterous, a typical lavish Jules Verne-style adventure full of youthful wonderment and hilariously dated effects. The movie is a kind of no-talent competition in which the acting, script, direction and camera work vie for last place but remains as upbeat as its exuberant charm allows for. With the great pairing of an overbearingly British Peter Cushing and a surprisingly pudgy Doug McClure battling rubber-suited monsters and subterranean species, it remains a blast throughout, even if the movie seemingly wanted to give more character to Caroline Munro's heaving cleavage than anything else in the picture.

One restless evening, I sat down and composed a short letter, just for fun (this was obviously before I’d made any friends), that read WAKE UP! in bold text at the top. The body of the letter was a plea for the reader to wake up from their manufactured existence. It explained that they were actually lying in a hospital bed, surrounded by loved ones, and that the message had been implanted into their self-constructed, artificial reality with the intent of illuminating the truth to them. People don't just become addicted to the game, it takes precedence over the physical world and even has an impact on it: even fame and social position are determined by the virtual, not the real. reviews.text: A lot of talking heads, but some great ones: Pam Grier, bell hooks, Larry Cohen, Gloria Hendry, Fred Williamson, Mario Van Peebles, and more relate their thoughts on the blaxploitation genre and its effects on African-America and Hollywood. It has some great pieces that give context to some of the classics of the genre, and it has some interesting perspectives from Grier, Afreta Shakur, and Hendry especially. The political and social context of blaxploitation films isn't always inherent to the movies, so having that lens to interpret them with is fascinating.

Despite being one of the most expensive films of the late Roger Corman's entire career, it is nonetheless the epitome of low-budget, exploitation fodder, done right. His guiding hands know exactly how to sell this sort of material. There's action, romance, heaving cleavage, violence, explosions, pathos-filled death scenes and a surprising amount of philosophy, what's not to like? It certainly helps that John Sayles's…

I’d take this over-flared, over needle-dropped, over-cast, over-baked monstrosity over any TRANSFORMERS movie any day, sue me. reviews.text: If I had to show someone the 1990s in movie form, it would be Beavis and Butt-Head Do America. It's all here: television addiction, guffawing teenage apathy, nonsensical toilet humour, grim satire, Jerry Springer-esque sleaze, a very MTV trip out sequence, and Chelsea Clinton. This is one of the few movies that — much like its titular characters — I laugh almost constantly throughout. I love that the film's protagonists have no idea about the actual plot of the movie that is going on in the sidelines. Everything happens around them as they mindlessly shuffle across America finding double entendres in every sentence, causing horrific highway accidents, watching donkeys shit, and wah-cking off in caravans. This movie really shouldn't work, but, outside of the South Park movie, I can't think of a better feature length adaptation of a television show.

This one is even set in 1983 (the year of Videodrome), for greater authenticity. The trouble is, Cronenberg didn't make 110 minute exercises in tone; even at his most abstract, there's a sense of narrative purpose and characters you can invest in. It's not that I'm against opaqueness in films, cinematic fever dreams whose primary appeal is audiovisual, but if you're going down that route, they need to be texturally interesting and not so one note. reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: Antonioni's final feature film is a sprawling, trawling, rambling mess. More soporific than engaging. More distracted than visionary. A collection of several thinly-realized stories that never add up to much beyond a yawn, patched together by elusive memories and the pall of awkward sex. Like IDENTIFICATION OF A WOMAN (1982), and 8½ (1963) before that, the story follows an artist searching for inspiration for his next movie. He wanders aimlessly around an Italian city hunting for his feminine muse, mumbling in stilted philosophical voiceover that feels about as intangible as the clouds.

reviews.author: Josiah Morgan
reviews.text: Reality through images, the only things trusted are those enforced as true once documented on camera. Antonioni's compositions are mysterious; architecture all seems endless and incontestable, men and women are made minuscule against the backdrops of dim interiors. There's none of the precision that makes Antonioni's early films (and the little work that would come after this) so fascinating, which may be Wender's fault - there's not much of interest here outside of the stuff Antonioni does. As typical of his work, its at its most tender and emotional (not necessarily best) when skin touches skin. Improves as it goes on.

reviews.author: Nick Newman
reviews.text: All of Antonioni's movies are about vibes, sometimes literally, never more than here. A series of events bordering between tangible experience and mere impression, vignettes for which only a director unable to speak could be responsible — "the true image of that absolute, mysterious reality that no one will ever see."

reviews.author: Robert Motherwell
reviews.text: Final feature film by Michelangelo Antonioni is far from his best work yet it remains indomitably his own. A director, who's obviously modeled after Antonioni himself, wanders around Italy where he observes small romances take place-whether these stories are meant to be real or just imaginative creations of the director is unclear-we the audience are given the chance to join this director in his meditation on love, desire, and a failure to communicate. Despite strong compositional work the film hardly boasts any of the cinematic power Antonioni showcased earlier in his career-still, with a cast that includes John Malkovich, Sophie Marceau, Jean Reno, Peter Weller as well as a strong music score by Van Morrison-the film still comes off as a deep work of passion-even if it's a quiet one. Despite its subtlety there are some surprising moments of dramatic power.

reviews.author: Miguel Marías
reviews.text: Más allá de las nubes y nuevamente La noche (1960) y El eclipse (1962) es ahora evidente que Antonioni tenía y sigue teniendo una visión cinematográfica muy personal. Este enfoque, que siempre fue minoritario, es hoy no ya algo excepcional, sino una anomalía, todo un síntoma -por contraste- de la enfermedad generalizada del cine actual, que es la vulgaridad y la consiguiente falta no sólo de ambición o preocupación estética, sino hasta de una estética y de la permanente búsqueda de formas expresivas que es lo único que mantiene vivo un arte. Esto puede significar, simplemente, que la mayor parte del cine ha renunciado al arte incluso como aspiración; que en su obsesión por el éxito económico se ha convertido…

reviews.author: Blair Russell
reviews.text: It only seemed right to view some blaxploitation during Black History Month. I’ve known of Black Caesar for awhile, yet it wasn’t until recently that the film became available for streaming. It’s a Larry Cohen joint that began as a project for Sammy Davis, Jr. (!) where a man short in stature would become a gangster a la a 30’s film like Little Caesar. However, Davis found himself in trouble w/ the IRS so instead Fred Williamson became the lead and the script changed to fit a former pro football player. From what I’ve seen, this is likely the best he’s ever been on screen.

reviews.author: BeardofTsu
reviews.text: The film grabs your attention right from the start with an engaging mob hit involving a shoe shining. When the James Brown scores kicked in, I was completely hooked! Fred Williamson walking down the street to "The Boss" perfectly captures the essence of cool, showcasing why Blaxploitation remains an unparalleled genre. One particularly memorable scene is when Gibbs puts shoe polish on the corrupt, racist cop as he beats him, all while the cop sings "Mammy, Mammy." It's a moment I won't soon forget. I watched the European cut, which includes a scene where a street gang attacks Tommy Gibbs - this scene was cut from the US version after the decision was made to create a sequel. Overall, it is much more than your run-of-the-mill Blaxploitation movie thanks to the performance of Fred Williamson in this gritty entertaining character study. HELL UP IN HARLEM might be next.

We basically watch him ascend the ranks of the streets from a shoe-shiner who does favors for the mob to bonafide badass #1 gangster in all of New York in the style of those Golden Age Hollywood gangster pictures from the 30s, up through the revival of such films in the 80s and 90s. Except here, Tommy is never able to outrun the marginalization and racism he fought to escape throughout his entire life. By the end, he is right back where he started: beaten and battered…

reviews.text: Bava's beautiful Gothic folklore infused tale of terror may not be as shocking today as it was upon release; but is just as breathtaking. The black and white cinematography, Gothic set design and foreboding score result in a feature that is just so black. The story has a few holes and drags a little in the third act but the design of the film is always enough to keep things interesting. The film is rich with symbolism and plays around with the rules of the genre; given that it's never really clear if this is a witchcraft film or vampire film. Lewis was a raving Bible freak who made anti-drug films.” They’re both right. BLOOD FREAK is the greatest thing that ever happened to Miami, an extraterrestrial dispatch that combines the innocence of 1930s exploitation with the cynical nihilism of post-Manson hate culture. Filled with unsettling violence, uninformed depictions of “reefer parties,” and a killer with a giant turkey head, the movie’s disturbing grandeur will never be equalled. If Jesus died for our sins, it was all worth it because we’ll always have BLOOD FREAK. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.text: Christ, I haven't laughed that hard in some time. Preposterous anti-drug film from the early 70s that's quite possibly the shoddiest thing I've ever seen. Mexican Elvis turns into a turkey-headed man after eating an experimental turkey while already 'addicted' to dope after a couple of tokes on a spliff. In a hallucinogenic fugue state, he runs around killing people and draining their blood. Proceedings are occasionally interrupted by a squinting man with an improbable moustache in a wood-panelled room, chain smoking and providing a running commentary on the shit you've just witnessed. There's a great bit near the end where he has a coughing fit and you think it might be about to make a point about the dangers of smoking, but nah - he actually just has a coughing fit and the director couldn't be bothered to re-take it. This is why the 70s were king.

This one takes a few ideas, but it's mostly original. The whole "mummy" aspect is just a concept in a story that takes in ideas of the occult and astronomy, as two Egyptologists obsess over resurrecting an evil Egyptian queen...for some reason. If the appeal of SOV movies is that they feel more 'real' than those on shot on film, then this shatters that reality like a brick to a coke mirror, as shot after shot is interrupted by wipes and dissolves that don't take the movie anywhere except back to the same shot in progress. reviews.author: bummer_buddy
reviews.text: I haven’t seen this since college but it’s as pervy and bizarre as I remember! One of my favorite parts of this movie is that there are so many conversations that are cut off mid-sentence, I had no idea it was because the producers demanded they go back and re-edit what was initially a campy titty horror comedy…into a more serious, “marketable” film. I think we all know how that worked out for them. I submit that in the spirit of “The Streisand effect” (when an attempt to suppress information brings national attention to it) we add “The Boardinghouse effect”—when an attempt to tone down material results in something far sillier and less marketable. Someone should make a letterboxd list…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Perhaps not quite the best De Palma movie (I might give the edge to Carlito's Way or Hi, Mom!), but it is THE Brian De Palma movie. Split diopters, mirror surfaces, garish and distancing set design, intricate camera movements, and sexist depictions that viciously target the heart of mainstream cinema's inherent misogyny. It's all part and parcel of De Palma's techinque, and it's all pushed to the breaking point in this recursive Moebius Strip of exploitation. Scorsese said of BDP's Scarface that it was really about Hollywood. Body Double makes that point unmistakable. It all coalesces in one great sequence in which the post-New Hollywood, Reagan-era Hollywood is linked to MTV empty aesthetics and outright pornography through some tawdry art direction, music video edits-on-the-beat, and meta lapses. Also a withering critique of the misogyny of seemingly nice-guy protagonists as much as the violent villains from whom such men attempt to save women. Vicious stuff.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: In a previous Letterboxd review I faulted the final act of this movie for succumbing to genre expectations after the exciting first hour of racially motivated cathartic humor. Thinking about it in terms of Fred Williamson's aims as a screenwriter and actor, I can see how deliberate this is: He wants to be the star of a Western, not a "black" Western. The confrontational name and the "get whitey" intro grabs your attention so he can show you how serious he is about playing the hero role straight. If Hollywood wasn't so racist (is that the right verb tense? probably not) he would have forayed into the role of mainstream action star. He had to do things his way, though, and godamn if he isn't all the more enviable for it. (for real, though, that final act is still kind of weak by comparison)

reviews.author: John (Magic Rat Movies)
reviews.text: Here's a deliriously entertaining ode to the sort of spirited, gory, cheap and cheerful exploitation epics of the VHS era. Bounty Killer is brilliantly bonkers, the film Neil Marshall's Doomsday wishes it was, a film Robert Rodriguez should study for pointers before any further Machete outings, a gloriously in your face mash-up of Mad Max rip-offs, spaghetti westerns and Faster Pussycat Kill Kill patented ass-kicking femme fatales! This is energetic, endlessly inventive, full-throttle B-movie nirvana overflowing with rampant creativity and tasteless tongue in cheek humour. Hell, it's even a film where the villains are big business white collar drones embodied by Gary Busey! Seriously, what's not to love about this crazed, kinetic cult classic in the making, which is infinitely better than any film with a former member of Coronation Street in a leading role has any right to be!

It's often so bad it's good, just as intended. It's delightfully over the top and campy, and the violence gets really bloody and gory in a ridiculous and fun way. I've been looking for ages for a film like this that's actually this good. Also, this director really, really loves women in high heels and boots.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Brewster McCloud (Bud Cort) lives deep underneath the Houston Astrodome, but his dreams rise much higher. He aims to fly. Not in a plane, but with strapped-on wings he’s designing—encouraged by a mysterious woman (Sally Kellerman) who may be his guardian angel. But BREWSTER MCCLOUD, Robert Altman’s wild, anarchic cult favorite, isn’t about dreams as much as it is about the highs and lows of humanity. It’s a serial-killer mystery. A frenetic car-chase flick. A crazy circus-finale comedy. Shelley Duvall makes her striking screen debut as the tour guide whose seduction of Brewster may lead to his undoing.

reviews.text: “i’m gonna make you rich.”What a statement this thing is. Sam Peckinpah once said this was the only film he made exactly the way he wanted to make it. After studio interference and compromises on even his most celebrated work, this was the picture that came closest to his own vision. You can feel it. Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia plays less like a movie than a manifesto torn from an open wound, with nothing held back. It is bleak, grimy, funny, strangely tender, and so emotionally exposed that it almost becomes uncomfortable. He went south of the border to make it, beyond Hollywood’s reach, obsessing over the right bars, the right faces, the right scorched landscapes…

But there are positives to take away from this glorious mess of a film. Some solid, if not terrific, performances abound. Vincent Cassel does what he does best-- act dastardly. reviews.text: Peter Yates' Bullitt is about as realistic as a police procedural is going to get whilst still being engaging. Steve McQueen is fantastic, he always makes everything seem effortlessly cool! I read McQueen actually modelled his character on Zodiac hunting Detective Dave Toschi, who helped inspire DIRTY HARRY too and was played in ZODIAC by Mark Ruffalo. The famous 10-mins car chase sequence is obviously memorable & influential but that foot chase and airport shootout in the climax goes even harder, the third act in particular is a masterpiece in escalating tension. (reminded me of Heat' climax).

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes

Exciting nail-biter of a car chase: stylish soundtrack for build up, great sound editing for chase-proper, great choreography and editing throughout, easy top five contender.

You can see the influence of Bullitt on Mr. Pakula, Mr. Fincher, Michael Mann, Ms. Bigelow. California Split might be the ultimate in this idea, giving us in the audience the vicarious thrill of a an exciting night of gambling, but the focus is totally different from what it would be in a conventional film. Gambling is an eminently cinematic activity, giving clear emotional stakes to clean, fundamental onscreen action, but Altman is markedly uninterested in the false drama and statistical impossibilities of movie poker. reviews.author: Harry Ridgway
reviews.text: A thing of rich and raw beauty isn't usually found in cinemas at this time of year. It's predominantly a period when brash blockbusters try to numb our minds and perfunctory cash grabs attempt to pry open our wallets. But John Michael McDonagh's Calvary defies this logic vehemently. It's a film that's imbued with staggering gorgeousness, verisimilitude and a whole heap of panache. Not to oversell it, but Calvary is to John Michael McDonagh what In Bruges was to his brother, Martin. It is, and I predict will be, one of the finest films of the year.

reviews.text: "Captain Kronos: Vampire Hunter" is a 1974 horror film Brian Clemens. A feature within the notable Hammer films cannon, "Captain Kronos" intermixes gothic vampire horror stylings with that of romanticized swashbuckling adventure. Ironically upon release, the film became somewhat of a conundrum to sell on the perspective audience because it didn't really fit the typical build of a single genre. It's a little bit of Alexandre Dumas flavoring in style with a companioned element of Errol Flynn. Now mix that concoction with a more subdued and sexualized European style of Jess Franco/Jean Rollin but not as forced in terms of abstract and you might have your placement of landing. And, though I think the film's weirdly widely mentioned connection to spaghetti westerns is severely overstated, it is nevertheless both refreshing and a hell of a lot of fun.*

reviews.text: Very much a Spike Lee film: conflicting discourses allowed to collide as the films picks subjects, characters, ideas, stylistic tics, everything Lee thinks might ressonate in his big tapestry. Much like Get on the Bus, Lee's best non-New York film, the space here is a complete abstraction which actually increases the feel of competing ideologies in a race to the finish line that is unreachable. It is more pointed and angry than anything he has done since the much maligned She Hate Me. I will never get why so many of his best stuff gets acused of being messy or ham-fisted given that as often happens he has little interest in conclusions but just allowing those collisions to open up new avenues.

reviews.text: I've never seen a movie like this, a screwball homage that fully transubstantiates the genre's breakneck pace and flaunted sexual mores into a more contemporary and ironically repressed context. That in an of itself is not without precedent (Bogdanovich, May and others others did it years earlier), but Rudolph completely mutates the pace along with the surroundings, maximizing the sense of despair that would erupt from the screwball if not given an animated outlet of expression. The film boasts many aesthetic delights—its openly quasi-musical, frequently plunges into giallo-esque reds—but both its comedy and its tragedy derive from the monotonous grind of the characters' lives and the way that their gnarled, interlocked romances only exacerbate their unfulfilled loneliness. At times it's…

reviews.text: The seduction of performance. In each gesture and every enunciation a drama is staged, whether transitory or for keeps, with nighttime as a dais for these sordid scenes. Sex, both foregrounded and backgrounded, affecting arrangement and acting as an objective foundation for our myriad mutual understandings, yet even when stronger feelings start to take hold, it is always there, lingering like flickering signs and streetlights—lurid and bright and hot as a wink—influencing the action betwixt players. Not a love triangle but some strange sort of trapezoid with its messy, rhomboidal leanings and uneven sides; what this story reveals beyond the fundamental intricacies of human interaction, the follies of interconnection, and fate’s sense of humor, is the peacock dance we all…

Something to day about these neon 80's sets and Teddy Pendergrass soundtrack that creates an aesthetic to this L.A. backdrop full of hookers but it's the lovers that struggle to hold on to love. I enjoyed the whole cast for it's quirky engaging narrative that only Alan Rudolph can deliver. I feel like this is a more jaded aged "The Graduate" in a way especially with that ending.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: the insularity of obsession, a tiny little red-light district just for your imagination. rudolph's ritualistic repetition of signature sounds for each locale gives choose me a phosphorescent glitz, wind chimes and saxophones, half-in and half-out of reality, it is a strange movie that plays with cliches but not for the aim of satire, it is more like when you listen to a song and create a visual story in your head to go along with the tune. it reminds me of chantal akerman's toute une nuit, both films about the illicitness of intimacy while distantly stoking the internal fire of these lonely hearts, embracing the paradox of love's essential relation to madness and irrationality, people moonlighting as their desires under the safety of dusk, going against their better judgement for the sake of that palpitating warmth in a cold postmodern world, the sacred amidst the sordid -- "you're not alone in the dark."

Such a beautifully offbeat film, glowing with warm lights and soft music that centers on lonely bodies trying to make sense of what they desire. The neon-lit, perpetual-night setting feels so in tune with the gentle weariness of these wounded strangers who are tired of being alone, but aren't quite sure how to handle all the uncertainties that come with letting someone in. Overall atmosphere is very intoxicating, the sense of intimacy and loneliness coexisting in the film's late night world makes everything feel so interesting throughout. I've waited years to watch this and it was absolutely worth it💕

reviews.author: Derek
reviews.text: Citadel is an imperfect yet pretty fun Irish horror film. It reminded me of a lite version of The Brood seeing as though it's about evil children like entities that are born from negative emotions. The only difference between the two is that in The Brood, the creatures are born from anger and rage, while here they are born from trauma and fear. They were similar enough that there is no way that it was on accident, but despite The Brood being the far more superior movie, Citadel was still a good time. Whereas The Brood was fantastical and over the top, Citadel is steeped in harsh realism, which I really enjoyed. The movie is set in the bleak setting…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A profane funeral for western civilization. Unlike other Fulci’s end of the world scenarios, this doesn’t move towards cracking reality, but start with a series of disparate parts and allow them to cohere. It is also unique in that characters actually seek their destination instead of stumble into it. There’s a mourning feeling throughout, a ritual of passing. Most of the violence happens very late and there might be less of it, but there’s also a lot of sorrow. As often in Fulci he just finds images from eyes bleeding to a phone covered in maggots to heads squelching that are charged with power. One of Frizzi’s better scores as well.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: I guess it's not surprising that this would feel more brutal and terrifying than ever, but it's still a triumph of editing and in-camera film techniques. The woozy focal lengths that communicate feverish brains combined with those insert shots of hands on public transport poles or faces smeared with cold sweat are so paranoia-inducing. The hard cutting of the film only makes it all so much worse; the smash cut from Winslet weakly trying to hand her coat to another dying patient to her corpse sealed in plastic and being placed in a mass grave is among the most singularly unpleasant, profoundly unnerving moments in cinema history. Soderbergh's cold precision as a filmmaker, and Martinez's metronomic score, epitomizes the steady progress of the human response, but at every turn it's emphasized how impossible it is for humanity to get ahead of a disease. At the moment it certainly feels like the best horror film of the last decade.

I still think a little more subversion of those images would probably drive the point home better, and as always Bakshi's shaggy style can be a little hit-or-miss whenever his characters actually have to speak. reviews.text: A film that so thoughtfully and effortlessly allows us to experience and find love in this family and life in ‘70s Brooklyn. Spike Lee is an absolute genius. His eye, talent, and raw portrayal of everyday life is brilliant to watch. It’s personal and kindhearted and the care Spike Lee has for his stories adds so many layers and so much beauty to his films. A film as hectic and roaring as it can be intimate and soulful, giving us a look at the highs and lows of family and neighborhood dynamic. The tough moments were heartbreaking and so realistically accurate and raw that my stomach couldn’t help but feel knotted. Dreadfully emotional at times while equally as heartfelt and tender at others.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Highly questionable depiction of African revolutionary uprising in this bleak and ultraviolent men-on-a-mission movie, using the 1960s Congo Crisis setting with the same tact that a 30/40s Hollywood Western might show you native-on-settler violence. But despite that, Powell & Pressburger cinematographer Jack Cardiff (whose poetic and vibrantly artificial lensing of The Red Shoes and Black Narcissus is iconic for a reason) makes the transition to directing quite competently and delivers on a gorgeously widescreen photographed episodic series of pulpy and nasty macho adventure action setpieces that manage to evoke things like The Dirty Dozen and Where Eagles Dare obviously, but also Lawrence of Arabia, The Train and The Wild Bunch.

reviews.text: Holy hell! If, like me, you've always thought of "The Wild Bunch" as the film that introduced stylized ultra-violence to the modern Hollywood vernacular, make a date with 1968's "Dark of the Sun." Featuring Rod Taylor ("The Birds") and NFL hero Jim Brown, this is a unflinching Men on a Mission flick about two soldiers of fortune who plunge deep into the Congo to rescue a mine company's workers—and some $50 million worth of diamonds—only to come face to face with an inferno of face-melting violence and inhumanity. Another great cult flick I wouldn't have sought out or even heard about if it weren't for the Letterboxd fam.

MacDonald himself thought so, too, reportedly saying he “was pleased to find it only semi-rotten.” Ed Waters’ script is fairly faithful to the novel and character. McGee isn’t a private detective, but rather a beach bum who occasionally takes on clients as a “salvage consultant” when the mood strikes him or funds run low. reviews.text: First rewatch since tearing through thirteen of the McGee novels during quarantine reveals this to be a note perfect adaptation of MacDonald’s Floridian noir spirit. No lengthy character intros. Barely any backstory. You’re simply dropped in the middle of Travis McGee’s seventh mystery and forced to keep up, just like the books. Ahead of its time, even if Robert Clouse directs it like a beach bum spin-off of MANNIX.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A cheap and mean neo noir exercise taken from a John D. McDonald novel that served as Robert Clouse debut feature. The complex plot is beyond Clouse’s control as things move awkwardly from one major scene to the next. There is one classic brawl between Rod Taylor and William Smith: intelligently staged, blunt and very physical, it came and goes with a furious energy that is not that common in American thrillers of the period.. It is good enough one can easy imagine Warner execs taken a look at It and decisdng to give Clouse the job of making Bruce Lee’s very Chinese mix of nationalism and narcissism go down more smoothly to Western audiences. As often happen in B thrillers of the period the lazy bluntness of it adds to the feel of nasty low life authenticity.

reviews.author: Auteur
reviews.text: George A. Romero's masterpiece. A subversive anti-capitalist manifesto, spot-on indictment of consumerist culture and desensitization, and an exploration of the social construct vs. human nature debate, masquerading as a nail-biting zombie apocalypse thriller with some of the greatest gore effects of all time, Dawn Of The Dead is not just one of the best horror films ever made, but also one of the greatest artistic statements from a filmmaker at the top of his game.

reviews.author: cinemasauron
reviews.text: From the director of Night of the Living Dead, the cult classic that single-handedly changed the landscape of horror genre with its effective take on a world overrun by reanimated corpses, Dawn of the Dead arrives as the follow-up chapter that adds even more elements to this post-apocalyptic world while further evolving the characteristics of the living dead.

reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: In the wake of the gargantuan success of Jaws, studios and production companies decided it was only fair they try to make their millions on cash-grab film efforts aiming to reproduce the results of the box office phenomenon. Generally described as “nature runs amok” films, most of them were big business at the drive-ins across America during the seventies. Even big-time directors got in on the action. Director Irwin Allen, best known for his disaster films (Towering Inferno, The Poseidon Adventure, etc.), directed the 1978 Michael Caine vehicle The Swarm, in which killer African bees descend on American cities. Director William Girdler, while a lesser-known name, was no different even though his aim was much lower than Allen’s: the B movie exploitation circuit.…

reviews.text: As much as I want to love Days of Heaven more (and don't get me wrong, it is arguably the most visually breathtaking film in Malick's catalogue), I can't help but feel the choppiness played out behind the scenes - literal years of editing and postproduction - manifest itself in the pacing. There's an odd mix of in media res sequences coupled with the now-traditional meditative abstract breaks that effectively cause a jerkiness and stuttering in the narrative progression. It doesn't destroy the film by any means, but it adds to my feeling that there is an extraordinary story hidden here, fragmented, glimpsed, but never appropriately focused on due to whatever issues caused such a headache in the editing booth.…

I didn't choose the school highest on the US News and Report rankings. Instead, I picked the school where my version of blackness would be most readily accepted. At the Ivy League school I visited, I was the only black person I saw outside of the airport during my two day stay. At another prestigious school, my social circles were already predetermined by my hometown and my race. I was tired of being the only black kid in the class. reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: An intersectional treatise turned into a feature length film, which is... kinda the best thing I could ever say about a movie? As much a primer on how to survive as it is an indictment of white supremacist culture, as much a complex look as a didactic essay, as much a coming-of-age college story as a political diatribe. It's very difficult to write about this the way I normally write, because normally I am prising ideas out of a film, chopping up text and subtext as I bounce off an idea. Here, the ideas are all text, and the subtext is... not mine to address. At least, I don't think so. The title--and the direct message here--is certainly explicit enough…

reviews.author: Rida
reviews.text: Representation isn't about scaring politically correct white artists into including POC characters in their stories to satisfy some imaginary diversity quota. Representation is about getting to make films like Dear White People, and in creating an environment in which filmmakers of color can get the backing to make films about their communities. It's incredibly refreshing to see complex, ambiguous characters with hyphenated identities taking center stage in a film. It's almost enough to make me want to overlook the numerous weaknesses in the film itself. Almost.

reviews.text: Subterranean homesick blues. Gary Sherman’s London Underground one man cannibal jam boasts one of my favorite opening credit sequences/scores ever, a 7 minute long take of the cannibal’s victims/dead relatives that ends leaving a dimly lit tunnel, and Donald Pleasance as a scenery chewing police inspector. My type of cult jam, strewn with raw meat bodies via an underground corpse graveyard and just enough of that procedural flare that I dig in small doses—Neato stuff for 1972, especially that small, but memorable tango between Christopher Lee and Donald Pleasence.

reviews.author: Branson Reese
reviews.text: Wish I could find more to like in this downbeat, acid jazz drenched snapshot of NYC in the mid 70s full of actors whose heads looked carved out of dried up apples. But this really is a conservative piece of art. Look, I'm not opposed to conservative art. It's getting made whether I like it or not and I've loved plenty of reactionary slashers so it's not like I'm up on some high horse, here. I'm no liberal. This movie's real sin is that it's slack and ultimately pretty boring. It's The West Wing without any screwball dialogue. But instead of owning Republicans with facts and logic this is a movie about owning minority teenagers with bullets. Ultimately they boil down to the same message: I'm right and these other people are so wrong that they must be destroyed.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Classic revenge movie about a mild mannered architect who becomes a vigilante after his wife is murdered by vicious street thugs. The film works thanks a strong focus on the character. His awakening which sees him realise muggers are bad and guns are a good tool for getting rid of them is calm and measured; and fascinating to watch. The way that the film explores the vigilante theme is interesting too for the way that the revenge isn't focused on the perpetrators of the original crime, but crime in the city in general; which also allows the film to provide a broader commentary on the city itself and local police force. Charles Bronson is spectacular in the lead role and he really lifts the material with a powerhouse performance. This is top quality gritty seventies cinema!

Richard Friedman (PHANTOM OF THE MALL: ERIC’S REVENGE) directed the New York crime drama in 1983. It received a minor four-walled theatrical release in Phoenix, Arizona in 1984 before Prism Entertainment put it out on home video in 1986.

reviews.text: One of the most intense and fascinating noir films I’ve ever seen. The film distills the essence of the genre with almost feverish urgency as if it were always one step away from total ruin. It’s something that goes far beyond the narrative of bad luck and cruel fate, it’s about the energy with which Ulmer directs his camera and his characters, transforming the scarcity of resources into an aesthetic of pure existential despair.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: Some unscrewed heads at the 20th Century Fox greenlight department gave Dirty Mary, Crazy Larry a go, and it has taken grindhouse and hot rods aficionado Quentin Tarantino to make sure it has never been forgotten. “Vanishing Point” had been a hit (another Q.T. favorite, I prefer “Dirty Mary”), and so Fox was souping up the formula with a slightly bigger budget. You got Peter Fonda in the getaway car after a supermarket robbery, Adam Roarke as the would-be level-headed brains behind everything, and Susan George as the slutty eye candy who wants you to forget she’s not a slut and she’s all in for anything resembling danger.

reviews.text: "Dirty Mary Crazy Larry" is a 1974 crime film directed by John Hough. What starts early on as more of a meticulous heist feature eventually gives way to more of a daredevil road racing movie. In all this the film is a presented good time for the causal fare of things, something that really resonates with the drive-in flavorings that were prevalent in the era. I don't quite think that its overall balanced, but nothing too much to nitpick to get away of the general amount of fun.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This one may be late comer in the Hammer Horror cycle, but it absolutely shows the studio at their imaginative best. Roy Ward Baker's film is a play on the classic Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde story, with the murderous personality this time taking on female form. Despite the camp nature of the concept, Dr Jekyll and Sister Hyde is absolutely played straight. The film never indulges in any silliness; playing along similar lines to the original novel but with the gender of the Hyde personality reversed. The fact that "mister" rhymes with "sister" seems to be more important than any comment on gender roles, though the film does make the most of its salacious concept. The initial transformation scene…

reviews.text: Continuing with the tradition of amazing on-camera transformation effects of Jekyll to Hyde, this is the first movie in my mind to really match the Fredric March transformation from 1931 which uses lighting and colored makeup to create a one-take change. Here, Roy Ward Baker uses a single take in which the camera spins around Ralph Bates, head in his hands, before a mirror, and when he looks up, he is Martine Beswick, done simply by changing the angle of the mirror so that it shows his back, but Beswick's reflection. Watching the scene enough times you may catch the corner of the other actors' sleeve just coming into frame as they both stand up. It's a triumph of simplicity.…

reviews.author: Aberrant Ghoul
reviews.text: Oh, this is such cinematic comfort food. It's like being wrapped in a warm, Technicolor blanket, as you're lulled into a restful sleep, transported into a dreamscape awash with a luscious, gothic atmosphere. It easily sits alongside the 1931 Dracula and the 1992 Dracula, as one of my all-time favorite Dracula films. Peter Cushing is great, as a younger, more action-oriented Van Helsing, and Christopher Lee is so damn menacing as Dracula. Sure, it takes its liberties with the original story, but it all works great. It focuses on the important moments, moving along at a brisk pace, with more action than most Dracula adaptations. And that climactic battle between Dracula and Van Helsing is glorious.

A surprisingly fun entry after a run of weaker Hammer Draculas. the idea of dropping Dracula into 1970s london shouldn’t work, but it mostly does, even if it feels a bit like the Count got lost on his way to a different film, which you can definitely tell was to try catching the attention of a younger 70s audience

reviews.author: Tentin Quarantino ☭
reviews.text: Most bad-ass action film I've seen since...well...The Raid. Similarities will be drawn between the two films for sure, but they remain their own entities in spite of the similar concepts. Where The Raid is more or less an excuse to have fight scene after fight scene (not complaining), Dredd feels like an actual story with its own characters and its own world. Alex Garland's script is tight, and full of great moments. The look of the movie is unique and wonderful. Karl Urban was magnificent in the eponymous role. I loved how the whole story felt more or less like just another day for Dredd. Widespread conflict and global stakes were not necessary. The rookie was very well integrated into the story and provided a much different type of sidekick role than usual for this genre.

reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: An infectious good-mood in film form. This is all unadulterated mismatched-buddies action fun. And something that can’t be described as anything less than a blast. It’s a rare blend: one that manages to successfully mix Hong Kong action sensibilities, interesting characters, enough of a story so that its easy to follow but still not entirely vapid, funny dialogue, explosions and more spinning flipping kicks then I ever think I’ve seen in a two-hour time period before. Mostly down to Mark Dacascos, who is like a magnificent whirling dervish on the screen. He’s great. And so is Kadeem Hardison as the other part of the buddy pairing. Although, no disrespect to them, Brittany Murphy almost steals the whole thing with her gloriously unhinged role. It just all adds up to something that’s relentlessly entertaining.

(The instinct this has to get Cage for the lead role is basically everything wrong with it, even if there's some obvious fun to be had with him because he's the best.) Did marginally enjoy spending some time with my good buddies Tom Atkins and William Fichtner I guess.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Its boundless empathy in the arena of mental illness and its full commitment to building an absurdist reality out of whole cloth make Drop Dead Fred positively Shyamalan-esque. Decades later, the film has the cult it deserves, but the critics who’ve panned it would do well to take a second look. What appears to be a broad, juvenile comedy in passing is actually quite a sad and sensitively-spun story about one woman’s arrested development barreling headfirst toward a truly destructive nervous breakdown. Trapped in a state of emotional object permanence by a controlling mother and a repellent boyfriend, she recedes into the fantasies of her youth to discover a new narrative by which to reframe her life. Fairy tales never satisfied Elizabeth Cronin. Her problems have always been too large to fit into that tiny box, and she needs Fred to smash the living daylights out of it.

reviews.text: Should be completely impersonal, but it's not. Should be a minor work, but it's not. Should be shown in film schools - for students to see how to take on a project completely for hire and make it completely theirs. All the tropes are there somehow - body horror disguised as gory action scene for example - but also families, offices and social networks, how those networks define characters and in reverse how character definition can be completely deceiving. But that's just the surface: if a viewer is aware of the central twist late in the movie (the best films get even better on repeat viewings) the film shifts from being the ultimate modern-noir genre flex to continuing Cronenberg's fascination…

By all accounts, Wood did have robust heterosexual appetites, but... surely there was something more complex going…

reviews.author: Alex Kittle
reviews.text: Set in a post-apocalyptic world without memory, Claire Carré's EMBERS is fittingly meandering and dreary. It follows a group of unconnected individuals as they cope with the effects of a worldwide epidemic, with most survivors left to wander around aimlessly, constantly re-experiencing things after forgetting them. One couple wakes up each morning asking "Who are you?" and must piece together their relationship through guesses. A former neurologist attempts to combat memory loss but finds himself doing the same work over and over again regardless. A teenage girl and her father survive with memory intact in a high-tech bunker, aiming to preserve human culture and legacy, but their isolation leaves the girl miserable.

reviews.author: Shikhar Verma
reviews.text: Embers is a post-apocalyptic story where the entire human race has succumbed to mass amnesia. Their memories are bound to be lost with the passage of small fractions of time. Following a group of vignettes, Claire Carré's film explores deeply ambitious questions with great subtlety and acquisition. Embers follow a group of people trying to cope up with survival and wishes to understand human tendency in a world where everything seems temporary. It investigates human nature in the most prolifically imaginative way. While it doesn't seem to have a certain closure to everything it brims-up, Embers work because of its visual style and a singular narrative flow that brings every scattered thing together.

It begins as a battle royale TV game-show and mutates into an escape film as the laconic antihero Shannon (Al Cliver) leads a telepathic mutant (Moira Chen) and her oracular son to safety.

reviews.author: Laurie Orla
reviews.text: Endgame was the first Italian post-apocalyptic movie I ever saw and remains my favourite one for that very reason. Somebody in my family thought it was a good idea to rent Endgame and leave an impressionable five year old alone for an illicit viewing of this radiated spaghetti trash. As a result an unhealthy obsession was born...Despite being a shameless rip-off of undoubtedly superior films, this was by far the coolest thing I'd ever seen up until that point. Although in retrospect the most unhealthy aspect of my childhood obsession with Endgame was that I immediately began to idolise Ron Shannon (Al Cliver) as the dynamic anti-hero I most wanted to be.As an adult, I still appreciate the…

Though it doesn’t hit the highs in terms of thrills and gets ridiculous at times, the fast paced screenplay and its solid characters keep it interesting. On the other hand, they don’t make such movies anymore, making you only crave more for such 90s styled action thrillers. Reason why the movie has aged well. A solid watch.

reviews.text: You've reached the darkest pit of hell when you've become such a Monty Python completist that you seek out all the group members' horrible solo projects - Splitting Heirs, Yellowbeard, The Rutles 2: Can't Buy Me Lunch, all that shit. As with the Beatles, you see what the individual Pythons brought to the group by studying their solo work. This Terry Jones effort has some of the atmospherics and playful, anachronistic approach to history that marked Holy Grail and Life of Brian, but without the diamond-cut timing and rigorous comic logic that marked Cleese's writing, without the visual imagination that Gilliam had when he was at his peak, and without the form-bending experiments that the whole group were interested in…

reviews.author: MichaelEternity
reviews.text: Jolly high fantasy with Python-esque humor dotting an otherwise sincere quest narrative. Looks like a spoof but you're actually supposed to care about what happens and believe in the magical mystique of all this Norse legend stitched together. And I did! Fantastical medieval sagas were a defining '80s genre, and while "Erik the Viking" isn't exceptionally funny or particularly grand, it is amusing and at times elaborately produced; I mean it's streets ahead of other off-brand Monty Python swashbuckler comedies like "Jabberwocky" and "Yellowbeard", at least.

We focus on The Bronx once again; a ruinous hellhole under the control of various gangs, and now subject to the 'The Corporation' who have plans to gentrify the area, by way of exterminating everyone that lives there. The plot in this one is basically just a loose thread, which the director uses to string a tirade of action against. And it comes thick and fast - vehicles exploding, gunfights, helicopters shot from the sky, flamethrowers and more besides. They send extermination squads called "Disinfestors" to burn, gas, or "relocate to New Mexico" the few bands of civilians who try desperately to remain in their homes. When they make the mistake of burning Trash's parents alive he embarks on a crusade to bring the remaining stragglers and gangs together and go on the offensive against the tyrannical corporation and the political apparatus that enables it.

reviews.text: Captures the craziness of that era in Italian film better than I anticipated and has a real loose charm to it. Really nails it for the most part although it loses half a star for some awkward animation that didn't really need to be there. Otherwise, it's impeccable in the choice of interviews and structure, with some truly bizarre anecdotes about Italy in the 70's that will turn your hair white. Not surprising that Henry Silva and Franco Nero are the most interesting but I was also really impressed with the stories from John P. Dulaney who's more of a footnote in the genre than a star. Lots of great surprises like that in this doc.

reviews.author: JSlattery
reviews.text: Hugely entertaining love-letter to the 'poliziotteschi' genre..the ultra-violent,definitely non-PC Italian cops and robbers films of the 1970's.Director Mike Malloy..a familiar face from the bonus features of many Eurocrime DVDs and blurays..is the perfect guide to this macho universe populated by motorbike-riding handbag snatchers, sweaty, double-crossing pimps and no-nonsense,slap happy and invariably moustache-toting cops, often played by either Franco Nero or his dollar-bin clone, the wonderful Maurizio Merli! Nero is among the interviewees, as are various, often imported stars of the genre such as Fred Williamson,John Saxon,Richard Harrison and Henry Silva..Silva is as gaunt and scary looking as ever, but he's an unexpectedly witty and droll interviewee, who'd have guessed? Even if you've only a passing interest in the genre I can't recommend this doc highly enough, it's every bit as good as 'Not Quite Hollywood ',the tribute to Aussie exploitation films of the same era..and that's high praise!

reviews.text: Maybe my favorite Cronenberg now - layers and layers of "spaces" overlapped until the distinction between the virtual and the real can no longer be distinguished. This is constructed so meticulously - placing characters within a virtual world, governed by virtual laws - but this also depicts the virtual-nature of our basic standards of living: you wake up, you eat, you go to work, you have lunch, you go home, you have dinner, etc. In-between, everything becomes a game: alliances, relationships, sex, even eating food. By the end, we have no clue whether we are seeing a "game" or "reality." But it doesn't matter - for Cronenberg, they're one and the same. Masterpiece.
