reviews.text: Family Plot is exactly the kind of twisty, convoluted, humorous caper the Coens would later excel at, but in the Master’s hands, it’s surprisingly talky and static. You can sense his age with this one, during lengthy scenes of characters extensively discussing the plot but saying very little along the way. More often than not, it feels like a made-for-TV movie of the time, which isn’t a bad thing, but as the final Alfred Hitchcock film, it’s a touch underwhelming. Deserved props go to the inimitably glamorous Karen Black, the agreeably punchy John Williams score, and a bonkers setpiece involving a car careening down a mountain that must be seen in all its wacky, breakneck glory to be believed.

It’s a movie about what it’s like to be with people who share your fervor for something that most other people in your life (or the world) think is a waste of time. Those other movies are all disappointing on some level, but FASTER, PUSSYCAT not only fulfills its checklist of sex, violence, and rock n' roll, but it also adds qualities one wouldn't even expect were possible in this realm of filmmaking. The self-consciously pulpy dialogue dances between the oddly poetic (Dan Clowes's ears perked up at "like a velvet glove cast in iron") and the sophomoric pun ("everything we touch is hard"), always with a certain cadence that's easy to identify but nearly impossible to recreate. reviews.author: WraithApe
reviews.text: Maybe I need to give The Editor another shot, cos this batshit crazy homage/piss-take of old school Troma grindhouse excess was pretty damn impressive considering its miniscule $10k budget! It nails that grimy SOV aesthetic and goes full bore with the gore. It took me a while to get on its wavelength; seemed at first like it was gonna be a bit tryhard, pushing edgelord territory, but the writers' sense of humour really grew on me as Fuchman's reign of terror intensified. It's uneven and purposely taboo-smashing, featuring incest, anal rape, genital mutilation (one scene in particular is hellishly cringe-inducing - you'll know the one I mean if you've seen it), baby-stomping, religion-baiting, and it's gory as all get out, but isn't that exactly what you want from a midnight movie?! Simultaneously the silliest and the most extreme thing I've seen in a hot minute!

reviews.author: autocinephilia
reviews.text: Father's Day is the funniest exploitation film ever, and not in an unintentional, so-bad-it's-good sort of way. Father's Day is a perfect black comedy, and the mix of hardcore exploitation and surreal comedy is measured perfectly. Both the comedy and the violence are exaggerated to their limits, and I have no qualms about saying that this might be the most violent film I've ever seen. This is an exploitation for the most die-hard fans of the genre.

reviews.text: When Richard Lester directed this movie, he was only 52, and with it, he was pretty much done. And while this film is not entirely successful, it does show he can still successfully corral multiple elements without losing control of the story.

Bennett MIller's masterpiece revels in the unspoken, mulling through silence and emptiness in a world where everything is left unsaid. The film resembles the quiet pattering of a slight rain-storm, slowly adding more and more rain until the thunder strikes, leaving the audience shaken in a way that very few films accomplish.

First episode is more interesting because it puts a relatable situation in front of us; it doesn't try to be a statement on language/cultural barriers. During the second episode, however, everybody that is key to the plot finally speaks English when nobody did before. It's flat-out entertaining and smartly-written Polanski (for the most part) with really intriguing mystery pieces in the best old-school way, and with the best piece of trivia between Ford and Polanski I have ever heard regarding what the title of the film should have been.

reviews.text: "From Hell" presents a dark story behind the Jack the Ripper murders of prostitutes that suggests it was something more than acts of extreme violence committed by a madman. Like an Italian giallo that shows how sick society has become at its uppermost levels, "From Hell" takes you into the heights of London society and how it was permeated by anti-Semitism, arrogance, and the sanctioned license to commit barbaric medical experiments just so long as they were done on people at the bottom of the social ladder, especially prostitutes, and its secret societies of "gentlemen". It's a dark painting with a lot drops on it that weave the danger of the dark alleys of the red light district of Whitechapel…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: As a work unto itself, From Hell is mediocre and unfocused, conjuring Gothic images of foggy, gaslit London nights broken up bafflingly by Rob Zombie-esque grindhouse montages of blades, splashes of blood and split-second glimpses of carnage that actively undermines whatever dread the film elsewhere tries to conjure. It plays out in look and movement like Brett Ratner's take on Red Dragon, consistently undermining itself for the sake of bad music video editing and an insistence on making an unambiguous hero out of a detective whose moral and psychological instability are meant to be explored in more critical terms.

reviews.text: 100-word review: Scotland Yard inspector Frederick Abberline investigates a series of gory prostitute murders, during which he becomes infatuated with one of next likeliest targets. The perpetrator is Jack de Ripper, but who's hiding behind the esoteric moniker? From Hell is a murder mystery playing dress-up. The period piece context is curious, but blunders a little at being veritably grounded in the portrayed time and place. The way it addresses how prejudices obstruct reasonable police-work is respectable though (there's an explicit lesson to be drawn here that converts well to contemporary affairs), and so is Johnny Depp's uncharacteristically subdued performance.

The story is told from the perspective of the investigating inspector Abberline and from the prostitutes who fell victim to the probably most famous serial killer in the world. reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Easily superior to the first Ghost Rider, but not nearly as wild or intense as a Neveldine/Taylor Nic Cage superhero movie should be. Everything with Ghost Rider himself is better this time, down to the dirtied-up design of the character and his bike, but he’s not onscreen very much. And while Cage has his moments of inspired lunacy, he’s actually weirder overall the first movie, where he has an inexplicable Elvis accent and more pronounced personality quirks. (This time he talks like Nicolas Cage and restricts his freakouts to a handful of scenes.) At just 90ish minutes with only a couple of significant action scenes, Spirit of Vengeance feels like something whittled down from a darker, scarier, stranger, more satisfying movie.

reviews.text: Still stand by my original video essay on how this formally explores human insignificance (wow, just realized how long I've been doing this for, Christ) but was once again blown away by the human-scaled patience and simplicity of Edwards' camera compositions and movements. The moody images and build-up/release are perfectly calibrated and there are so many great uses of the Spielberg Oner, all of which combined gradually invite you into the portent nature anxieties and accentuate the already pretty unbelievable VFX work. (Crazy what hiring people who know the strengths/weaknesses of CGI and letting them economically manage the location shooting accordingly can do for a movie.) Only American Godzilla movie that's genuinely interested in leaning towards the anthropological and melancholy in the same way the original film did, while also featuring rock solid monster/disaster blockbuster setpieces worthy of a Jurassic Park or War of the Worlds movie.

Always living a humble life even though she appears to be an attractive person both externally and internally, Wyckoff never found herself in a relationship or even losing her virginity going up into her 40's. reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: Would it be out of line to call Good Luck Miss Wyckoff Sirkian? While Wyckoff has plenty of hard-hitting exploitation elements baked into its core*, there’s also a deep well of compassion for its central character, including rightly placed indignation for how Wyckoff’s community treats her for engaging in a sexual relationship with a junior college athlete, who also happens to be black. This is a film loaded with heavy material, and despite having an ending most viewers will see coming a mile off, the tragic journey of one lonely teacher still manages to hit hard thanks to a wonderful lead performance from Anne Haywood, and the confident, melancholic direction of Marvin Chomsky, who elevates the material by masterfully mixing high and low brow art to create a chilling exploitation effort that’s nigh impossible to look away from.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: One of the saddest movies I've seen in recent years, a rewatch brought out just how many times Miss Wyckoff (Anne Heywood) needs the support of friends, family, coworkers, community, anyone, but ends up at best with terrible advice and at worst... well, it only gets worse as the movie goes on. The distancing effect of making this a period piece / Sirkian melodrama pastiche doesn't do much to temper just how devastating it is. As with all good melodrama, the artifice of the BIG emotions, incidents and performances is all a container to smuggle across some brutal truths about (tiny things like) the human condition.

reviews.text: Seriously devastating, the melodramatic equivalent of a perfectly-paced horror shocker that starts working on you in the first scene and never lets up. Mean-spirited provocation is tempered by genuine emotion and compassion, on the part of the filmmakers if not most of the people in Wyckoff's life. Ignores the fact that in the pre-Civil Rights era black men were routinely murdered for the crime of simply looking at white women (adding yet another brain-bending complication to the dynamic between Wyckoff and Rafe), but that could be an intentional barb against a complacent white liberal audience or something.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: A damn near Sirkian adaptation of William Inge's eponymous novel, GOOD LUCK, MISS WYCKOFF is a devastating melodrama, playing out like a slow build horror movie where repression is the bloodthirsty monster in the room. The titular '50s Kansas schoolteacher (Anne Heywood) begins to experience menopause at thirty-five, bringing an overwhelming sense of loss to a life already completely bereft of sexual contact. Her local physician (Robert Vaughn) recommends she see a therapist (Donald Pleasence) in another town, all while her catty colleagues (including a still-luminous/venomous Dorothy Malone) whisper to one another and speculate as what exactly is wrong with the gradually deteriorating woman. Despite advances from a friendly (albeit married) bus driver (Earl Holliman) who attempts to start up…

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: GOOD LUCK, MISS WYCKOFF is a strange piece of work from an admittedly strange time in history. There are some various years to take into consideration when discussing this: it takes place in 1954, the novel it is based on was published in 1970 and the film was released in 1979. Right there you are covering a period of twenty five years of American history and a pretty potent quarter century at that, if we're discussing racial relations and gender equality. And we are.

reviews.text: A feverish delirium of film noir, a raw and unrelenting explosion of desire and destruction, in which the camera fearlessly follows its characters as they spiral into absurd violence and passion. The story of Bart and Laurie (the reluctant gunman and the femme fatale with blood in her eyes) unfolds in a very predictable way, but it feels right, is lethal and lyrical. Laurie is one of those ultimate archetypes of the fatal woman: a fusion of magnetism and manipulation, leading Bart to his downfall with a whisper and the promise of eternal love. It’s impossible to look away from her burning presence, the embodiment of danger wrapped in silk and gunpowder.

reviews.text: One of the all-time great examples of B-noir pulp being elevated by intelligent craftsmanship, and also in the running for the most aptly titled film ever made. A proto-Bonnie & Clyde doomed lovers-on-the-run armed robbery thriller given a forceful, expressive and psychosexual charge from an uncredited and then-blacklisted screenwriter Dalton Trumbo who directly ties the perverse American tradition of obsessive gun fetishism with the romantic passions of youth + exhilarating nature of the crime-action genre formula; an idea then sharply and kinetically realized by under-sung B-movie technician Joseph H. Lewis who (with the help of regular Howard Hawks cinematographer Russell Harlan) replicates all the propulsive excitement and lethal attraction these characters feel via pure style.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: I. I didn't realize until watching this adaptation the degree to which Hamlet is Claudius' story as much as it is that of the titular melancholy Dane. Trapped by his own ill-fated ambition and lust, Claudius is unexpectedly sympathetic, a man unequal to the situation to which he has condemned himself, but also unable to dismount and cut his losses. In the end, he's more victim than actor, drawn ever-forward by his flight from the judgment that dogs his steps, fleeing Hamlet through the mechanism of further violence and deception, beyond hope that it will end in anything like the serene victory of which he's long dreamed.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Walter Hill's debut feature is a very well made drama about a street fighter in the depression era. The film is very much a sign of things to come for the successful director. The setting is well felt - costumes, cars, locations etc are well on the money. The plot, which largely surrounds a fight promoter and his troubles with local houdlums is interesting - but by far and away the best aspect of the film is the street fights. They are all very raw and hard hitting - the sound effects are awesome. Every punch is extremely satisfying! I love how the fighters are featured too - the biggest man isn't necessarily the best. Charles Bronson is perfect for the central role - quiet, capable and very understated. James Coburn gives excellent support as the smarmy promoter. It all boils down to a fitting conclusion. Hard Times is an all round good film and well worth the time.

reviews.text: A juicy morsel of the California 60’s, but also an exercise in bewilderment and a great contribution to the P.I. genre, paving the way for the later, greater entries of postmodern lucidity, like The Long Goodbye and Inherent Vice. Newman remains cool and sarcastic, snickering his way through most of this mystery, but when things get serious, they get serious — the investigation of love in times of trauma and the theme of how far men are willing to go for their women intersect one another. Everyone seems head over heels for each other to the point where it becomes a confusing blur of names and faces, but then there’s Lew Harper, plodding his way through both a divorce and the most dangerous case of his career. Underneath all that love are entanglements of cold-hearted deceit, and Harper knows it best. Sometimes you just gotta say, “Aw, hell.”

reviews.text: Usually, when a film has a tone that's all over the place, it can take me out of the film entirely. Not with Headhunters. For this film, the film uses it's tone and audiences expectations to it's advantage to make room for plenty of twists and turns. It starts out as a serious, straightforward crime drama and then as the plot thickens, it transitions into something more gory, bizarre, and even darkly funny. It kept me on the edge of my seat not only wanting more but guessing what would happen next. That's just one of the reasons why I loved this film. It's also well acted, well directed, superbly written, and exciting from beginning to end. It's loads of fun and one of my favorite films that 2012 has to offer.

reviews.author: Deckk
reviews.text: 100-word review: This darkly comedic Norwegian thriller is one to certainly leave a lasting impression thanks to it's uniquely intense rendition of the genre. At its core, Headhunters explores themes of deception, identity, and the consequences of greed. The protagonist, Roger Brown, is a corporate headhunter who leads a double life as an art thief to support his lavish lifestyle. The film takes viewers on a rollercoaster ride as Roger's meticulously crafted world unravels when he crosses paths with a ruthless ex-military man. The black comedy emerges from unflinching portrayal of absurd situations and the characters' desperate attempts to outwit each other.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Lazy Sunday afternoon with GOD BURT. This '80s Las Vegas noir absolutely ROCKS and is over 100 minutes of nonstop Burt. We've got Burt choking down liquor and drowning his sorrows. Burt doing gags and deadpan laffs teaching Peter MacNicol to fight. Burt gently but firmly taking no nonsense. Burt doing a running jump-kick and disarming his foes using only edged weapons (he doesn't use guns). Burt winning and losing $100,000 in one night. Burt putting himself in the crosshairs of certain death because it's the right thing to do. Burt looking like a leather chair and sounding like a full-body massage.

reviews.text: Burt Reynolds is laconically dead-eyed throughout. Look at his mug on that poster. That’s it. That’s the only face Burt’s gonna pull for you over the course of the entire runtime. Woman he’s known since she was in braces gets brutally sexually assaulted and beaten? That’s the face he's gonna make. He wins big at the blackjack table? That’s the face. Achieves his lifelong dream? That’s the face (actually the closing scene is quite fun). The rise and the fall, the good and the bad, the dreams and the nightmares of Vegas, pre-LED lit Disneyfication... it’s all the same to him. It’s all gonna come to shit one way or another, nothing’s ever stayed good in his life long enough…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: In which apparently six directors (including, briefly, Robert Altman) take a crack at legendary novelist-turned-screenwriter William Goldman's Las Vegas for-hire mercenary/gambling addict loser neo-noir pulp novel, and all lose out to the charmingly weary and career-declining middle-aged Burt Reynolds, who ended up punching the credited director so hard he broke his jaw and probably should've just directed it himself after that. The end result is a bit of an episodic mess that alternates on a dime between fading 70s tough guy character study crime movie, a sad gambling addiction drama, a goofy buddy hangout movie, to eventually the kind of sloppy, violent trash of this era you could imagine starring Charles Bronson and having a Cannon logo on it.

It feels a bit unnecessary from a story point of view. I would imagine the movie was rushed into production because of the success of the original. But on its own, it’s a well-made and fairly entertaining Blaxploitation Crime/Drama. It feels a little repetitive and fails to take the character in interesting new directions. But if you have seen the original and enjoyed it, as I did, it is worth checking this one out as well. But keep expectations in check.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Black Caesar is a great movie because it's actually a smart character study disguised as a blacksploitation gangster movie. Hell Up in Harlem loses some of its prequel's singular, tragic focus on the rise and fall of Tommy Gibbs, but it's still a smart and ambitious Larry Cohen film, and it makes up most of the slack thanks to an array of wild set-pieces. I won't waste time listing them all but my favorite one is probably Fred Williamson killing one of his foes at Coney Island with an umbrella-turned-spear - it's shot like a Hitchcock murder and it climaxes with a gusher of animated blood. But the thing I really love about these two movies is that they create a world where violence always has consequences, even if it's really fun to watch.

Hell Up in Harlem definitely features the guerilla style filmmaking practically throughout with many packed streets while the movie is going on in the middle of it. Williamson's enemy is the corrupt district attorney Mr. DiAngelo played by Gerald Gordon who wishes to control the drug trade in Harlem while Julius Harris as Papa Gibbs seems to be more and more of a badass as the film goes on. reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Weirdly enough, the world of High and Low contains fundamentally good people. There is an evil criminal and heartless businessmen, but when things get tough, the people do the right thing. High and Low is rarely subtle in its class allusions, but it gives us sympathy for the wealthy lead, even after painting him callously when we realise the monetary value he initially places on the lives of different children. This is a film of affluence and poverty, of hierarchical systems within society (like the poor man tough on his child but meek when facing his boss). If a rich man exists, there must exist those who are poorer.

reviews.author: Remobo
reviews.text: I can't make any excuses...I love this stuff. Back in the day, when I was first sifting through the trash left out on other country's curbs, I proclaimed myself to be a huge fan of giallo. After further digging, I found that what I truly was, was a fan of Poliziotteschi. The machismo and swagger of Spaghetti Westerns turned up to 11, minus the spooky hoo-doo nonsense of, say, your Three Mothers trilogy; plus all of the car flips, gut shots, and face slappings serving as warrants that could only come from the country that brought you "The Mafia" ®.

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: To me, this is Enzo G. Castellari’s greatest film (and he’s had some great ones), and one of the essential, if not THE essential Euro Crime film. It’s right up there with Fernando Di Leo’s Milieu Trilogy, any of Umberto Lenzi’s films and Castellari’s own stuff like Street Law and The Big Racket. Franco Nero stars as one of the angriest, most violent cops in the genre’s history and no doubt was the basis for Maurizio Merli’s Inspector Tanzi character in later films, right down to the blonde hair and blue eyes. Castellari opens up High Crime with an elongated car chase and the film never really lets up from there.

reviews.text: Never made it more than a few minutes into this one before, and now I remember why: it's horrible. Just one terrible gag after another. Brooks is very transparently trying to be Monty Python here, but the thing is, Monty Python was six guys with very different sensibilities, so there's a system of checks and balances in place, and you're only seeing everyone's best stuff. This plays like if Monty Python was just Eric Idle's bits. That said, I think it's nice that all the famous Gen-Xers who grew up watching this on TV got together to make a sequel miniseries with Mel. I like it when people respect their elders. I hate thinking about grandpa feeling lonely at the nursing home.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: From a production standpoint this is one of the more impressive Mel Brooks pictures, lots of those gorgeous matte paintings that would come up later in Spaceballs, and big set-pieces like the "Spanish Inquisition" musical number. Comedically, though, this is Mel's "drunk dad" period, and while it's often very funny, it also feels a little too mean-spirited in parts. Probably not any more offensive than Blazing Saddles on paper, but where that movie had a very sturdy satirical framework for most of its vulgarity, this feels more like spitballs. Dad comedy legends like Jackie Mason and Henny Youngman get cameos, just in case there was any doubt on this point.

reviews.text: Looks like absolute shit through the lens of 1986 which means that through the lens of 2019 it looks like beautiful, weird, late night space trash. Unfortunately it isn’t really funny at all. Would kill to be a contrarian about this one but it’s just a boring pile of sleaze in the comedy department which is a real shame. This feels like the kind of movie you rediscover and it’s like “oh man these frustrated comedy writers were way ahead on this one!” but actually people in 1986 had a perfectly functional sense of irony and this isn’t some hidden gem that went over their heads. The whole thing feels like somebody making a Monica Lewinsky joke in 2003. If this was made today Howard would be a CGI duck who says “that’s not a thing.” So I guess we should be grateful for what we have. Could always be worse.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: It's hard to imagine that anyone thought people would go for this. Even the guy who wrote it couldn't seem to juggle its whiplash tone from the director's chair, a pulpy sci-fi mess that hurtles between cornball self-aware ribaldry and high-concept adventure. It seems perfect for someone like John Landis (who I believe was offered it) but there may be no way to make this really work. It's entirely too long and barely coherent, but it also features some terrific stunts and special effects (the stop-motion monster at the end is absolutely spectacular), a lot of terrible jokes I find both amusingly stupid and amusingly inappropriate, it's extremely pervy (Lea Thompson may be the first woman I ever thought was pretty), and the John Barry score is frequently indistinguishable from his best Bond work. I'd say it's not for everyone but it's probably not really for anyone.

reviews.text: The last scene is a big misstep; it not only announces the movie's major theme, it actually has the lead character say the phrase "Let's make a statement." It's not only clunky, it's totally unnecessary; even without it, it's perfectly clear what the film is about. This female voiceover artist (writer/director Lake Bell) who can't get work in a male-dominated industry is a stand-in for gender inequality in *all* of Hollywood. For a while, her voice is literally silenced. To Bell's credit, the message comes through without the exclamation point. I just wished she had trusted us to get it a little more.

reviews.text: The widescreen compositions of the middle third are obviously quite striking, Carpenter and his DP giving his subjects so much space that they're dwarfed by their surroundings. The terrifyingly towering church and even the main street of the town itself, everything is domineering and suffocating and terrifying. What bumps this up to something truly masterful, though, is the editing in the final third. The film becomes this freakish whirlwind of unnerving nonsense, time and place disappearing and reappearing in the blink of an eye. Thrilling stuff. I didn't even mind the "meta" self-reflexive narrative trappings which so often like nails on a chalkboard to me. It's all executed so well. @TheHorrorMaster indeed.

reviews.text: In my experience over the years, when a director releases a "Director's Cut", it is normally because his vision and the studio producing it invariably clash over certain issues, usually an excessive running-time which could prove problematic in the theatres. Some directors have become synonymous with them, most notably Sir Ridley Scott, who tinkered with a number of his own films, some of them years after their initial cinematic release, and Peter Jackson's LOTR's trilogy, where his Extended Editions were just extraordinary. It goes back much further than Scott and Jackson however, with everyone from Howard Hawks to Sam Peckinpah, Sergio Leone to James Cameron, either releasing their own vision, or an original version of something the studio initially meddled…

reviews.text: You may have heard that there’s a scene in Steven Spielberg’s Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull in which the cinema’s most iconic archaeologist survives an atomic blast by hiding inside of a lead refrigerator. The incident occurs about 20 minutes into the grizzled whip-cracker’s fourth feature-length adventure—widely considered to be the series’ best (note to self: fact-check this later)—and it follows a scene in which a small squadron of Russian soldiers infiltrated Area 51, unveiled an alien corpse, and got derailed by an arthritic part-time college professor who’s so bad at his job that . . . well, these were supposed to be his office hours. So it’s safe to say that, even before the scene in question, Kingdom of the Crystal Skull, like the earlier films in its series, doesn’t feel particularly beholden to realism.

reviews.author: theironcupcake
reviews.text: Sports movies are a dime a dozen. Most of them follow variations on the same plot, usually tracking a path toward redemption for an athlete or team in need of a first or second chance to prove their worth. Inside Moves, which is Richard Donner's favorite among the films he has directed (he is especially proud of the poster that advertises rave reviews), utilizes a slightly different formula by functioning as a character study with far more emphasis on platonic and romantic relationships than on tournaments. Not all of the gears fit together, but the parts that work do so wonderfully.

reviews.author: MichaelEternity
reviews.text: Probably the most tucked-away Richard Donner joint since he became a commercial artist, or at least tied with 1993's misleadingly depressing kid-power thing "Radio Flyer". But this one's actually worth seeing. It's one of those largely aimless and scrappy slice-of-life dramedies owing to the movement of simmering naturalism from the '70s. After crippling part of his body in a failed suicide attempt, John Savage befriends a bunch of fellow handicapped older guys in a bar in downtown Oakland, and basically it's just about him restoring his peace of mind through this camaraderie, finding a place where he belongs and navigating some relationship turmoil with both a lady friend (Diana Scarwid) and the bartender who dreams of being a basketball star…

reviews.text: Adapted by Daniel Mainwaring from Jack Finney's 1954 sci-fi novel The Body Snatchers, this film ingeniously positions sleep as a liability and an adversary. Falling asleep is natural relaxation and a prerequisite, but here it's the mechanism of termination, with arguably it’s sweeping themes simultaneously incorporating commentary on McCarthyism and of the threats of social consonance. It's director Don Siegel, one of the outstanding Hollywood genre directors, took merely nineteen days to shoot the movie and it involved no second-unit work. Invasion of the Body Snatchers is a harrowing cinematic nightmare which possesses one of the most extraordinary conclusions ever filmed.

reviews.author: A.A. Dowd
reviews.text: One of my favorite movies. As a thriller, it's basically perfect, masterfully building dread over its first hour, before sending its richly-developed characters on the run and turning all of San Francisco into a hostile organism. But I also remain in awe of how well the film works as cultural satire (it's much better in that respect than the original), as witty comedy, and especially as a doomed romance. Is there a more strangely moving expression of affection than finding yourself unable to destroy the alien double of your beloved? The look on Sutherland's face when the woman he loves literally crumbles in his arms is almost too much to handle.

reviews.text: Umberto Lenzi’s epic caveman adventure was a lot more fun than I expected. George Eastman is killing it as the villain – not only does he have the perfect physique for the part, he also seems to have a blast wearing his lion-head and killing people with his new invention - the sword. Surprisingly light on gore or sleaze, especially coming just a year or two after Cannibal Ferox, but there are a few fun split-head effects. It still confuses me that these movies were even a Thing in the early 80s.

reviews.text: I don't understand how anyone could see this and think that American Sniper is unambiguously endorsing Chris Kyle's view of the world. Like that film, like Jersey Boys, Eastwood here is on the side of a delusional American, but not his delusion. Perhaps contrast to Oliver Stone's Nixon, which attempts to understand its subject by building up pity for him, rather than empathy. Eastwood lets his Hoover indulge his own myths about himself, poking holes in the facade at opportune moments, while still allowing him a genuine humanity. We get Hoover as he saw himself and Hoover as he was and it's left to us to decide what to do with that which is irreconcilable.

reviews.text: Caught in a very awkward disconnect that blends children's fantasy, pocket-sized kaiju and Takashi Murakami's unmistakable superflat aesthetic, Jellyfish Eyes struggles to find a stable footing and becomes so muddled at points that it is all but impossible to discern why anything is happening. The visual design is undoubtedly the film's strongest aspect, with each one of the weird and wacky creatures popping against the muted, almost sterile human environments, but the effects are so lacklustre and stiff that they all become this horrifying blend of adorable concept and nightmarish realisation. At times, the imagery feels closer to an art installation or a horror attraction than a children's film, undoubtedly thanks to the combination of Murakami and Yoshihiro Nishimura's backgrounds…

reviews.text: Django Prepare a Coffin is unlike most of the Django series for the fact that it was intended as a legitimate follow up to Sergio Corbucci's original film. Beyond that the main thrust of the plot is fairly standard Spaghetti Western revenge fair, which sees the title character on the hunt for justice after his wife was killed by a crooked politician. We then see Django become a hangman with a hustle - he's saving men from the gallows and putting his own gang together! Quite how he gets away with this for so long is anyone's guess, but the film rides with the preposterous plot for the first half. It never really capitalises on the outright goofiness of it,…

The film is one of the many "Django" (1966) repeats in a long line varied adventure tales, but in that vein, it is one of the more prevalent examples within this. Sergio Corbucci originally incepted the character, and the first film exhibits the infamous Franco Nero in the lead role. reviews.author: Nilknarf
reviews.text: For being the far off future of 2001, space technology didn’t seem to advance very far from 1962. Oscilloscopes, geiger counters, reel-to-reel tape, and paper printouts. I liked the blue and yellow space suits, very retro cool. This movie started out like a Star Trek episode and remained so for its entirety. Stylistic planet set. The plot line was sometimes silly and the script lines was sometimes humorously entertaining. I liked everyones awkward pronunciation of “Uranus”, maybe they should of chose a journey to the eighth planet because saying “Neptune” is a safer pronunciation. There was some awkward edits and general scene malaise. This was billed as a horror movie so I gave it the nod for October, but really there was not a lot of horror. The claymation stop-motion ‘rat’ monster looked more like a rabid cyclops squirrel. Extra half star for the out-of-place retro cool folk song sung on the end credits role by Danish musician Otto Brandenburg.

reviews.author: Nakul
reviews.text: Watched Peter Jackson's King Kong for the first time in forever. It rules so hard. This movie is extremely underappreciated and doesn’t get talked about as often as it should. An unapologetically melodramatic, romantic, indulgent, and a grand old fashioned adventure story realized with genuine artistic flair. Epic in every sense of the word, with a truly colossal scale to match. Every penny of it's crazy budget is shown on screen through stunning visual effects & cinematography. There are so many scenes where Jackson's horror roots are on full display, stylistically and technically. Also, that T-Rex & Kong fight sequence goes so hard, one of the best action sequences I've ever seen. A lot of people hate-circlejerk over its runtime, but it has excellent world building and characters with actual motivations and development.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: God, I love this movie and I don't care who knows it. What turned out to be Jackson's last gasp as a filmmaker of true vision and excitement, which is all the more impressive considering he takes a limited and already-remade concept and strips it of its underlying racial metaphor to simply delight in the thing itself. But this just bursts with energy, from a well-defined human cast with across-the-board strong performances (even an arguably miscast Jack Black acquits himself well by turning his naturally buoyant energy into something curdled and mean) to its amazing creature designs. To this day I'm wigged out by the bug scene, with its glacial, almost oneiric scoring and the slow pace of the beasts…

It's rife with bad acting, dumb comedy, boring action, and a story that's light on coherence or intrigue but heavy on the racism, and it's really just a 100 minutes of shitty set pieces strung together in a way that's incomprehensible. I don't even particularly like the 1950 version of this film, but at least that King Solomon's Mines had some redeeming qualities to it and wasn't just nonsensical, cheap Cannon junk like this.

reviews.text: Weekly reminder to independent filmmakers: you can make a movie about whatever you want. You could even make a straight-faced epic about a motorcycle riding Renaissance Festival troupe if you thought you could do it with sincerity. George Romero did, and it bears his fascination with turning small communities (be it zombie apocalypse survivors in a shopping mall or Society for Creative Anachronism on Wheels) into microcosms of America at large. Rather than establishing a utopia just to destroy it, here Romero seems more optimistic that staying true and not selling out actually will give a permanency to the ideas espoused by the good king Ed Harris (his best performance?). The temptations of money and fame that plague the troupe…

The atmosphere is pure gothic horror. The style and sets are absolutely great. The monster itself is a real disgusting mess aswell - certainly one of the more original takes! It does take a while to get going, and honestly most of the interest is in the final third but there's always enough to keep things entertaining. The beautiful Rosalba Neri takes the lead role and excels with it - just…

Contains some genuinely beautiful colors and FX work and I have never laughed louder in my life than the generic tough brooding cop robotically explaining his tragic backstory so that he can have forest sex with the pop star.

reviews.text: This is one of those movies that people will describe as "so bad it's good" (surely the Terminator/South Sea Queen of dumb shit to say about a movie), and I get where they're coming from - there's some goofy stuff going on here, with a lot of truly weird performances and creative choices all around, and two leads who fall in love while sharing romantic chemistry roughly equal to that of Arnold Schwarzenegger and Linda Hamilton in the original Terminator movie. But don't be fooled: This is a one-of-a-kind blast to the synapses, and one thing I'd forgotten in the three years since I saw it last is how great it looks - atmospherically shot with the kind of literally explosive action that makes you feel happy you're alive. Fuckin' A.

reviews.author: Aberrant Ghoul
reviews.text: A Charles Band production that predates Empire and Full Moon. The kind of dreadful B-movie nonsense that feels like it was made to be featured on MST3K. And, in fact, it actually did get an MST3K episode. And I wish I'd watched it that way, because it's largely kinda dull on its own, aside from the delightful stop-motion aliens (which didn't get nearly enough screen time). Too much of this feels like some languorous summer hangout film, until the protagonist (who I swear must be allergic to shirts) turns into a laser-canon-wielding mutant zombie thing and blows a bunch of shit up before a weirdly anti-climactic and rather abrupt ending. Oh well, this was also the screen debut of Eddie Deezen, for whatever that's worth.

reviews.author: TheAzhdarchid
reviews.text: Easily one of the unironically better B-movies I've seen, simply on the basis that its themes are deeper than a puddle. I mean, they're not deep like a lake or ocean, so maybe like pool deep? But the execution of Billy being pushed around all his life only to go on a murderous rampage once he gains power is more engaging than the bluntly stated and surface level anti-authoritarian message in King of Kong Island, the awkwardly inserted communist politics in Planet of Storms or whatever the fuck the theme of The Incredible Petrified World was supposed to be. Plus, the stop motion in Laserblast is fucking awesome. I miss when low-budget films used it.

reviews.text: Absolutely stupid brilliance. A magnificent, reflexive, fun, schlocky "love letter" (hate the phrase but it's true!) to action films. The first hour of this is so divine, and the second half dives into strange meta-commentaries on celebrity that I had totally forgotten. Charles Dance is fantastic. And this thing is cameo city– a buncha random appearances that make you feel like they just sent a massive email to anybody who was available. Do not understand the crossover audience for some of these gags, but that just makes me love them more. A big chunk of the script for this Arnold Schwarzenegger action film is references to The Seventh Seal. For who? For me! (I have not seen The Seventh Seal. Not enough explosions.)

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A lifetime of baggage is hard to stuff into just a single suitcase. Crawling around our respective rocks, poking a head out from below every now and then to confirm that the world is in fact still turning. It always is, whether we come with it or not, and sometimes we feel we have no reason, no incentive to keep on spinning, keep cycling, through each day, long and breezy—calming to the point of numbness—which manifest a need not to die, but to live, or die trying; to find that internal justification for an existence. But if we do find it, will it be too late? Maybe the reason itself is all that mattered, regardless of where our ashes may fall.

The ever closing loneliness here calls back to Edward Yang's The Terrorizers while the genre; romance aspects call back to Wong Kar-wai or even a downbeat version of Postman Blues. Thailand has never looked this sad, everyone is sad. The last lizard stays even in the most uncertain of times.

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: contextualized in their respective careers, this is a much better film for Hill than A Fistful of Dollars is for Leone (and, on a certain day, better than Yojimbo for Kurosawa) — the source is laid bare here, with Hill less concerned with updating (or changing) narrative beats and, instead, opting for more impactful action (Willis constantly duel-wielding handguns with unlimited ammo as if he’s emulating a prohibition era Chow Yun-Fat in a John Woo movie) set against a legitimately perfect Ry Cooder score that can give Morricone rare competition; likely destined to be Hill’s most consistently underrated movie

reviews.text: Melville's personal connection to the WWII resistance film as gangster tragedy in Army of Shadows makes that one a more affecting gut punch, but this is probably still the purest, most pared-down, and undeniably influential expression of his love of the cutthroat economy of old American crime movies and the hardened, distrustful, unsentimental, and solitary worldview/philosophy that he lived by. Taking the basic narrative structure and cool genre storytelling/design choices he loved as a kid, and honing them to his own specific interest in the lonely criminal-as-craftsman: their post-war isolated male psychology, their sense of spartan stillness and detachment, their meticulous adhering to certain self-imposed rituals and processes, their icy, ruthless calm and over-mannered sense of control even in their…

When the frame can be focused on a face that so clearly tells a story of its own, the symbiotic relationship between director and performer evolves beyond the expectations of standard storytelling.

reviews.author: Matthew Christman
reviews.text: There’s an easy critique to make of Lincoln. It’s the latest in a long line of popular retellings of the Civil War that puts white men at the center of the narrative, marginalizing the very people who fought and died for the recognition of their own humanity. It’s more pernicious endorsement of the Great Man theory of history and all its attendant, authoritarian implications. It’s an easy critique because it’s essentially correct. If someone condemns Lincoln because they are too distractingly annoyed by this, I completely understand, and there’s really no arguing with that reaction.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: You know, you don't see an animated film maudit all that often, but that's pretty much exactly what we've got here: a financially disastrous attempt to make a Japanese version of an American animated feature (and before the Disney Renaissance had reignited interest in American animation, even). It showcases the strengths of neither form, but the strange intermediary thing that it is feels very little like anything else I've seen, and there's something compulsively watchable about it, even when it's utter nonsense. Weirdly underplays its surrealism in a way that makes it more authentically weird, and the abrupt shift from bubblegum cutesiness to family-friendly horror right around the midpoint knocks it off-balance in a way that feels authentically dreamy even if it's narratively inexplicable. I am very happy that I never saw this as a child.

Still, Lonesome Dove never ceases to impress me. The whole cast is superb, and Robert Duvall gives one of the best performances of his career. The characters and story are very memorable. The dialogue is excellent as well, adding to the film's authenticity. The technical aspects (especially the cinematography) and production design are truly remarkable, for being made in 1989. It's a truly engrossing experience, that's worth the 6-hours. When it comes to westerns, Lonesome Dove is simply one of the best.

reviews.text: A very funny, if not overly scattershot, black comedy from the poison pen of the oft ribald George Axelrod. Frustratingly this naughty somewhat underseen satire never truly fixes its focus on any one theme, be it youth culture, high school, parent child relations, religion or the movie industry. In its barely coherent attack on everything (an “act of pure aggression” goes the tagline) something is lost. Tony Richardson’s take on Evelyn Waugh’s The Loved One, a sort of caustic cousin from the previous year that’s equally broad, manic and tasteless, beats it in look, execution and bite. Quibbles aside Lord Love a Duck is still a pretty great comedy. Tuesday Weld as Barbara Ann Greene the ultimate cashmere sweater girl…

This is pretty much the basis for my running theory that comedy is incredibly hard to get right (and prevent from aging like milk) specifically because so much of it tends to rely on the attitudes and parlances of the day, all but destined to be long-distant relics that can never really be appreciated as intended unless you happened to be in the midst of the zeitgeist that birthed them.

reviews.text: Lucky Number Slevin, by director Paul McGuigan, throws a half dozen plot threads at you in the first ten minutes or so. A bookkeeper is shot while on the way to his car in a parking structure. Bruce Willis (who makes sporadic brief screen appearances) is a mysterious stranger at an airport that strikes up an unusual conversation with a sonny boy, something about a “Kansas City Shuffle.” A nine-to-one odds horse takes a dive at the racetracks. Another unexplained character is shot coming out of a bank. And then there’s Slevin (Josh Hartnett) who has been mistaken first by a neighbor, and then by two thugs that want to take him to a gangster’s hideout.

reviews.text: It hits me sometimes. When I stop thinking about what I'm doing right now and let my mind adrift, let myself stare towards the distance. The horizons always seem to elicit these thoughts, memories of loss from long ago that still sting beyond the grave I buried them in. Gazing outward I see landscape, but just as much as the subject am I gazing at the aspect of distance itself. Sky meets ground. Meets city, meets trees, meets mountain and sea. There is always a meeting, of heaven and earth, somewhere out in the distance that cannot be reached and cannot be grasped. But it can always be seen.

Maborosi’s story is superficially simple: affected by the death of her grandmother and her husband’s inexplicable suicide, a young Osaka woman starts new married life, along with her son, in a remote seaside fishing village, but finds the past continues to trouble her. Eschewing close-ups,the narrative draws the viewer in gradually, so that, as Tony Rayns says, intimacy is earned, not frivolously given. reviews.author: SnowboardJunkie
reviews.text: Have you ever been in love with someone and they choose a path which seems completely out of character? It comes crashing into your life with all it’s intentions leaving you helpless to do anything about it. You gave your heart to this person and perhaps you deserve understanding. But it’s not a place that you can find your way back to, even by some miracle. The earth has come apart and the divide much too great, leaving you stranded on the other side. Maborosi is that unknowing that lingers in your gut long afterwards. It’s that moving forward and finding peace in a place you never thought you’d be. And what you find is, that being able to understand life isn’t always as important as the willingness to try even when you don’t.

reviews.author: Hungkat
reviews.text: In essence it's a film about grief, seen through the view of the ocean, through the frame of a window in a tidy, unoccupied room, and experienced through silence and absence. People say time heals everything but it's not completely true. Grief, as if dulled by time (a long time it is), may become less intense and manageable, but it's never really gone, and not even the sea can wash it away. However, despite how painful the grieving process may be, the experience of watching Maborosi is akin to having a warm shower - tranquil, quiet, and meditative.

reviews.text: Major League will always hold a special place for me. I grew up playing a lot of baseball, and while there are plenty of dramatic and poignant films about the sport, there aren’t nearly enough that are funny. That’s especially relevant with this one, because as much as I enjoyed it, the majority of the kids I played with loved it too. Sure it’s got its share of poorly aged jokes and characterizations, but when I think about how often me and a bunch of other dumb teenage boys would quote the better lines from this one while playing ball for hours on end, I can’t really help but hold this one close to my heart and give a slightly better rating than it probably deserves.

reviews.text: "Theatrical" tends to get used (by me and everyone else) to describe movies that take place in small, carefully blocked sets with acting styles clearly derived from the stage. But Margaret feels theatrical in a way that cinematizes the sorts of things that stagecraft has to fake by insinuation, capturing the overlapping dialogue and din of being characters surrounded by an entire city of people. In fact, the true conflict of the film isn't Lisa vs. the bus driver, or vs. her mom or even vs. herself. Connery’s charm always teetered on the edge of gilded danger which is used with acute prowess here. Tippi Hedren’s performance proves to an intriguing portrayal of buried traumas — swimming between stark mania and prim repression. reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: In many ways the ideal Anthony Mann film. Just a platoon behind enemy lines trying to reach point B. The Korean enemy secondary to the landscape itself, shot in some Californian exteriors, transformed by Mann's camera into this unforgiven terrain. The film dramatizes that idea time and gain while reducing everything else besides the back and forth between Ryan's lieutenant, a war pro trying to do the job with as little causalities as possible, and Ray's cynical sergeant. Even the title is spare and minimum (the Brazilian distributor thought it was so plain they went into the opposite direction and called it "Those Who Know How to Die" which kinda fits too). It is less a death march than a sacrificial one, men offered to the land, so the conflict can keep going. So, one of the few honest war movies.

The top ten might surprise others, with my penchant for B-Westerns including Lesley Selander, Gordon Douglas, and George Sherman, alongside the staples of Spielberg, Sir Ridley Scott, and Hitchcock. Following this film, Anthony Mann will join that top ten, with this being my 18th film from the man that was fired by Kirk Douglas just weeks into the production of Spartacus. Mann is without a doubt one of my favourite directors, just his Westerns with James Stewart would have secured that, but the deeper I dive into his filmography, the more…

reviews.author: Raphael Georg Klopper
reviews.text: Anthony Mann doing a Sam Fuller type of war movie drama, and still finding his place seamlessly to evoke the best of his abilities. If there’s something completely refreshing behind Men in War’s very basic premise of the lost platoon behind enemy lines and the high ranking officer butting heads with the lower ranked sergeant about their war tactics relationship; is having its almost bleak nihilistic and unforgiving viewpoint of the conflict. Savored by Mann’s usual traces of the morally shaken characters, the hard-edged violence, and unnerving nail-biting tension, reaching horror-thriller territory here.

reviews.author: sallitt
reviews.text: Men in War. I really vibrate to it from the start. Mann has such a strong sense of visual documentation, established even in scenes of intense drama (and there aren't any other kinds of scenes in this movie) - his images seem almost abstract, yet are subordinated to a sense of place. And there’s such great dignity in the Ryan character: he reveals his thoughts and feelings to his subordinates without relinquishing control; his unusual friendship with L.Q. Jones plays like a relationship of equals. Whereas his nemesis Aldo Ray is daringly conceived less as a character than as an embodiment of the irrationality of war. The script credit is to Philip Yordan, but he seems to have been a front for Ben Maddow: the writing is superb, and is matched by a focused, intense direction that goes beyond what Mann had done previously, opening a new phase of his career. (24 May 2025)

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: My dim memories of the cheesy Japanese STAR WARS knockoff I watched on VHS nearly 25 years ago did not prepare me for something so spectacular. Narratively completely baffling but graphically nearly identical to, say, a Leiji Matsumoto anime from around the same period. Go look at the character designs and backgrounds for GALAXY EXPRESS 999 and then watch this. Same thing. Loaded with gorgeous, elaborate sets and costumes and featuring some of the loveliest & most complicated miniature work i've ever seen. I may never be able to tire of watching these chunky plastic starfighters in space dogfights, suspended on wire tracks, slingshotting around asteroids. The illusion may not be as convincing but the sense of speed and motion here rivals and occasionally even surpasses the Death Star trench run. Such a beautiful movie.

reviews.text: A dense quasi-montage of a film that captures the history of Japanese cinema, the romance of celebrity, and an existentialist appreciation of the journey in a beautifully animated series of flashbacks, this film is the confluence of reference and reverence. It has a respect for cinema--and Japan--while also being able to depict both without canonizing them. Knowing a little (a Wikipedia entry's worth) about Setsuko Hara's life, I can see the parallels here, though I appreciate she merely served as an inspiration. Chiyoko's persona matches neatly with Hara's "Eternal Virgin" persona, and the appealing notion that her career was based not on a desire to create but to seek some ideal figure neatly sidesteps the seedier (and endearing) suggestions some…

reviews.author: Erika
reviews.text: After watching Gods of Egypt and having my brain melted by the pure insanity of it, I was delighted to see that Moonwalkers was the type of insanity that I like. Drugs, violence, Ron Perlman, movies inside movies, Stanley Kubrick, Moonwalkers was my type of movie. It's almost like this movie is poking fun of the popular conspiracy theory that it's based on. It's messy as all hell, the tone is all over the place. One minute it's a stoner comedy and the other it's a gangster film. It will certainly turn off some people but I felt that it made the movie a lot more fun. The cast is incredibly charismatic and Ron Perlman delivers a terrific performance. Moonwalkers is such a relentlessly energetic and colorful movie that it never once lost my interest.

reviews.text: A film with shots so breathtaking that the entire audience would gasp collectively, but also a film that's desperately in need of an editor. Normally I'm not one to criticize shallowness of narrative, but as much as I loved the performances in this film, even those can run out of steam a little bit when the audience is forced to endure the same sort of strange, goofy behavior and (as everyone else has mentioned) grunting for a bloated 150 minutes. Not my favorite Mike Leigh film but certainly his most beautiful and, in general, one of the most visually stunning films of the year. Dorothy Atkinson is absolutely hysterical.

reviews.text: sprawling but never disorganized or lacking in intimacy. this has to be somewhat autobiographical on Leigh's part, with so many characters either unduly frustrated or even perhaps overly impressed by Turner's insistence on what they see as quotidian. the details are what make both artists' work so vital.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: Probably one of Mike Leigh's most visually beautiful films, as every scene looks so real and atmospheric and seems like a deliberate choice to mirror Turner's paintings. It's an incredibly slow affair that looks into Turner's life, but it does offer an interesting portrait of the artistic mind, and by the end, it did offer a portrait of someone I had no prior knowledge of, and it succeeds on that front. It's a film that demands patience, and even if it lost me at times due to its pacing and emotional distance, the presence of Timothy Spall makes this a good enough watch, down to his portrayal of a character who is equally gruff and eccentric and is portrayed in an honest, flawed fashion. Overall, it's a beautifully crafted film and a departure from many of Leigh's films, and even if it's not one of my favorites of his, I still appreciate Spall and the artistry here.

reviews.author: Harry Ridgway
reviews.text: It's only fitting that Mr. Turner takes on the texture of an ambulatory painting that brims with precise orchestration and vivid expression. It beautifully hums and flows like the artwork on display - not just as a superficial marvel but as a profound reincarnation of J.M.W. Turner's eminent yet occasionally objectionable life. Unlike countless biopics of recent, Mike Leigh's stunning epic boasts copious clarity and a seamlessly paced narrative that creatively circumvents the trappings of the genre. Incandescent and entirely immersive, Mr. Turner echoes the enchanting artistry of Turner with its own spellbinding piece of magnificence.

reviews.text: Gimme a bullet to bite on and I’ll make believe it’s you. Abel Ferrara is a prankster at this point in his career, seeing just how many buttons he can push and how many bridges he can burn down, but he does so with a real attention to the kinds of fires he wants to start. In Woody Allen’s Manhattan (1979) there’s an image of young love with the Queensboro bridge in frame accompanied with the kind of music Woody Allen likes, and Ferrara recreates the image in Ms. 45 but makes it a violent one, as if to say this is my New York City. This is a film for the litter that people ignore, the bugs people step on, and for the lives that have been ruined by people who don’t pay attention to the kinds of fires they want to start.

reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: Jeremy Saulnier's first feature, years before Blue Ruin and Green Room, is a micro-budgeted amateur indie cheapie, but it's still so recognizably his work, with incompetent, desperate characters locked in a tense push-and-pull situation with each other, and some startlingly graphic gore. A shy nebbish finds an invitation to a "murder party" and shows up to discover that the "artists" who planned the party want to murder him, and things get ridiculous from there. It's openly a dark comedy, made by Saulnier and some of the friends he used to make backyard home-video movies with as a child. (The making-of video, which includes scenes from those childhood projects, is an adorable must-see.) Not a fantastic movie, but an enjoyable background to Saulnier's later work.

reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: Even though Murder Party, served as Jeremy Saulnier’s Hollywood calling card, it’s still impressive how much of his style and penchant for well-staged, ultra-violent set pieces was present in his debut. Even though the film carried a micro-budget, the way Saulnier whips his camera around to execute the film’s set pieces makes it easy to see how Murder Party shares the same DNA with Blue Ruin and Green Room. That said, my main takeaway is art students are insufferable and have deep ceded emotional issues. Don’t be fooled — even when the cute girl from class is dressed like Pris from Blade Runner.

The film follows the story of the English vessel Bounty, en route to Tahiti to embark some plants. reviews.author: legolas
reviews.text: The 1962 Mutiny on the Bounty is the Technicolor fever dream of Hollywood's prime with a richer, wider reinterpretation of the 1935 original, bespangled with spectacle and overpurchased with ambition. And to its credit, it's gorgeous to behold. The production is first-rate, from the replica Bounty, hand-assembled for real, to the splendiferous, painterly set pieces of the South Pacific, every frame shouts big-budget prestige. Raging ocean storms, idyllic island paradises, vibrant Tahitian rituals with 6,000 extras. It's all there, all the elements of a big adventure epic.

reviews.author: Fabian
reviews.text: A massive historical epic the likes of which were produced excessively in the early 1960s, with highly inflated budgets and troubled productions, contributing to the inevitable decline of the Golden Age of classic Hollywood cinema. This remake of the 1935 Best Picture winner is overlong, oversized and a chore to get through, with a rightfully dismissed performance by Marlon Brando front and center—not to mention the fact that this somehow snagged another Best Picture nomination despite being very middle-of-the-road even in terms of historical epics. Some nice visuals, a sprawling score and good cinematography are not enough to sweep you through these three hours of ever-increasing boredom; despite a major climax, the film is too unfocused to be worth more…

While the primary Flaming Carrot character is not featured, his side character team, which became an ensuing spin off series, the "Mystery Men", became the featured focused build that would lead to this film. reviews.text: At a glance, Natural Born Killers has the potential to mislead. What seems like a full-blooded thriller packed with gratuitous brutality is in fact more profound; more intelligent than what its exterior and hateful critics may imply. It's personality is satirical, predominantly lampooning the media for their embracement of serial killers and near veneration of the activities they conduct - all done for the sake of ratings. Oliver Stone is clearly a staunch combatant of such behaviour and as we all know, if Oliver Stone disagrees with something, it's almost guaranteed he'll make a film to argue his perspective. Some may call him his work propaganda, but you can't deny his skill and innovation.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Miyazaki's most hellish vision of nature's ability to push back against the waste and ruin of Man. Eden as a vision of paradise lost: an unspeakably beautiful world utterly fatal to humans. The minutiae of the film is so fascinating: the careful documentation of Nausicaa dumping a shotgun shell around the eye of a hardened, giant bug and sparking a flame to loosen the lens, the way that living Ohms move with the segmented, undulating motion of caterpillars. Its sense of scale is exquisite, and the use of both horizontal and vertical space to de-emphasize the importance of people against a world that has evolved past them is suitably unnerving. And through it all, hope shines, finding in its heroine a figure seeking to find the balance for man and nature to coexist without one killing the other. My favorite Miyazaki.

reviews.author: Bruno Youn
reviews.text: Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind is another masterful work from Hayao Miyazaki, presenting a story that truly hits you right in the feels. His take on a post-apocalyptic world covered by wastelands and a poisonous forest called Sea of Decay with giant insects inhabiting it is just so peculiar and wildly imaginative. I loved all the rich mythology involved and how Nausicaä has a genuinely powerful bond with the creatures as well as nature itself. She is such a kind, fierce and caring protagonist that you feel attached to the character right from the start. Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind manages to deliver an incredible sense of awe while also having a beautiful and touching message so I could not recommend it highly enough!

reviews.author: Jan
reviews.text: No Good Deed tries to sell itself as a tense home-invasion thriller, but the logic just doesn’t hold up. First off, a fugitive on the loose breaks into a woman’s house, and she’s oddly kind and trusting, barely questioning why she’s letting a stranger in. Then comes her friend, who can’t help but overly sexualize Idris Elba’s character, making the scene feel unintentionally awkward. The acting is bland, and the so-called “thrills” feel more like a spoof than suspense. This isn’t the kind of movie that keeps you on the edge of your seat. Its the kind that makes you impatient and just ready for it to be over. The only redemption is the twist at the end, revealing that their partners were having an affair and both characters were unknowingly intertwined. It’s a clever touch, but it can’t save a film that never truly finds its footing.

reviews.text: Released shortly before All About Eve, Joseph L. Mankiewicz's No Way Out is a drama focusing around the theme of racism in the USA. Luther Brooks is a black doctor given the task of treating two brothers that have been shot during a robbery. When one of the brothers dies, the surviving one blames Dr Brooks for the death. The film is bolstered by a pair of powerhouse performances from Sidney Poitier, making his debut, and the always excellent Richard Widmark, who absolutely excels with his portrayal of the vile white supremacist at the centre of the story. The film makes its points without being overly preachy. The film focuses on the characters and situation which ultimately makes the message…

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: My dramatic increase in appreciation of this wild film is due to the precise and hilarious commentary by film noir expert Eddie Muller, and an immediate rewatch of the entire film with said commentary. It humbled me, and proved how an even close first watch of a film is never enough. It doesn't always work (some scenes have clunky extension, other atrocious patches of dialogue sound like a stubbornly white poptimistic rendering of Black life), but when it does work (Sidney Poitier's performance, Widmark's expressionistically racist tirades, certain lighting tricks like a quasi-sci-fi white light/fear-of-a-black-planet moment during a race riot, the ending), it soars. What a debut for Poitier!; here, he establishes the perfect metaphor for his unfairly beleaguered film career.

Not just Lennie’s or George’s, but Candy’s, Mae’s—everyone clinging to the same fragile idea of something better, knowing deep down it probably isn’t coming. I read it and instantly fell in love and got to watch a stage production with George Costigan and Matthew Kelly too in the early '00s. But the only film adaptation I'd seen was the 1992 version with Gary Sinise and John Malkovich. That's good, but this one has to be the absolute definitive take.

reviews.text: Two drifting ranch hands blow across California during the Depression. Lenny (Lon Chaney, Jr.) is huge, hulking and slow-witted, with a childlike innocence; George (Burgess Meredith) is his protector: a smart, selfless man who's happy to keep telling that same old story: one day they'll own their own place, and Lenny can pet the rabbits. Having fled the town of Weed (it isn't a marijuana metaphor, but imagine if it was), the pair pitch up at a ranch fairly teeming with trouble, most of it coming from the owner's son Curley, and his sexually frustrated wife (Betty Field).

reviews.text: Of simple construct comes one of 2014's most enjoyable flicks; another Australian picture which manages to capture, fun, heart and emotion in its grasp. Paper Planes announces its conventional structure from the beginning of its running time, but never loses its charm along its bumpy and desperate road. So whilst lacking finesse and anything that one could consider original (part its intriguing premise), it's the performances, the energetic writing, the imagination and the wonderful setting of outback Australia that prove to entrance the viewer and not let go until the final note.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A patient, regretful, soft-spoken neo-western odyssey about getting "lost in a deep, vast country" where nobody knows you for half a boy's lifetime, about memories so painful that deliberately repressing/forgetting them and wandering a shameful purgatory is far easier than saying them out loud... Let alone actually trying to fix what you might have broke in a movie a long, long time ago. One of the most soulful and sad movies I've ever seen, containing some of the most vibrant loner poetry desert landscape/urban architectural photography ever committed to film by Robby Müller, and made all the more beautiful and haunting by the aching twangs of Ry Cooder. The choice to basically never put Stanton or Kinski in the same room as one another (with clever visual/sonic use of cars, home movies, phones, window glass and reflections to make this possible), even in that final scene, is one I'll be thinking about for a while.

reviews.text: Wish I had something cool or unique or insightful to say about this thing, but sometimes it's like reading Hegel or something where you end up rewatching a sequence a second time just after it happens just to make sure you got everything. More spin-off than sequel, basically pure speculative science-fiction with all the "genre" sucked out - a vision of a highly technologically advanced, first world country entering martial law. reviews.text: Perversely contains the actual robot fighting to the final half hour of a two-hour film, but in the process dramatically expands Oshii's thematic ambitions and political/techno-existential ideas pointing directly to their summit in Ghost in the Shell. The film slams on the brakes about halfway in to lay out its ideas in almost excruciatingly blunt detail about how Japan's postwar prosperity is the product of a foreign occupation that permanently denies the country a military capable of anything other than a defensive war even as Japan's booming industries directly profited and raised the nation's economy by helping to supply those occupiers' war machines elsewhere. But the gliding montage of rotted post-industrial buildings that accompanies this monologue turns political fire into…

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: "It's been half a century since the last war. Neither you nor I have experienced a war. 'Peace.' Peace is what we are supposed to defend. But what is the peace of this city, this nation? The all-out war and the defeat. The US occupation policy. The Cold War under the nuclear umbrella and the proxy wars. And civil wars that still go on in many nations of the world. Ethnic clash, military conflict, blood-drenched economical prosperity created and sustained by those countless wars. That's what's behind our peace. Peace created by an indiscriminate fear of war. An unjust peace that is maintained by having the wars elsewhere, but we keep denying ourselves this truth."

reviews.text: There's a moment, about a third of the way through, where the music rises, the sky is pastel behind a static shot of a derelict warehouse, and you realise that a gear somewhere has shifted subtly, and you're really watching a film essay about the ambiguities of postwar Japan. Then almost as soon as you've noticed, the music fades, and you are set back down to continue with the narrative. It's effortless, and beautiful, and is just one of the ways that this film assumes the form of its predecessor, then blows it up from the inside.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: watched both cuts of this back-to-back, they're basically two separate movies that should be each considered on their own terms. theatrical cut is more hardboiled, action-packed and has a playful vibe, with gibson narrating and getting a lot more quips in against these shitheel badguys. director's cut is more emotionally restrained, grittier, more violent, with a brighter and higher contrast visual palette, and overall is closer in thematic presentation to the previous 1967 adaptation of this novel, point blank. one feels like a great pulpy 90s action-thriller, the other feels like an edgy homage to 60s/70s crime films. in my view, the theatrical cut is overall a more interesting package, and still retains the tight pace of the original director's cut while cutting out some needless domestic abuse scenes and a lackluster ending. stick with the theatrical, but the director's is an interesting curio.

Does however get a decent bump from its supporting cast (including Bill Duke and William DeVane!) and the nasty gunfights.

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: Richard Lester's Petulia gains in beauty, strength, and power the more ways you can see it: backwards, upside-down, watching scenes in piece-meal, on your phone, on your laptop, in 35mm, with friends, with family, by yourself, after a breakup, with your new partner. It's meant to be taken apart and put back together again, like each one of Lester's lost lovers: a wild woman, an insecure man, two hollow shells. It towers as a hallmark of depressing romances. Romance, but never romantic.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: On trying to feel something in a commoditized world. What is the place for human connection when even freedom is just a stylistic choice? Gestures move from play acting to painful longing. Memories and (un)possibilities of future dissolve into each other. Piece by piece the possibilities of drama strengthens despite its world in flux. Places can be sterile on one shot and contain a world of sadness in the next. Richard Lester fragmentary style might be very indebt to Resnais (for all the beauties of Two for the Road this remains the masterpiece of the late 60’s Hollywood goes New Wave moment), but the film seems to point to late Resnais as much as applies his earlier stylistic tics. All three leads do career best work. This is a film of total desolation but somehow a slight of romantic hope remains: one can always leave with a last impact on each other.

reviews.author: Josh Gillam
reviews.text: Filmed in San Francisco in the summer of 1967, Petulia was made in the middle of a moment, but rather than the breezier antics of his early 60s films Richard Lester examines this relationship story, and lets it get messier and darker on the way, capturing something of the era differently than you’d expect.

reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: Petulia is a fascinating portrait of American society in the legendary (mythical?) San Francisco Haight-Ashbury neighborhood circa 1967*, just as the counterculture reared its head and embarked on a Summer of Love. The story centers of two San Fran denizens going through radical personal change, mirroring and certainly impacted by the larger unrest of American culture at the time. Julie Christie plays the titular character, Petulia, an unhappily married young woman and tuba aficionado who meets and becomes besotted with an older surgeon (George C. Scott), who’s grumpy and adrift himself, recently becoming separated from his wife (Shirley Knight) of many years. Each are struggling mightily with their own specific and acute sense of ennui and find themselves attracted to…

reviews.text: Spectators to their own lives: seeking something about which to care; something that matters to them; something that is important. Lost and frightened, they impose their desperation on others, asking both strangers and intimates to carry the weight of their expectations, hoping that, this time, something will happen that they feel.

Both George C. Scott and Julie Christie are great and elevate this material into another realm. Be prepared for disillusionment and heartbreak but maybe just a little hope.
