reviews.author: Alexander Walker
reviews.text: Truth is obscured in Richard Lester's land of make-believe where people wear tight-fitting turtleneck sweaters, eat luxury tapas and live in modernist apartments adorned in ostentatious geometric design. People view an increasingly violent world through ' dummy' television sets. Nothing feels real. Internal greenhouses keep plants sealed behind steel and glass. The warm glow of flower power is slowly diminishing. We have entered a time capsule of a period where everyone seems dazed and confused. This isn't science fiction. It is late sixties San Francisco. When ' Petulia' was released the Summer of Love was a fading memory. Peace-loving revolutionaries were no longer greeted with open arms, but shunned by a paranoid community suspicious of passive resistance and non-violent ideology.…

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: The summer-of-love 'far-out-man' vibes and the flashy Nic Roeg cinematography including silent flashbacks inserted into the narrative, date this Richard Lester directed romantic drama. But the story and the acting and the satire of late sixties America manage to overcome these drawbacks (and the ludicrous and unnecessary sub-plot of the 'adoption' of a Mexican boy).The writer of the novel it was adapted from hated the film, probably because Lester hated the novel so much he changed it to reflect what he wanted to say about the America of the time.George C. Scott gives a restrained well-rounded performance (even though he seems far to old for his 'mod' clothing) and Richard Chamberlain gets away from his TV matinee-idol image playing an abusive husband. Julie Christie is Petulia, an English, San Francisc-based socialite trying to escape her brutal marriage.Julie was my first 'pin-up' actress and here, as in many films of this period, she is stunningly beautiful.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Blast the ground with yellow powder. Insert men in full-body white suits. Shoot against the bluest sky. Overload the senses with color, with broad strokes, without fine detail. It's just three blankets of hue, bold and direct and bright. Zoom in. Show fine details of insects. Watch them, timelapse them, animate them, delve into their movements, make their movements part of the plot, part of the themes, part of the atmosphere. Make the audience feel the insects all over their bodies. Make the audience squirm. Keep it sterile; keep it aloof. Keep it heavy, but not opaque. Keep it ominous. Keep it scientific. Show the violence, show the gore, but keep it clean. Almost bloodless deaths. Drain the victims, strip them bare, scour their flesh and leave their bones. Leave dust. Show the swarms. Show the insidiousness. Show the breakdown. Make the audience question. Build the tension to Phase IV. Dissolve.

reviews.text: I love how the many characters and their relationships only gradually come into focus, in much the same way as McCabe & Mrs Miller and Nashville. For example, Oxblood Oxheart and his Agnes Skinner-esque mother are seen quietly dining at Rough House’s restaurant and milling around Olive Oyl’s engagement party and a lot of other places long before they really figure into the plot in the boxing scene. There’s no scene announcing what, exactly, Wimpy’s deal is. He’s just always hanging around, looking for hamburgers. Probably no one knows how he became a regular at the Oyls’ dinner table.

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: What in fuck is this movie? Popeye is up there with the strangest studio movies ever made. A rambling, aimless nightmare that kind of beautifully captures the spirit and madcappery of a Fleischer animation while also relentlessly alienating the viewer. Characters repeat lines over and over. Most dialogue is muttered, meaningless, or talked over. Every action is deliberate, wobbly, and utterly bizarre. With his disgusting prosthetic arms, Robin Williams is a surprisingly excellent Popeye. Paul L. Smith is a walking horrorshow as Bluto. But Shelley Duvall as Olive Oyl blows everyone out of the water. She not only looks exactly like the original character, but every movement she makes gives her the appearance of a flesh and blood cartoon. The music by Harry Nilsson, much like the rest of the film, is as jarring as it is oddly wonderful. As completely unwatchable as Popeye is, I think I love it?

Public Enemies is an enormous film and in my opinion arguably Mann's richest, constantly shifting & intertwining thematic outliers and formal conceits - it's yet another film about Baudrilliardian prison simulacra, but also a film on the birth of modern surveillance & the FBI, the birth of modern celebrity, a character study of Dillinger himself, the end of a certain romanticism & how all these points shaped the America which we know today. reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: In 2006, Mann by pure happenstance aligned with David Lynch and Pedro Costa in providing a canvas for experimenting with the limits of burgeoning digital video technology. In 2009, you could argue that he made an equally inadvertent pairing with James Cameron in testing the new format on an epic scale. But if Avatar is a massive tech demo, Public Enemies is an attempt to see how the grammar of film itself might be manipulated to shake up even the oldest genres in cinema history.

reviews.text: I've gone from disliking this film to loving it to now finding it one of the best of the last decade. A crime movie that foregrounds the allure of iconic criminals while thoroughly countering it with a brutal vision of single-minded crooks and equally simple cops. (In an amusing twist, it is the nascent FBI that is seen as far more nefarious by the public at large in this movie, distrustful of a Depression-era government body formed, in part, to fight those who took a vicarious revenge on the banks that lost everything for so many people.) It also feels like a ghost movie, lingering on a body falling from the running board of a getaway car, or the last, cold breath billowing out of a dead Babyface Nelson. Utterly exceptional.

reviews.author: Ian West
reviews.text: Mario Bava’s grime crime thriller. An intense on the run road trip to no hopes-ville and a vast departure from the more colorful gothic tales he’s best remembered for, holding back his more audacious visual style in favor of claustrophobic action and tight tension that suffocates—upping the crazed suspense level well into the danger zone and resulting in the most manic panic themed nightmare into nihilism he’s ever done.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Mario Bava’s ride into grindhouse hell remains one of his best movies even if he shortchanges most of the surface pleasures one associates with him. A parade of awful scummy behavior and extreme sweaty close ups of vile men. Some of the 70s nihilism and easy ironies can feel a bit pat, but this is a masterclass of expert blocking and propulsive editing turning the inside of hijacked car into a catalogue of humanity’s worse behavior. It is a crime film that is somehow scarier and more vile than any of Bava’s better known horror films and in its own way as much a triumph of style than something like Kill, Baby, Kill.

Don’t ever allow me to get that pretentious again). Mia Farrow’s squeaky voice works comedically, but it’s perhaps the only flaw of the picture, if you can call it that. I almost wish Allen went more melancholic with this one, it’s DNA is so similar to Barry Levinson’s Avalon, except it never allows melodrama to sneak into frame, even moments of drama are followed by a new happy memory.

Earlier this month, Insomniac launched a spiffed up HD remake of the original game, and thought that it might be a fun idea to promote it by partnering with Rainmaker Studios — an animation house responsible for 11 Barbie movies and "Escape from Planet Earth" — in order to create a feature-length film that essentially told the same story. reviews.author: Daniel Kibbe
reviews.text: RED 2 piqued my interest with a quote from a trailer: "the only summer movie without giant robots, superheroes, or aliens. Just the best there is". And that statement rings true for the most part. It's generic story coated with the charm of faded stars back in action. It succeeds in delivering some old-school action, and some laughs, but fails to deliver a truly compelling story. John Malkovich and Anthony Hopkins are the clear standouts in this all-star cast of old folks. They're easily the best parts about the film, with Malkovich providing legitimate laughs. Like I said, the plot is generic, and everything you'd expect, but its refreshing to see an actual human story told this summer. It's fairly funny, and fairly entertaining, making for a surprisingly decent film.

reviews.text: RED is just fine. The action is uninspired and the humour isn't particularly funny, but the final act is fun enough. There's probably an argument to be made about the glamourisation of CIA operatives (our lovable hero literally "toppled governments") but honestly RED is too shallow for this to matter. The film makes no sense and is filled with silly plot logistics. The early 2010s feels like a generation ago, with big films like this being so much smaller in scale and so filled with terrible music. The best thing in RED is the great cast, though it must be said that John Malkovich steals the show and has the most fun. However ultimately all that RED shows is that even older actors can be the leads in generic, bland action movies.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A case study in what a director does: put on Manhunter (the same material, same cinematographer) and observe what that film does with space, sound, architecture and light. How dynamic the visual style is and how much subjective interiority and perversity it mines out of wordless atmosphere. Then throw on this film. By all “objective” measures probably a perfectly okay, expensive middlebrow procedural with an overqualified cast. But far more frustrating to me than a “bad” movie because we get to witness the same scenes (frequently beat-for-beat, line-for-line) with the knowledge that they can be incredibly expressive and now they are among the flattest, dullest, most literal-minded and unimaginative the genre has ever given us. I hesitate to even use the word imitation when describing how generic and pointless of a remake this is because it doesn’t even appear to be trying. I guess that’s Brett Ratner auteurism.

reviews.text: Alan Rudolph starts with a very typical Fatal Attraction scenario and manages to build a slippery film that is both attentive to human mystery and emotional raw. It slowly goes from confounding to painful as the film careful moves toward a confrontation that is immediate and felt as few genre films are. So many things here are very calculated for effect (the blues score, Anthony Perkins presence as the stalked man, the careful structural absences), but it never feels like an exercise, it is open wound just too real. I do like how even after we get some answers for its blank spaces, the world remains unattainable. Geraldine Chaplin (who is amazing here) did it a bit after Noirot, and Remember My Name feels like what a Rivette film would look like if he was American.

Rudolph’s specific eccentricities and dive bar melancholy made him an all time favourite for me the second I saw Choose Me, and I’m so glad that feeling of adoration continues here. this one doesn’t shy away from darkness or unhealthy dynamics, it knows that everything here is on borrowed time, that the events of the film even happening have destined these beings to a harder life, but there’s beauty to be found in the moments before it all tumbles down.

Robert Webber is the leader of the French Connection is actually the heel here; no, not Alain Charnier. The French Connection was an actual drug trade way back when; their foe that they wish to take out is not Popeye Doyle… it was Inspector Clouseau.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Retconning the events of Pink Panther Strikes Again as being evidently a mentally disturbed hallucination of Chief Inspector Dreyfus's, this makes more overtures towards being an actual movie rather than just a series of gags. The problem is that all of these overtures fail and many of the gags are either weak variants of familiar favorites or just offensive and/or embarrassing. There's a hint of humiliation in all comedy, of course (probably why the discipline attracts so many neurotic, damaged personalities), but it's nevertheless depressing to see Peter Sellers, possibly the finest comic actor of his generation, subjected to one extremely stupid disguise after another, especially when the series has run as low on steam as it has here.

"Certo Agora, Errado Antes" mostra duas versões de uma mesma história, com acontecimentos parecidos, mas não idênticos. Os detalhes fazem toda a diferença. O filme reflete sobre como cada decisão, mesmo pequena, pode levar a caminhos inesperados. Não há grandes reviravoltas ou cenas de impacto. Tudo acontece de maneira simples e natural, sem pressa. O ritmo é devagar e pede paciência do espectador. Diferente dos filmes de Hollywood, este segue um estilo mais contemplativo, típico do cinema asiático, focado no cotidiano e nas sutilezas da vida.

Stacey Keach stars as Pat Quid, a cultured truck driver with a pet dingo who comes to believe that he's sharing the road with a serial killer driving a green van. The nods to Hitchcock are numerous but the film still manages to take on a life of its own through the setting, lead performance and a wicked sense of black humour. It's a rather gentle ride - aside from a macabre sequence involving pig carcasses, the film largely stays away from providing any shock value, preferring instead to build interest through the characters and central situation. Loved so much of this setup, Keach’s wild personality and his penchant for talking to himself, the sassy faceless dispatch voice and the eclectic score that modulates between classic adventure score, military march, and suspense thriller. reviews.text: I'm thrilled to have finally seen the new 3D restoration of this classic film, which is new on Blu-Ray. If you care about cinema, you really ought to buy it. I promise I'm not being paid to tell you this, I just believe strongly in the product. This movie's flaws are many and well-documented, but it's amazing how much better it becomes in 3D. Shots that once seemed totally pedestrian suddenly come to life. Whatever else he got wrong, Phil Tucker had the right instinct to make a 3D movie in Bronson Canyon, which is so full of rocks and trees and hills and other things that make for a dense and interesting 3D frame.

This is especially because it is an early example of the independent film, specifically designed to take advantage of the 3D film market. Shot on one of the most shoestring budgets that one could find, the makers of the film couldn't even afford a full robot costume for their antagonistic Ro-Man Extension XJ-2 (or Ro-Man for short) character. Instead, you get this humorous use of a gorilla suit with astronaut helmet…

reviews.text: This could’ve so easily been another cynical ‘70s dystopian melodrama, but it also layers on this thick melancholy and insight about used up athletes. Even without all the heavy handed corporate/sociological commentary, it’s still a damn good sports film first. The matches are just incredibly staged and viscerally brutal (even 40+ years later), and James Caan brings this real muted, weathered sense of worth to the central gladiator. Love all the Kubrickian classical drops, piped in so even the characters can hear the portentous soundtrack to their lives. This holds up better than most of the post-2001 studio sci-fi that became so popular during the early half of the decade.

As much as it feels camp there is some solid rhetoric to today's day and age albeit in a distant past foil of the future. I can't say that the story gets to a truth that a gamer can break the game but it feels like a lot of sci-fi novels of the time to hold that potential that the written word can find truth and set you free. It's dry and very stylized and I think that's what I enjoyed about it as well as James Caan's performance but it is a little long. I do have to say I liked the fans T-shirts and the battle sequences. Totally worth watching for a vibe and a questioning of the computer age. So check it out before A.I. deletes this review;)

reviews.text: You can take the man out of the war but you can't take the war out of the man. One of Schrader's many lonely, isolated, tortured character studies taken to some cathartically gruesome revenge-action extremes by Flynn who’s just one the most effectively spare, blunt-force filmmakers around at this type of thing. Devane gives one of the best psychotic, dead-behind-the-eyes chameleon pretending to be a real person performances ever and young Tommy Lee Jones in this should be in the canon of sad 70s hot guys. The final shootout is one of the straight-up nastiest of its era, and even more perverse when you realize the larger idea being worked through here is one of violence as a bonding or healing tool for a traumatized generation of men. "I'll just get my gear."

reviews.author: Leon Staton
reviews.text: Gainax is no longer famous for its early works—the least of which known might be Royal Space Force. Defining points in their timeline, like Evangelion and Gurren-Lagann, are more mainstream and attractive overall within the anime industry the studio has influenced. On occasion, remnants of the past creep in from the early days when intrepid anime fans like Toshio Okada and Hiroyuki Yamaga convinced their colleagues that vision mattered more than experience. A movie like Royal Space Force would rarely if ever come from a more economic, less daring era of Japanese animation—that being the current period of limited-animation TV fanservice and carbohydrate productions. When I first heard that the old guard of Gainax is going to do precisely that,…

reviews.text: It's no wonder Coppola tired so soon and so easily of classicist filmmaking....he's completely consumed by emotions and so he tries to find a way to express them. In other words: this man is intoxicated, completely wasted on cinema. He lives, breathes, eats cinema. This is the middle film in this 1980's monumental trifecta (the others being One From The Heart and The Cotton Club) of total aesthetic, sensory reaction. This one is so utterly aestheticized, stylized, explosive that it's easy to forget there is a very precious coming of age story here.

reviews.text: The older I get, the more I swing away from Coppola's New Hollywood string of canonical classics and the more I gravitate toward the freewheeling experiments of his work in the '80s and beyond. Rumble Fish is as much of a sensory experience and technical show-off as One from the Heart, the impressionistic flip-side to the more standard coming-of-age tale of The Outsiders. Its plot is not so much thin as vaporous, forever taking the shimmering, ectoplasmic shape of something solid before a slight breeze disrupts the form. It is a film carved out of various images and sounds of youth, blending '50s greasers with contemporary fashion, expressionistic renditions of West Side Story gang fights with a soundtrack heavy on…

reviews.text: Honestly, "Season of the Witch" wasn't that bad, although it's definitely the second-best film with that title. This film came out the following year after another medieval witch/folk tale, "Black Death," starring Sean Bean. Both tell a fairly similar story of witchcraft being at the centre of the black plague. Whereas "Black Death" had its Knights seek out the source of the Witch in a faraway village, "Season of the Witch" sees Nic Cage and Ron Perlman transport a young girl (who's been accused of causing the plague) to a faraway village and stand trial.

reviews.text: 400 leagues in six days? Um, that's 230 miles a day, three or four times what you could expect from people on horseback who have to stop to eat and sleep. But this film has bigger problems than errors in simple math. The plot and dialog are sloppy, pedestrian and predictable ... it's tough making a good film with material like this, no matter who's acting or directing. On the plus side, Nicholas Cage and Ron Perlman are always fun to watch, Claire Foy is good at playing angry, spunky gals, plus there's good support from Steve Graham, and Robert Sheehan ... everyone does their best with the awful script and it's these actors who give the film what little appeal it has, along with some fairly nice production design... but it doesn't help much, the film's still probably worth a pass.

reviews.text: I could very easily be a contrarian here and say that this was exhausting, overly long, and not particularly enjoyable, but I'd be lying. I had gone in as somewhat of a sceptic due to its reputation; however, it's safe to say that my scepticism wavered fairly quickly upon pressing play. This was monumental. I felt as though I was watching a documentary due to its authenticity and realism. A blockbuster on an unfathomable scale that never lacks excitement or the use of complex emotion. Beyond the potent philosophy and depiction of human emotions, this was surprisingly very enjoyable. Pretty much the blueprint for big-budget action films. Everything is perfect, from the set-up to the (deliberate?) anti-climactic ending. This is a rare occasion where such immense praise is more than warranted. What a picture! What an experience!

reviews.author: Eddie White
reviews.text: Some films try so hard to be cool and just aren't. She's Gotta Have It just drips cool from the minute it starts to the very end. As searingly honest, hilarious and lively as it was when it was released in 1986, this film does so many things ahead of its time. It follows the story of one Brooklynite Nola Darling as she simultaneously dates three different men, refusing to commit or to be 'posessed' by one of them. It feels like the Annie Hall of 1980s for me. A feminist, jazzy masterpiece direct from the mind of a young Spike Lee. Beautifully directed, edited and scored and featuring raw but charismatic and memorable performances and unique characters. There are so many great lines that stick in your head and so many truths about love, relationships, men, women and sex told as they are. All cinema fans must watch this gem.

She's out there willing to make mistakes, and so is he, from the jump.

reviews.text: At a certain point learning about history just reduces people to statistics. Shoah is so vital because it tries to make history be about people again. It is a reminder of how seriously we should treat history. It is an act of historical record, letting survivors and witnesses to the Holocaust speak. Their words are preserved here, and even when interviewed through a translator the translator is not edited out, allowing the original answers to be heard exactly. Shoah is not a history lesson, nor does it examine the origins or events of the Holocaust. Instead it is a document of what people saw, collected through individual testimony. reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Shoah is a profound achievement in documentary filmmaking as well as a heart-wrenching memorial about the Holocaust. It features long lingering images of the countryside around the Nazi death camps which create a perception that even nature still hasn't recovered from the terrible events which transpired there, let alone humanity. Directed by Claude Lanzmann who chooses against utilising sadly all too familiar archival footage to communicate the atrocities; instead, he decides to linger on the expressions of observers, evildoers and the survivors of this terrible chapter in history while additionally exhibiting vacant synagogues within the communities that were once occupied by Jews.

The screenplay by Luigi Cozzi claims to be based on Edgar Allan Poe's "The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade," but this wacky thing takes only the most superficial inspiration from that satire, and is more a spiritual cousin to Cozzi's Hercules movies for Cannon. Legend has it Cozzi was initially refused a directorial position, but when credited director Enzo G. Castellari turned in an unusable 3+ hours of footage, they had to call in Luigi to turn it into something resembling a narrative feature. His solution was to present it as a bedtime story read by mom Daria Nicolodi to his own daughter, Giada, and to have her narrate…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Little bit of Hitchcock, giallo, Rosemary's Baby, slashers and what would eventually become the psychosexual science-fiction of Cronenberg going on here. Creates a very strong formal tension between De Palma's classical Hollywood thriller style and the shocking violence/bizarre, sensationalist modern detail that he populates it with. The climax of the film that combines three different psyches battling it out in extreme close-ups, real memories, implanted flashbacks, POV/split screen images, and fake archival footage which are also dreams (??) before exploding into sex and violence is nothing short of insane. That no one really solves the central case feels quite appropriate with how this movie is designed to make you feel.

reviews.text: Another Hitchcockian crime film from De Palma draped in sleaze and a sort of tabloid sensationalism, this film falls slightly too far on the side of trashy at times while indulging heavily in De Palma's favorite influences. Like Body Double, this film owes a debt to Polanski as well as Hitchcock (though the former is much more present in both). Hitchcock toyed with his share of risque or over-the-top material, flavoring his storytelling with it, but De Palma seems to go the other way, flavoring his sensationalism with tension-fraught storytelling.

It's a bunch of situations strung haphazardly together, never quite coalescing into a complete narrative. Every character gets their arc, but everything feels much too patchy for the film to be a fully satisfying experience. I was never bored, however, and swooned over the detestable Jake Ryan, so I can't say that I didn't enjoy the film, but it did leave me disappointed, like, is this it? This is just going to be one of those forgettable in-between films, the sort of thing you can't summon up the passion to either love or hate. Meh.

reviews.text: Stephen King's Paul Schrader's Cat People. Half baffling, horny melodrama between incestuous, shapeshifting hairless werecats who drive fast cars and "drain the lifeforce" of virgin girls... Half goofy action creature feature with Mädchen Amick as the beautiful popcorn girl at the Aero Theatre who finds herself in a series of insane, peddle-to-the-floor setpieces filled with silly rubber suits, ridiculously gory murders (by eye-gouging, hand-tearing, bone-breaking, corncob-stabbing?? etc), and an army of squaded-up, slomo-leaping warrior felines led by a vengeful tabby cat named Clovis. Intensely moronic but somehow manages to sustain itself even after clearly suffering some weird form of coked-up fever dream brain damage of various King tropes and hangups—Garris commits to them so fully the whole final reel which should probably collapse on itself instead sort of rocks. Great final shot and Enya credits drop. Cameos include: Mark Hamill, Ron Perlman, Clive Barker, Tobe Hooper, Joe Dante, John Landis, and King himself obviously.

reviews.text: Smashed hits incredibly close to home. It has long stood out to me as an indie gem—one of those rare films that tells the truth without embellishment. It captures the emotional dissonance of addiction with such raw clarity. Watching it often takes me back to a time in my life when I was struggling to stay sober while in a relationship that made it nearly impossible. We enabled each other constantly. The line between love and codependence blurred until neither of us could recognize it anymore.

Satirizing beauty pageants seems like an easy target, and it is, but what Smile does to layer everything is shine its spotlight on the adults involved in the Santa Rosa ceremony. Their lives are a pit of denial, none more so than Bruce Dern in a…

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: It's almost unbelievable that so gentle a satire can land with such an emotionally powerful wallop (like an iron glove cast in velvet, to rearrange a quote from Faster Pussycat, Kill, Kill, Kill). It's a cumulative effect that is patiently built, scene by scene, across a wide cast of characters. The ambition seems to be nothing short of deconstructing the "American Dream" by detailing how its pursuit has emotionally crippled an entire small town and negatively affected the values of contestants in a beauty pageant. Somehow it achieves all of this while still remaining consistently funny--even venturing into a teen sex-comedy subplot--never feeling forced or overly self-serious and never resorting to mean-spirited mockery. Everything feels really natural. Even the comedic…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Michael Ritchie's Smile is very nearly perfect, a laugh-out-loud funny satire that is unashamed of its heart, and grants many of its targets a wholly unexpected degree of grace and complexity. Particularly astonishing is car salesman/beauty pageant judge Big Bob Freelander (Bruce Dern), the characterization of whom treads a knife's edge between buffoonery and realism, and who ends up unable to either hide or resist what he believes to be his inherent kindness. It's an incredible performance, one made possible by Jerry Belson's audacious, breathtakingly sharp writing.

Ironically, I had somehow flown over this film in its relevancy but upon research I found that this film holds something of a notorious build. My viewing for sure reaffirms this film as I can confirm that it at least ends on a very polarizing note.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Tonally uneven yet still utterly engrossing revisionist Western, whereIn Candice Bergen’s former wife of a Native warrior leads a green Union grunt across hostile Cheyenne territory after her army escort caravan has been decimated by raiders displeased that America has again encroached on their land. I mean, the only reason you’d adapt the real life Sand Creek massacre the movie concludes with (a savage, disproportionate response to the Natives’ murderous raid) in 1970 is to use it as a stand-in for ‘Nam era atrocity. A cynical “this has happened before and will keep happening throughout time” exploitation polemic that I naturally loved every minute of.

reviews.text: I believe the reason why Terrence Malick's aggressive cutting and fracturing of his footage -- the self-destructive, almost imploding nature of his editing process -- neutralizes his narratives and consequentially makes them feel so complete (as opposed to traditional narratives), is because of the way in which our minds perceive, dissolve and rebuild experience through memory; our lives, some so deeply incomplete and yet still the most generally complete notion that we're capable of considering, are but fragments and deconstructions and reconstructions and, thus, the crafting of this sort of splintered cinema is what renders his films so conclusive and absolute, for all we have to compare them to are our own shattered and superglued existences.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: There are a small handful of filmmakers I would describe as Joycean. Terence Davies, despite never shooting in Ireland, captures the physical reality of Joyce's books: the creaking interiors, the spiritual weight of real and emotional death, the way that alcoholism and rage is both the manifestation and perpetuator of lower-class misery. David Lynch reflects the author's pathologized sexuality, the warped, half-glimpsed chimera of lust and repression that distorts perspectives into horrorshow abandon. (In more ways that one, Lost Highway resembles Finnegans Wake converted to film noir, replacing that book's transcendent motion with more base impulses of murder.) Add to that list Terrence Malick, who (since The New World, at least) has tackled the more probing, elemental, associative side of…

His method is fundamentally opposite to how we're meant, or how we've been taught, to perceive "character" or the presence of bodies & minds on screen; rather than observing the whole of an individual, a complete picture of a person, and re-tracing our steps to uncover the smaller, more intimate psychological details of the individual's inner clockwork (the popular "character approach"), we're instead presented with those…

reviews.text: Forms a pretty solid, miserably bleak Charlton Heston sci-fi dystopia trilogy with Planet of the Apes and The Omega Man, and though perhaps overshadowed by the legacy and even more iconic twist ending of the former this still very much holds up for me. Namely Fleischer’s structuring of this as a sweaty, conspiratorial procedural where a jaded detective (selfishly indulging himself of every meager pleasure left to be wrung out of our synthetic commercial food processing and environmental hellscape; vegetables, showers, and women mostly) is given a radicalizing front-row seat to the corporate cannibal machinery horror he helps serve and maintain.

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: Soylent Green is one of those sci-fi films that keeps you thinking, "We'll get there," so that whatever negative reaction it elicits, it will never be indifference. As for me, it became a certainty that Harry Harrison's prophetic vision of 2022 would become a reality sooner or later. The opening credit sequence is a simple but effective way to establish that the urban nightmare featured in the film is a logical continuation of the uncontrollable population increase.

reviews.author: Chris Cabin
reviews.text: A desperate, horny detective mostly abandons his job in post-apocalyptic America to get laid, take showers, sleep, and eat lettuce and hobo stew with his elderly research assistant and one of the chief suspects in the murder case he's working, whom he is also boning. He is then, of course, stunned to find out this horrible world can only go on as is through systemic executions, cannibalism, and ongoing suppression and oppression by the state against the people. The good times are fun and all, but I was wishing for a little bit more dread and layered uncovering to support the outlandishly bleak premise, a bit more time showing what is left of the old societal structures, and what has happened to its overseers and heralds. Fleischer, per usual, directs the shit out of this, and its mostly his decisions - and Edward G. Robinson - that really make the final 30 minutes sing.

reviews.text: Roger Corman’s gloriously shameless sci-fi romp, is a guilty pleasure that delivers more fun than it has any right to. Corman, the king of cutting corners, recycles so much stock footage from his earlier Battle Beyond the Stars flick, sometimes you forget which film you are watching. The space battles, ship models, and even James Horner’s score are lifted straight from Battle, with its boobie shaped ship and froggy looking enemy crafts exploding in the exact same way. The plot is pure B-movie. A 10-year-old kid accidentally stows away on a freighter stolen by a ragtag crew of space pirates led by the gruff Captain Hawk. After a shootout with “The Company” (because every sci-fi flick needs a faceless evil…

Being not absolute bastards, our Space Raiders decide to return Peter to his family once they're done with some business, but some fellow pirates, led by Zariatin (Ray Stewart) realize just how much a kid like Peter might be worth. Meanwhile, the Company, which Peter's father works for, sends a Texas class ship out to bring the boy back...dead or alive, but probably dead.

reviews.author: _pashabo
reviews.text: There are films that are not just underrated -- they seem hidden in the folds of history, as if someone turned off the lights in a room and left the audience wandering past. Space Raiders is one of those films. Partially assembled from recycled footage of Battle Beyond the Stars -- another of Roger Corman’s strange whims -- it nevertheless manages to become something far more cohesive. And when you finally turn on that light, you realize that all this time there lay a true cornerstone of 1980s space culture.

Note that I never saw the film again on VHS after the one theatrical viewing; that is perhaps a sign of what my opinion was as a kid… I really remembered nothing at all. reviews.text: I can see why this feels like for-hire work when you look at Kubrick's filmography but when compared to other old-fashioned analog epics this is honestly among the more beautiful and intimate of them with finely-tuned performances from some reliable greats (Douglas, Laughton, Ustinov, Olivier, etc) and insanely gorgeous spectacle sequences that simply serve to amplify fast and Trumbo's material which was clearly inspired by their blacklisting and is very emotionally engaged with its basic ideas of class solidarity and spectacle/violence as both tool of entertainment and revolution. What an ending too! With the path of literal and ideological freedom lined with corpses. Glad I decided to blindly pick up the new 4K blu-ray (one of the best-looking ones I've seen so far tbh) and finally get around to this one.

Mesmo sem a costumeira liberdade artística que conseguiria alguns anos depois, Kubrick realiza um excelente trabalho, construindo sequências maravilhosas e narrando uma história extremamente cativante com sua habitual competência. A luta pelo direito das minorias sempre esteve presente nas telas do cinema, mas trazer essa discussão na década de 60 transformou Spartacus em um épico que rompeu com o estereótipo de filmes de gladiadores.

reviews.text: Wait, how was this not higher on my watchlist? A troupe of stage actors gets locked in during a rainstorm with a deranged killer on the loose—doesn’t sound that unique on its surface, fine. But what if all the kill-count-fodder characters were memorable, well-written, sassy theater kids? What if the script was filled to the brim with phenomenally self-aware dark humor? What if the lighting, coloring, and general outrageousness mirrored the serial-killer-based play they were already rehearsing? What if the faceless slasher donned a fucking GIANT OWL HEAD PIECE and stumbled into the theater’s tool shop, finding a litany of potential murder weapons ranging from an axe to a power drill to a goddamn chainsaw? What if he utilized each…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: From its opening moments, this film declares itself to be a masterpiece of style (screencaps here; spoilers within). It toys with a neon, cocaine kind of atmosphere, but it is firmly rooted in giallo mystery, slasher suspense, and Hitchcockian flair. It is theatrical (how could it not be?), and there are issues with bad delivery and what I think was bad dubbing (?). The soundtrack is a bit mixed in quality. It occasionally lapses into characters doing stupid things, and the characterization isn't entirely profound. We get a few moments that show more than just a bunch of frightened people, but for the most part, it just has some surface personalities primed for emotional conflict and fear.

reviews.text: 100-word review: Using deadly weaponised thalaron radiation, the Reman Shinzon forcefully assumes Romulan Praetorship. Following the coup d'état, he professes a desire for peace with the Federation; the Enterprise is ordered on a diplomatic mission. Once there, however, our heroes discover that Shinzon is not only human, but also an acquaintance (of sorts). Nemesis continues the Star Trek tradition of openly debating ethics, this time focusing on a nature vs. nurture discussion with the characters of Picard and Data both being mirrored by duplicates of different upbringing. Unfortunately, that's all quickly abandoned in favour of an aimless, dull, and uninspired 'action' plot.

reviews.text: Terrific last-gasp of practical sci-fi about the impossibility of diplomacy amongst tribes with grudges that cannot be forgiven. Unusually cynical for a Trek and featuring a delicious turn by Christopher Plummer as a Shakespeare-quoting Klingon warmonger. This was released five months after Terminator 2: Judgment Day, and feels as though it could have been made 10 years earlier. But that never stops it from calmly, elegantly executing its story about old soldiers trying to survive. The older I get, the more Trek stories resonate.

reviews.text: Whether or not you enjoy Starcrash is going to depend on how much you enjoy naive art in general. It’s the kind of movie an imaginative 11-year-old boy might make if he had access to $4 million (in 1978) and some talented actors and technicians. It’s often clumsy and nonsensical, but it’s so enthusiastic and unselfconscious that it’s actually kind of charming and fun. It’s also weirdly compelling at times. That’s because the enthusiasm of the actual director, 30-year-old Luigi Cozzi, is infectious. Some of the talented folks he’s working with, such as a slumming Christopher Plummer, seem to be having fun with the material. John Barry turns in a surprisingly ambitious music score — one that anticipates his even…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Your first time was never that un-awkward. And outside? Come on. She woulda been so uncomfortable. I don't demand or expect realism here, but if you're going to make your entire film about virginity (blech), then at least have the decency to eschew cliched fantasies. For a moment, it feels like the film will portray this worship of virginity as the toxic thing it is, showing how creepily people talk about Lucy and of course the sexual assault (which is very uncomfortable to watch knowing this was goddamned Bertolucci). Instead, it reinforces the idea, romanticizing it and belaboring its point by contrasting her first time with her friend dying of AIDS, an unspoken statement that has connotations that do not sit well. What could have been a sweet, corny little film about a girl finding her father and love becomes a disjointed mess with a patriarchal view of sex.

Most of all, her character Natalie is crucial to the plot, which follows uptight but successful business executive Waymon (Joseph C. Phillips) who ask his friend & mailroom clerk Bobby (Tommy Davidson) to help introduce him to the free-spirited Natalie (Berry) and he'll put Bobby into the company's training program. While it is clichéd, this romantic comedy is still an entertaining film to watch and plus, you can't go wrong with a soundtrack that includes LL Cool J, Heavy D, Jodeci, Big Daddy Kane, Father MC and many others. Definitely a good, harmless watch.

With possible exception of In Living Color's Tommy Davidson who is also the only person who makes you Care that this movie has a point and wants to tackle a significant social issue. Specifically, black people judging each other on arbitrary "he's a thug because he wears his hat backward" type 'rules' rather than the classic, timeless Content of Character. reviews.author: Matthew Christman
reviews.text: I don't care that nobody seems to understand the plot. I don't care that it's didactic. I don't care that "serious people" find the geopolitical analysis puerile. I love Stephen Gaghan's Syriana because it's the only American film to seriously and thoughtfully engage with the "war on terror." Every other Hollywood product either exploits the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan as an easy background for action scenes or to make rather banal points about the traumatic effects of war on those who fight them. Syriana, on the other hand, examines the moral implications of our oil-based economy with deftly intertwined stories of terrorists, CIA officers and sheiks. There's just enough time spent teasing out the characters to make you care…

reviews.text: Another quality horror omnibus from Amicus. Tales from the Crypt begins with five characters lost inside a Crypt. This one works so well because the characters themselves are fundamental to everything. They are a morally dubious bunch, who pretty much deserve what they get. With the exception of the first tale, each segment has something of an emotional core. There's some real emotive use of POV shots for the short story based on a car crash, which also has something of Lovecraft's The Outsider about it. There's also spin on The Monkey's Paw, which puts a wife's desperation at the centre. The Patrick Magee story of a group of blind men taking revenge on the director of their rest home…

reviews.text: Five people taking a catacombs tour who discover they're about to be judged for their sins, as each tale torn-from-the-comics unfolds. But I have to say - poor Richard Green, I'm not really sure he did anything wrong except have a wife who is exceptionally bad at wishes. The rest of the bastards, though, deserve their fates. Among other interesting facts, I learned that dogs will kill and eat their owners if you don't feed them for a couple days, that schools for the blind have very robust shop class programs, that Joan Collins needs to massively upgrade her evidence planting game if she ever hoped to guest star on Columbo, and that Peter Cushing is an absolute treasure. His performance felt so personal, too, this is one to cherish.

reviews.text: Taras Bulba takes place in the 16th century, when Cossacks rebelled against the Poles who occupied their lands in the Ukrainian steppe. This had the potential to be one of the greatest historical epics ever, and it sports some of the best sword and saddle battle sequences ever shot on film. Unfortunately, it too often opts for a Romeo and Juliet story line, and while the Juliet character (played by Christine Kaufmann) is fine, the Romeo is terribly annoying. In the title role of the Cossack leader, Yul Brynner was made for this kind of stuff, but Tony Curtis, who plays his son (!), is woefully out of his element. Omar Sharif would star in “Genghis Khan” three years later, which had a similar aesthetic and was also in no small…

reviews.author: Jim Beaver
reviews.text: J. Lee Thompson's epic about the 17th century war between Cossacks and Poles is epic only in its action sequences, most of which are superb and quite grand. But the film spends far too much time on rather insipid misadventures of Taras's sons in school and in particular son Andre's romance with a Polish girl. Adhering only slightly to Nikolai Gogol's original novel, the movie has a wonderful look (despite an awful lot of process photography), but it's rather dull in the long stretches between battle sequences. Yul Brynner in the title role is wonderfully bombastic and flamboyant, but he gets far less footage than his two handsome but dull sons (Tony Curtis and Perry Lopez). What one remembers from this experience is the sweeping and truly impressive swarms of Cossacks gathering across the steppes (actually the gorgeous Argentine Pampas) to the brilliant music score by Franz Waxman. The rest of it is more pulpa than bulba.

reviews.text: North Korea is the setting for this Italian action movie directed by Ferdinando Baldi, who made four Tony Anthony films, including BLINDMAN and COMIN’ AT YA! Originally intended as a World War II movie set in Japan, the production was taken over by its North Korean investors, including none other than Kim Jong-il (!), who turned it into a commando movie with a vaguely sci-fi plot that makes as much sense as the title. One of its stars, Charles Robert Jenkins, was in the United States Army until he defected in 1965 to North Korea, where he was held prisoner with three other American soldiers for several years. Unquestionably, a movie about the making of TEN ZAN — something along…

reviews.text: In Nordkorea abgedrehter 08/15-Actioner der unspektakulären Sorte. Die Story um die Erschaffung einer Superrasse klingt zwar cool, aber es gibt weder Menschenexperimente noch eine abgedrehte Mad-Scientist-Story. Der Film plätschert relativ langsam vor sich hin, bis die Actionhelden endlich mal ein feindliches Lager in die Luft sprengen. Der Handlungsablauf ist uninteressant und auch die "Charaktere" könnten nicht belangloser sein. Die kargen, menschenleeren Landschaften Nordkoreas bieten definitiv keine gewinnbringende Abwechslung zu den Philippinen. Außerdem mangelt es an Actionszenen. Erst nach einer Stunde kommt der Film langsam in Fahrt. Es gibt einige Explosionen und das typische Rumgeballer nach dem Motto: "Die Bösen treffen nicht, der Gute trifft, die Bösen lassen sich fallen" - natürlich immer unblutig.Unfreiwillig komisch ist der Film leider auch…

reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: This isn't a movie. This is more like a visual album. Each murder is a track, "Bats", "Locusts", and so on, the Ten Plagues of Egypt, re-imagined in the style of a murderous Batman or Avengers TV episode. Vincent Price leads his mechanical band on the organ. The end credits might clue you in on who to root for and who is just part of the ensemble, organized into "Interested Parties", "The Law", "The Victims", "The Girl" (the wonderfully enigmatic and quite helpful murder assistant and violinist Victoria North), and "The Protagonists": consisting of Vincent Price as the abominable Dr. Phibes himself, and Joseph Cotton as Dr. Vesavius, the man he most wants dead. Dueling Doctors. Organs vs. Organist. Performance art. Play Somewhere Over the Rainbow when they bury me, for I'm going to see my beloved again.

reviews.author: demi adejuyigbe
reviews.text: It's a masterpiece. The best adventure film of the decade. Gorgeous, inventive, globetrotting, swashbuckling fun that only Spielberg could do. Caught myself going "oh shit, now this part is gonna rule" every few minutes over Zoom to make sure my friends took stock of every clever transition and oner. So much credit is given to Andy Serkis for playing apes and golems and all sorts of non-human characters that we ignore how good he is at just making a man like Captain Haddock feel real and lived in. Even the silliness of this film works so well– calling Sakharine "a sour-faced man with a sugary name" and giving him the pseudonym of "Shuggair Addeitiff?" Spielberg making a movie with a villain that looks like himself? Wonderful. Joyous. I live for this shit. Please cancel every non-Tintin project and put Peter Jackson to work on the sequel right now.

But when their plane crashes in the mountains , they find themselves in a battle against nature and some hungry wolves. Both Reeve’s and Arquette are good together, a little trivia it turns out Reeve’s could really fly . Holding several different flying license, which allowed him to do a lot of flying in film. I didn't know this film existed until recently and was excited to see a movie starring Christopher Reeve ... and directed by none other than George 'Mad Max' Miller. And then I checked Wikipedia while watching the movie and realised this was actually directed by a DIFFERENT Australian director also named George Miller. I couldn't believe it - what are the chances? At least Paul Hogan and P J Hogan, while both being Australians, were at least on different sides of the lens. No, this is George T. Miller, who had directed the well received Man From Snowy River a year before.

reviews.author: Wilson
reviews.text: The Aviator is a likeable film. It isn't particularly a good one, but it is an affable watch. Christopher Reeve and Rosanna Arquette star. He is an Air Mail pilot and she is his first passenger since he killed the last one (the film's prologue). She is rich. He is taciturn. They crash. It turns into an adventure film. It Happened One Night...after a plane crash. The film is neither rom-com, nor action film, but somewhere between both. It is a brisk 90 minutes and I like both Reeve and Arquette a lot, so I am giving it a pass, mostly, but it isn't really worth seeking out.

reviews.author: The Great Owl
reviews.text: File this one under “late 1960s drive-in movie that is so utterly wrong that it comes full circle and is right again.” A deputy district attorney is on the verge of a major career-making case against a murderer from a motorcycle gang while he drifts with bored resignation through an unsatisfying home life with his nagging wife, who is more obsessed with bridge games and dinner parties than she is with spending time with him. Enter Patricia Wymer as a teenage babysitter who seduces the district attorney, acquaints him with her freewheeling rock ‘n’ roll hippie lifestyle, and breaks up the monotony of his existence.

reviews.author: AuteurTheory
reviews.text: I don't know what I'm getting into, I've just had this Mill Creek Grindhouse collection sitting around for ages. All I know is this movie apparently had a sequel, which seems odd. _______________________________________For a shitty, 1969 exploitation film, the transfer is surprisingly clear- especially the audio. The look and aesthetic of The Babysitter is kind of like a perverse 1950s sitcom. Darkness and even violence lurk just around the edges of this average American household. There's a swastika reveal that shocked me. Look, I don't want to give this movie too much credit, but... I found myself thinking about Blue Velvet. There is some legitimate artistry hidden inside this softcore sleaze. According to letterboxd the director and cinematographer barely worked again, which is a shame. They had some real talent.

reviews.author: Mike Thorn
reviews.text: It's really not about the hapless leading couple at all. It's about the sleek but sinister edifice of modernity, literally built on the remains of recent atrocities. This modernity is physicalized by the great Karloff and his nouveau-Expressionist mansion, constant reminders of Lugosi's not-so-latent trauma. If these characters imagine their pre-WWI worlds as idyllic, even Edenic, then it only makes sense that The Black Cat veers finally into the Satanic. Look elsewhere for subtlety.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: A total creative coup to take the traditionally gothic setting of horror from this era and replace it with sleek, ubermodern architecture and decor. You can modernize your exterior and build over your atrocities, but evil is evil, evil persists. Supernatural? Possibly. Baloney? Possibly not. Nestled between WWI and WWII, this seems at once prophetic and reflective in its depiction of human souls ravaged by war, decades old grudges bubbling to the surface and causing collateral damage. When Ulmer lets the camera wander through the building as Beethoven plays on the soundtrack and Karloff orates, he's showing his filmmaking is just as modern as the architecture.

reviews.text: When blaxploitation films add Black to the title of a known property, like Blackenstein or Blackula - the films themselves usually have unique takes on the source material. Not so with Black Cobra, which is just the Sylvester Stallone film Cobra (1986) - if it was starring Fred Williamson. Minor variations including an embarassing Dirty Harry rip, and a total lack of sexual tension. Following the paint by number imitation, the Italian crew have made one of the stronger Williamson starring vehicles - but I spent the entire runtime appreciating how much better the Stallone film is. For these misgivings, I wish they had remade other Stallone films using the naming convention... Black Oscar would have been amazing.

reviews.text: 'The Black Cobra' is an okay Italian cop actioner with Fred Williamson fighting a biker gang directed by Stelvio Massi. I have yet to see a good Massi movie but this one had its moments.Fred's tough cop in the vein of Stallone's Cobretti and Dirty Harry is fun and it's nice that they gave him a pet cat. I also liked some scenes in the first half in which the biker gang terrorizes a couple on the beach (sadly it doesn't really go anywhere, but there was potential) and one where they break into a hospital to kill a witness. There is some action and violence but Massi once again can't quite pull it off well enough and it couldn't keep my attention in the third act. Fred would have deserved some better movies in the 80s but it's entertaining enough to hear him quote Clint Eastwood speeches almost word for word.

It's an honourable thing to do, but I'm not sure it's necessary. Every history is partial, every history smooths away edges and leaves things out, every history reflects the priorities of the people who put it together. reviews.author: triz
reviews.text: Realizado em 2011 pelo sueco Göran Olsson, “Black Power 1967-1975” é um pedaço de história, mais concretamente a história dos E.UA. e a sua relação com os seus cidadãos negros. Nas décadas de 60 e 70, uma equipa de jornalistas suecos viajou para os E.UA. para acompanhar as questões raciais da época. O material gravado tinha como propósito único o de ser exibido na televisão sueca. Assim foi e assim ficou esquecido durante mais de três décadas na cave da Sveriges Radio, a rádio pública do país. O espanto de Olsson ao se deparar com rolos e rolos de filmagens em 16mm foi tanto que, segundo ele, não teve outra escolha senão divulgar estes tesouros até então caídos no esquecimento.…

reviews.author: brotherdeacon
reviews.text: A capitalist media-widget designed to make money on the historical hipness of Black revolt. This information has long been public, with little to no serious change in the community. Celebrities, fashion and music may dress it up for 2011, but the disease of evolutionary amnesia will always win out. This is about as pertinent today as another re-issue of Woodstock, or better yet Wattstax (a more impressive film). To be lulled to complacency by history as mere data and myth is to spit on the graves of its martyrs.

reviews.text: Bei "Die Augen des Satans" handelt es sich um einen Science-Fiction-Film, der eine Alien-Invasion thematisiert. Die Gefahr geht dabei nicht von einer gesamten außerirdischen Spezies aus, sondern nur von einem Abtrünnigen. Dieser terroristische Abweichler hat die Gestalt eines fliegenden Gehirns, die Erscheinung ist dabei halbdurchsichtig und kann Anpassungen bezüglich Größe vornehmen. Nachdem das Gehirn die Befehlsgewalt über Körper und Geist eines Wissenschaftlers übernommen hat, demonstriert das Alien seine überlegene Stärke. Regisseur Nathan Juran spielt in "Die Augen des Satans" wie in den 1950er-Jahren üblich mit den Ängsten des Publikums und behandelt damals aktuelle Sorgen um Invasion und nukleare Zerstörung unter dem Deckmantel einer Science-Fiction-Geschichte. Die Spezialeffekte sind zwar besonders in Bezug auf das Gehirnwesen eher kostengünstig ausgefallen, doch die Besessenheit…

The camerawork also seems more fluid and leering than you usually get in these kinds of movies, and some of the images are impressively freakish. reviews.author: ChrisStuckmann
reviews.text: Rewatched this because Ben Stiller was a guest on David Duchovny’s new podcast Fail Better. He discussed how his “failure” with this film shaped his career. And indeed, I didn’t really like this movie all that much as a teenager because I wanted more of the Ace Ventura, Liar Liar brand of Jim Carrey. But it’s funny because all these years later, this plays like a highly original, unique blend of comedy and thriller, with an absolutely unhinged Jim Carrey in the title role. Stiller also shows early knack for visual ingenuity with a series of off-the-wall sequences such as the karaoke scene, or the hilarious Medieval Times fight. If you just watched Baby Reindeer and want something that’s in the same vein but lighter, this is it.

reviews.text: Retro futuristic aesthetics of a nightmare in total peril. Idle and abstract thoughts linger in dirty steampunk passages among rats and trash, a reverie of pensive agitation and isolation. An odyssey for a warped dream in beguile as they pursue such a phantasm of the core to the nightmare, every unique frame manifests of horror and an anomalous light of empathy. An insidious presence he reigns, a malaise for inept dreaming, a childish immaturity that spells doom in the realms of nonautonomy - one final dream to bring rapture.

This is a rather clumsy mix of slasher, psychological horror and supernatural elements. After the brutal opening, the film slows down to a snails pace. There's always plenty going on in terms of atmosphere, but not so much in terms of actual plot. The mystery with regards to the killer's identity is not difficult to guess, but Walker throws a few red herrings…

It's a testament that these nuts and bolts horror films have more going for them than most modern incarnations with their overdone special effects and elaborate, over obsessive plunging into the why and how of their monster's mythology. A shadow where it's not supposed to be still trumps all.

reviews.author: Sean Fennessey
reviews.text: Best first watch of 2021 so far. This had been a gap for a long time and its standing as a breathless, relentless visual orgy easily overwhelmed its reputation as a "shocking" studio production. Derek Jarman was still in his twenties when he created a production design that collided modernist style into a baroque 17th century French setting. Oliver Reed is in his terrifying but in the good way phase, symbiotic with Ken Russell on their fifth feature together. Russell's frantic whip-pans and high-angled framing of omniscient power and punishment irradiate Vanessa Redgrave's mad-eyed performance as Sister Jeanne, the scorned, manipulated tool of the church, to make this hysteria cinema at its most unrestrained. It's fun! (Michael Gothard as the zealot Father Barre is going for it bigger and more fearlessly even than Reed.) It's also a tidy artifact of false panic. Nude nuns, licentious priests, and ritual torture. Imagine that.

reviews.text: This film asks its viewers a difficult question. Can you truly look beyond the physical? See someone for who they are, not what they look like. In maybe his most accessible film, Lynch manages to tackle this subject with great skill, skirting the melodramatic here and there, but never getting preachy. He manages to get stunning performances out of Hopkins and, especially, Hurt. His performance is incredible. The humanity he manages to portray underneath those enormous amounts of make-up is breath taking. Lynch keeps everything sober, emphasised by the gorgeous black and white cinematography and allows his two leads to unfold a brilliant story about friendship, love and the human soul. It is a wonderful fairytale you should have seen at least once, in my humble opinion.

reviews.text: I described "Conan the Destroyer" as PG-for-1984, well, "The Golden Voyage of Sinbad" is rated G-for-1973, so Caroline Munro's wardrobe is barely there and Tom Baker's evil wizard draws blood from his arm to make liberal use of "the demons of darkness." John Phillip Law, of "Barbarella" and "Danger: Diabolik" fame, stars as the titular sailor, and he certainly looks the part of a matinee idol, but the real star here is Ray Harryhausen's dynamite stop-motion animation. I was particularly impressed by the creatures made of wood and metal, as Harryhausen goes out of his way to capture their distinct textures, and you better believe I was thinking the six-armed, sword-swinging Kali statute was like a Dark Souls boss.

reviews.text: I wasn’t prepared for how punishing The Great Silence would be. This is probably the bleakest Western I’ve ever watched. From the moment it begins, it establishes a world that is cold in every sense. The snow-covered setting isn’t just unusual for a Western; it feels like a deliberate rejection of the genre’s usual warmth and openness. Optimism barely has a chance to exist here. Everything feels harsh, stripped-down, and deeply cynical about the idea that the West was ever a place where justice naturally emerged.

Playfully black crime novels, so increasingly grim one can't help but smile - which remind me at times of Fargo (a comparison made more cartoonishly clear by the brilliant Tardi graphic adaptations). I can understand why Sean Penn might be attracted to the role of Martin Terrier - as the source material is a compelling character study of a tough guy stereotype that slowly unravels into a no longer posturing clown. The Prone Gunman could have been something special... instead we're left with palette swap Taken.

We have some nice locations here and they even travel to Hong Kong but really what makes this film is Castellari giving a balls to the wall mainly constant action movie that looks solid. Sure it lacks a little on the dialogue and it's not the strongest or most original of stories but it really does just giver. I think my favourite shot was when Fabio uses a corpse as a stick to get a gun and I call that thinking outside the box to bring us a memorable moment. That and a few inventive action scenes make this one to track down and enjoy if you like your action flicks. Thanks Keith G for the recommendation.

It runs a little long at over two hours, but I dunno… overdoses, jail breaks, Interpol, warehouse shootouts, David Hemmings, car chases, slow motion deaths, Fabio Testi, subway chases, and that insane airplane sequence… The Heroin Busters has no shortage welcomed eurocrime calamity and that’s exactly what I was in the mood for.

reviews.author: Flynch
reviews.text: Budget war nicht viel vorhanden, das Drehbuch war wahrscheinlich auch ziemlich dünn, aber Regisseur Enzo G. Castellari (Keoma; Riffs; Racket; Metropolis 2000 und noch viele andere) schafft es hier, uns die ganze Laufzeit bei Laune zu halten. Die (grausig, lustige) Kleidung der 70er, der italienische Duft vergangener Tage, Ex-Stuntman Fabio Testi führt viele seiner Stunts selbst durch, die Synchro ist herrlich politisch inkorrekt, und das letzte Drittel ist eine einzige Verfolgungsjagd zu Fuß, per Auto und Motorrad und zuletzt wird sogar waghalsig durch die Lüfte verfolgt. Und für die Ohren ist auch bestens gesorgt, denn die Gruppe Goblin steuert einen wirklich famos treibenden Soundtrack bei.Achja, David Hemmings (Blow up; Profondo Rosso) ist auch dabei.Alles in allem nicht der beste, aber auf alle Fälle ein über dem Durchnitt liegender italienischer Output.Für Freunde italienisch rasanter Unterhaltung, Undercover-Cops und speziell für jene, die Gefallen an der Mode der 70er finden.

It's really the best part of the entire film, which is a convoluted tale of cops trying to break up an international heroin ring.

Enzo G. Castellari brings his usual eye for composition and well staged action. A chorusy bass and bongo heavy Goblin jam over the soundtrack. David Hemmings angers a prostitute! reviews.text: Der Pilotfilm zur leider nach neun Episoden wieder eingestellten Serie. Wenn ich mich recht entsinne, wegen zu hoher Produktionskosten. Und die Serie hatte auch einiges zu bieten. Nicht nur, dass der Held mit einem futuristuschen Truck, aus dem sich ein Helikopter auskoppeln kann, über die Highways fährt, die Serie hat auch storytechnisch immer ein gewisses Science Fiction- oder Mystery-Element, das jede Folge zu einem ganz besonderen Erlebnis macht. Im Pilotfilm beschränkt sich dieses Element allerdings lediglich auf den Truck und den mystifizierten Highwayman selbst. Der Rest ist im Grunde typisches 80er Actionserien Material, wie es auch von A-Team o.ä. stammen könnte. Sam Jones verkörpert den Verbrecherjäger aber zusätzlich noch als herausragend coolen und über allem stehenden Kerl, den kein Wässerchen trüben kann. Ich hab die Serie immer wahnsinnig gerne gesehen und hadere heute noch damit, dass es nur neun Episoden wurden. Wenigstens eine schöne DVD Veröffentlichung könnte man uns doch mal spendieren.

reviews.text: I have never seen a war film quite like The Hill. For a start, there is almost no war in it, but that doesn’t make it any less brutal. I love how Sidney Lumet strips military life down to heat, dust, sweat, hierarchy and punishment, turning a British military prison in the Libyan desert into a pressure cooker where Army discipline has become indistinguishable from sadism. And like all the best prison dramas, it is really a study of power: who has it, who craves it, who hides behind it and who is destroyed by it.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: A forgotten gem of Lumet’s catalogue, a prison drama that enunciates the genre’s typical themes — crime and punishment, claustrophobia, man’s capacity for cruelty — with outstanding cinematography by Oswald Morris. The camerawork isn’t necessarily flashy — very little about Lumet’s work is — but it’s marvelously expressive, especially its treatment of “The Hill,” a giant mound of dirt in the middle of a British prison camp used to punish inmates who get out of line. It looms in the background of some shots, and serves as a perch to look down at the camp at other times, like an unfeeling deity is observing the proceedings. Plus, there’s plenty of subjective POV shots of the men going up and down the hill…

reviews.author: Lowe McKee

"Heat exhaustion," the Sergeant Major tells the doctor in a manner so indifferent you'd think he was talking about the weather.

reviews.text: Director Sidney Lumet is brilliant, and although this wasn't my favourite war movie, it was a very interesting take. Set during WW2 in a North African prison camp, a group of young British men are being held for a few offences, mainly being AWOL. They are tortured day after day in the hot sun, forced to run drills and exercises including running up and down "the hill". What's so unique is the fact that these men are being tortured by their own, something I hadn't thought about during war times. It also features a young Sean Connery who did a fabulous job along with the rest of the cast who apparently suffered as well in the hot Spanish sun during filming. It's an enjoyable film for sure, and one to watch for those seeking something different.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Directed by Peter Fonda, after the enormous financial success of Easy Rider, The Hired Hand has a free-spirited screenplay by Alan Sharp together with some attractive cinematography by Vilmos Zsigmond (The Deer Hunter). It features a touching performance from Verna Bloom and is fundamentally a revisionist western which sees Fonda, who also plays the exhausted drifter Harry Collings, withholding the typical genre tropes to capture the sensitivities of the narrative. This was an under-appreciated movie upon its initial release, and it’s all underpinned beautifully by a melancholy score from Bruce Langhorne.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Peter Fonda’s first film is unique among westerns of the time allowing his very personal psychodrama and exploration of his own body (this is very much an actor’s first feature, its true subject Fonda himself) to be informed by the 19th century setting but not much interested in genre tropes. Vilmos Zsigmond cinematography (one of his best) and the length dissolves still allow it a certain mythic status. The buddy movie dynamics is very much of its time (it is a romantic triangle in which poor Verna Bloom is set to finish way last) but Fonda and Warren Oates allow it to be realized with strong physical presence. The world here has a very Hellman like quality, the unattainable of everyone desires plays off in a harsh physical existence.

reviews.author: DallasFrance
reviews.text: The Hired Hand has a gorgeous Bruce Langhorne score and stunning cinematography-even by Vilmos Zsigmond’s standards. I’d give it four stars just for the opening scene! There’s a bizarre love triangle consisting of a Peter Fonda/Warren Oates bromance and Fonda’s deserted wife, played by Verna Bloom. Fonda never gazes as longingly into Bloom’s eyes as he does Oates, and Miles’ fortitude is wasted on a wobbly man.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: This opens with a dazzling view of a sparkling river that eventually draws back to show a wide landscape. This builds to a scene where three cowboys hook the body of a dead girl, marring the earlier beauty and suggesting this film's deconstructive agenda. (The body is never brought up again; it's just part of the landscape.) Full of cross dissolves, this film is intent on blurring moments together, fusing people, places into single images, reminding you of the transition of time, of change.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: A very 1970's New Hollywood western with strong Women's Liberation and Sexual Revolution vibes. Peter Fonda and Warren Oates were on a journey out West until their younger companion was shot and killed in a small border town. They decide to return to the farmstead where his ex-wife Verna Bloom lives, but she doesn't want him back, so they offer to work as hired hands. The emotional core is built around the question of whether or not Fonda and Bloom will get back together, whether they can return to their previous peaceful domestic life, a question which encounters two primary obstacles.

Harry (Peter Fonda), a drifter, returns home to Hannah (Verna Bloom), his understandably bitter wife, only to be drawn back to his old life thanks to the intensity of his relationship with Arch (Warren Oates), the man he's ridden with for his seven years. The story is not complex, but it is told beautifully with maturity and dignity. Its treatment of Hannah is incredible. Honda, in the director's chair,…

reviews.author: nathaxnne [goodbye <3]
reviews.text: Four stories in a House Of Horrors brought to you by Amicus Productions and writer Robert Bloch! Might you be: A writer haunted by their creation? A strangely familiar and alluring wax Salome in a Museum Of Horror? A cold and distant man scared of little girls? An aging horror star digusted with the cheap and inauthentic horror films of the modern era? If you answered Yes to any of the above you are more than likely to be found in The House That Dripped Blood! Of these stories, all are good or great. My favorite has Ingrid Pitt in a self-reflexive role! The Cushing in the wax museum is probably the best one, with eerie and lurid lighting. By setting all of the tales in one house, it was not only cost-effective, but added to the overall coherence of the movie, far greater than what might be expected from an anthology. Hail Amicus Portmanteau Horror! Hail!

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This is how you do an anthology horror film! The House That Dripped Blood puts the focus on the house itself. We begin with a Scotland Yard investigator looking into the disappearance of a famous horror movie actor, which leads him to an estate agent who regales him with four stories concerning the fate of the last four tenants. We get vampires, witchcraft, waxworks and a writer tormented by his own creation. It's all high camp in the usual Amicus style, but it's also exceptionally well produced. The stories themselves, written by Robert Bloch, are distinct and very well paced - neither feeling rushed nor outstaying their welcome. They share the location in common but they all have something outstanding…

reviews.text: This is my favourite Amicus film. Just by a hair though, as they have others that are exceptional also, especially From Beyond The Grave. A rare feat with an anthology film in that I love every tale here equally. From the creepy opening one, to the solemn, beautifully lit second with Peter Cushing, to evil kid section with my favourite part from Christopher Lee "Educational toys, not this!" and finally the humourous one with Jon Pertwee in his element as an egotistical horror film star making a really fun double act with Ingrid Pitt. With there just being 4 stories over 100 mins it doesn't have the rushed feel some can have, all are fleshed out wonderfully and could see how a couple of them coulda been feature length. The cast is great all round and a nice fun ending. Perfect candlelit October film.

reviews.author: Nakul
reviews.text: Robert Siodmak’s THE KILLERS is undeniably a classic film noir, and rightly regarded as one of the genre's best. Based on the short story by Ernest Hemingway. Hemingway actually credited the film for being “the only good picture ever made of a story of mine”. Delightfully engaging to watch. It's a masterful exercise in non-linear storytelling, filled with compelling characters. The suspenseful bravura of the opening sequence grabs you by the throat. Opening scenes reveal a world of strewn bodies and moody desolation as Dr. Robert Morgan (Vincent Price) goes about his daily routine of material repair (broken the previous night by vampiric hordes), weapon construction, and body disposal (that burning pit is searingly memorable). Accompanied by Price’s narrative overlay, the matter-of-factness of it all works beautifully, notwithstanding the annoyance of the film’s oppressively ubiquitous and largely unnecessary soundtrack. The film stumbles mightily in its flashback to pre-plague conditions,…

reviews.text: Dr. Robert Morgan wakes up once again to a bleak existence. His waking words are "another day to live through...let's get started." He spends his days disposing of corpses in a tremendous fire pit, scavenging for food, and trying to figure out where the plague touched ghouls hide in the day time killing them as they sleep. He spends his nights trying to find a cure while contemplating what it is that allows him to live while everyone else has become the walking dead.…

reviews.text: Clearly a sprawling epic, the set pieces are brilliant, and the scenery is breathtaking. Tom Cruise is Tom Cruise, and that is always a plus. Unfortunately, it is limited by the overuse of cliches—a story about the Samurai honour code and integrity that was clearly manufactured through the Hollywood system. Not to say it's disrespectful, but the tone feels a little off and over-romanticised. I also just think it’s a little dull at times. It does, however, manage to strike a pretty good balance between grand size and intimacy, and it definitely contains one of Zimmer's best scores. I had a decent time, but I don't think I'll be watching it again anytime soon.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Takes off like a rocket from zero to absurd. I went up to meet it at its own level, then it threw on the brakes and delivered one of those wonderful cinematic moments that stops time and momentum all together. It's a sequence involving two characters, some gauze, and a glass of J&B. It doesn't advance the plot, but it does serve as a reminder that movies are the greatest. It's about one character watching another perform, the kind of scene Jess Franco and David Lynch make sure to throw into nearly every single one of their movies. ...So I'm already doing joyous mental back flips by the time the aquatic sex scene that's shot, edited and scored like a spaghetti western hits the screen. Everything that came after that was just icing on the cake (puns mostly not intended). This is one wonderful, opulent piece of Eurotrash. I want to live in it.
