reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: Holy wow! The Laughing Woman is all kinds of magical! I've wanted to see this for ages. It looked right up my alley. I expected (and wanted) sleazy, super-psychedelic 60s Euro trash, and yes, this has all the sensory delights of a quality slab of Italian scuzz. There's nudity abound, a funky-as-fuck score, and lots of kinky sex stuff. But The Laughing Woman is also quite brilliant in its aesthetic execution and the jaw-dropping sexual power play between its leading "couple". This is a film that does several sneaky backflips in tone and I loved it for it. Its perfectly mad ending had me high-fiving my television with glee. This really deserves to be more widely seen. Criterion, can you please release this? Thanks.

For a long time, dysphoria made these feelings off-putting; pre-transition, my body danced differently with this kind of imagery. For a long time, I found it frustrating to see my fantasies so nearly displayed; masculine presence always denied me full immersion. Until I experienced a taste of my fantasies, these images seemed unreachable. Though there are many fantasies I have yet to indulge, even just a taste of them is enough to change my experience. reviews.text: I find it very hard to not watch this movie whenever I stumble across it (it’s currently on Netflix). As the years pass, I realize it is very close to my Platonic ideal of a Hollywood entertainment: Everyone is gorgeous and witty, and in every scene people are flirting or fighting or both. Most movies are lucky to have one actor at the top of their game. Zorro has Antonio Banderas, Catherine Zeta-Jones, and Anthony Hopkins all at their absolute peak. Plus, you have Martin Campbell behind the camera, one of the most dependable action directors of the last 30 years. It’s all pure pleasure. And why don’t more superheroes wear shirts with deep v-necks to expose their prodigious chest…

reviews.text: Fred ‘The Hammer’ Williamson films are so macho and testosterone filled that merely watching them will probably make your balls grow by two sizes. After blaxploitation fell out of fashion in the States, Williamson simply took his act on the road, with Italy being especially responsive to his talents. Perhaps because it got left behind in the VHS era and as far as I can tell never made it to DVD or Blu, The Messenger tends to get overlooked in favour of the Black Cobra series or his post-apocalyptic movies, when it comes to talking about Fred’s ‘eye-talian’ period.

It retains the camp synonymous with the brand, but they really pushed the boat out with the style and atmosphere - so many sets bathed in beautiful lighting. The Mummy's tomb and a swamp in the UK moorland being particular highlights. The story, which focuses on a group of archaeologists who ignore warnings and proceed to desecrate an Egyptian tomb, brings with it an interesting debate on the morality of doing such a thing. The film is essentially a collision between the ancient world's archaic beliefs, and the misunderstanding of the modern world, seeing everything as ripe for the taking. I loved that intro, but unfortunately, it strays too far from horror and more into an adventure flick, which honestly feels dated in its execution. It's just all over the place with what it strives to be, but at least you get a sometimes theatrical Heston performance, which makes up for any wrongdoing, and he easily anchors this film a whole lot. reviews.author: Deckk
reviews.text: 100-word review: The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes is a charming curiosity in Billy Wilder’s filmography, still carrying his graceful comedic touch here and there, even if more muted than usual. A Sherlock Holmes adaptation should, in theory, be fertile ground for Wilder’s trademark verbal sparkle, but here the humour feels intentionally softened, and the mystery at its core resolves with less satisfaction than one might expect from a Holmes tale. Yet that slight deflation seems to be the point: Wilder is more interested in the detective’s inner life, vulnerabilities, and blind spots (hence the title) than in a neat puzzle-box ending.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Of all the ’90s movies critics got wrong, this one might be their worst blunder. Even after I fell in love with Sam Raimi I waited a long time to watch this, mostly because it had been beaten into me that this was a shallow, superficial, melodramatic Western. In fact, it’s got one of the decade’s deepest casts — including Gene Hackman, Leonardo DiCaprio, Tobin Bell, Lance Henriksen, Keith David, Gary Sinise, Woody Strode, Pat Hingle, Mark Boone Junior, and a fabulous pre-L.A. Confidential Russell Crowe — plus a script full of sharp frontier dialogue, and Raimi applying all of his coolest camera tricks to Western gunfights. What’s not to love? Maybe people were just sick of Sharon Stone by 1995? (I seem to recall people turned on her around this time, but this is one of her better performances.)

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: I get the accusations of this as a shallow technique/pastiche exercise for Raimi but I don't care. His overly dynamic, exaggerated comic-book visuals punching up these particular archetypes and iconography is just a total blast to watch in action. Every extreme dutch close-up, or rapid-cut zoom hits in exactly the way it should and the organizing structure of a ridiculous gunslinging tournament keeps it constantly moving. It’s like a sped-up movie geek cartoon of Leone and Eastwood in the best way possible and the cast is so game for its gruesome-silly tone. Genuinely lost count of how many things it cribs directly from Once Upon a Time in the West and High Plains Drifter, and if you told me Hackman walked off the set of Unforgiven and directly onto this one I’d believe you.

reviews.text: When I was a ten-year-old brat I watched this movie on tv. The next day I found out from some of my classmates that they also watched it. We loved it so much that we copied the dueling competition from the movie. We would spend our breaks pretending to be gunfighters, holding duels, standing in front of each other and drawing our pens from our pockets. Whoever draw the pen faster would win. We each had our name inspired from the movie, like The Ace, The Boss, The Kid, Scars... well not Scars, no one wanted to be Scars! He was ugly and he stank! I was The Priest. I was pretty fast.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: The Searchers gives the lie to the supposed heroism of the Wild West mythos. John Wayne plays the same Indian-killing cowboy we've seen him play since the early 1930's, the image of a valiant savior come to rescue a bunch of white folks from the Native American menace, but here he plays it as explicitly racist, calling out the pathological nature of the traditional cowboy's racialized violence. Our heroes of the West were always outlaws who had to ride off into the sunset, but they were glorified outcasts, they were getting rid of the "real" bad guys. The Searchers shows this hero not as an altruistic warrior, but as a murderer whose positive effects on society are less purposeful, more…

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: Psychological epic on the psychology of racism, fascinating in dialectic with Griffith's Birth Of A Nation: racism as the product of fear of losing sexual superiority and the fear of race-mixing. Key that Ethan is pro-Confederacy: Martin fears Ethan wishes to kill Debbie but doesn't know why, Ethan fears Debbie has been 'contaminated,' resolves to kill her after learning she has become Scar's wife. Logically this should have no bearing, but for Ethan it's all about preserving the bloodline. One of the most damning indictments of American culture: and the extent that racism is fundamental to the conservative American psyche.

reviews.text: A visual and aural quest into the most mystical corners of Irish folklore. Possibly the most flawlessly animated film of 2009, though it's hard to tell in a year containing Coraline, Up, The Fantastic Mr. Fox, Mary and Max, Nine and A Town Called Panic as well. The story here is a beautiful and meaningful one, exploring themes such as the unknown and loss of innocence. Two scenes in particular, one that begins with a soft voice and another that begins with a flaming arrow, send this film up from being very good to a level of greatness. It takes quite an imagination to build a world so very wondrous and fantastical, so my hat is off to the filmmakers.…

reviews.text: A webbed and gnarled translucent watercolor sword and sorcery pastoral, furious with movement and activated Newtonian Alchemies. One of the jewels of the Annus Mirabilis 1982, The Secret of NIMH plays out like a crazed post-Disney, post-Rankin/Bass brew of Altered States and the Planet of the Apes TV shows. In the shadow of human civilization, the United States Government has given rats the capacity to use magickal and non-magickal technologies apparently not extant in un-DARPA'ed rat theories of global operations. This is the birth of the end of humankind's assumed hegemonic grasp on this world. Also, John Carradine as the most hypnotically terrifying animated owl ever.

reviews.text: An intriguing oddity rescued from oblivion by Mondo Macabro – not the voodoo horror/sexploitation film you might expect from the poster and synopsis. It's a fabulist melodrama that plays out at a languid pace. What I particularly liked about the Snake God is its poetic vibe and beautiful visuals (sharply edited by Bava regular Carlo Reali). Plus Nadia Cassini and Beryl Cunningham are gorgeous. Vivarelli gives the film a political subtext, but thankfully avoids didactism. All in all, a pleasant find.

reviews.author: SeanAloysius
reviews.text: Uma novidade no front: nada de mais, mas ainda uma novidade. Só o ritmo e as passagens insinuantes de um suposto terror para o terreno leve, não tão diáfano, do erotismo soft (como diria nosso querido Totò: "softíssimo"), canteiro de obras discreto da descoberta. Fronteira cruzada quase sem percepção, sem solavancos naturais de estrutura ou de narrativa, onde se abraça de vez e sem cerimônias o sobrenatural - bem no limite de uma outra fronteira, dessa vez temporal, que vem se inscrever ali sobre a palavra "Fine". A partir daí, Destino incógnito, Destino interdito. Bonito e sem charme. Honesto e sem penduricalhos. Visto numa manhã de domingo, dessas sempre soterradas pelo desencanto da semana à espreita.

reviews.author: William Cooper
reviews.text: I know a movie is good when it's enjoyable to watch on Pluto TV, which, for me, is the worst streaming app ever created. Seriously, the number of ads they have in one single movie is borderline criminal. At this point, I'm not sure I'll ever watch another movie on there. With that said, I'm a sucker for the spy genre, and this is one of the best ever made. This actually feels like what it would be like to be a spy. Nothing glamorous, just a day to day web of lies where your life is always on the line and you never get credit or recognition for your work. It also features an incredible opening scene and a haunting final one. Definitely worth watching, just preferably not on Pluto TV.

reviews.author: Lowe McKee
reviews.text: Espionage deglamorized. What heroes? There is no right side, there are no good guys. Just replaceable cogs in the political machine. The institution you put your faith in? They’d sell you down the river if it benefited them. This isn’t do the right thing, its winner take all. The Spy Who Came In from the Cold is refreshingly acidic in its view of authority. Perceptive in its understanding of power. Incisive in its language. There’s a courtroom scene in this that is as thrilling as anything I’ve seen in the last year. Stark black and white photography of a world that exists in moral and political shades of gray. You know, like our world. It’s much more interesting and intelligent than most movies in the spy genre. More than most movies, period.

reviews.text: By the mid 60s, spy flicks had taken a turn away from the slow mystery-thriller towards the more Bond-like action films that we all know and enjoy. The Spy Who Came in from the Cold falls into the former category and is, therefore, quite rare for its time. Based on the novel by the same name written by former real life spy, John LeCarre, it takes a realistic approach towards its subject and depicts a clandestine operation in which our hero, MI6-agent Alec Leamas, is tasked with taking down his archenemy, a high-ranking Sovjet operative named, Mundt.

reviews.author: Tim Fehrenbach
reviews.text: “is your sword for hire?”The title almost feels like it’s naming the entire genre. And one look at the poster seals it, this is exactly what you think it is. At first, The Sword and the Sorcerer (1982, directed by Albert Pyun in his debut) just feels like pure B-movie nonsense, or maybe pure B-movie magic, I’m not even sure. Tangled dark fantasy lore and high-energy, all-over-the-place action, dramatic, gleefully campy performances, paired with crazy visuals and practical effects that feel carved out of some strange, half-formed fantasy dream. The plot is both generic and weirdly messy, like it’s constantly slipping out of your hands.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Albert Pyun gets in on the wave of medieval fantasy that was greenlit in the wake of Boorman's Excalibur (Conan, The Beastmaster, etc) and does it with all the low-budget charm and ambition you'd expect. Occasionally a bit goofy and dull but makes effective use of color and gore FX and it's clear Pyun is a genuine nerd and loves this stuff which takes the adventurous tone he's going for here further than it probably would otherwise... Many scenes have the R-rated gruesomeness of Conan but with the light adventure tone of Star Wars and it's quite weird and fun. He's also displayed in almost everything I've seen from him thus far a solid eye for action that is well beyond the budgets he was given and this did not disappoint. The slimy demon magician make-up in the opening/finale and the triple broadsword that projectile fires individual blades off like a crossbow are both insane and wonderful.

reviews.text: After “Reign of Terror” aka. “The Black Book” this was the second Period Film Noir from director Anthony Mann. That is a Film Noir movie that is set in a historical period, rather than the 1940s and 1950s. This one also falls into another sub-genre, the "Train Movie". It deals with a detective played by Dick Powell (and ironically named John Kennedy) trying to prevent an assassination attempt at Abraham Lincoln. I have to give it to Mann, he really picked interesting and unique subject matters for his Noir’s.

reviews.text: "The Tall Target" is a 1951 film directed by Anthony Mann. A crime noir placed in the novelty of a historical setting, "The Tall Target" follows a New York City Police Detective named John Kennedy who finds himself caught up in an assassination plot against Abraham Lincoln. Obviously, we know the inevitability that history would actually bring in that regard, but this film is situated even before his tenure of President, when he was still the President-elect. Situated on board the train running ahead of Lincoln's arrival, Kennedy finds himself crisscrossing through the realm of sabotage and saboteurs. Additionally, with the entry of Lincoln and other factors like the Civil War precursory atmosphere, Kennedy really has to be careful who…

reviews.author: noir1946
reviews.text: Anthony Mann’s The Tall Target is a wonderful example of how a terrific film can be made on a low budget with a so-so cast. We know from the beginning that New York cop John Kennedy (Dick Powell) will keep the newly elected Abe Lincoln (Leslie Kimmell) from being assassinated, but the way Mann and screenwriters Art Cohn and George Worthington Yates establish and maintain the suspense is sublime. With most of the action set in a few train stations, with one set probably doing multiple duty, and on a cramped train, creating a claustrophobic atmosphere, and cinematographer Paul Vogel (Lady in the Lake, Battleground) drenching everything in noir shadows, Tall Target is constantly visually arresting.

reviews.text: some of the largest sets you will ever see are in the thief of bagdad; palaces towering over our plucky thieves and lovers like orientalist skyscrapers, designed with intricate mandala patterns and cathedric light shafts, a perfect setting for high-adventure! a very early film from raoul walsh, who would later define himself as the king of two-fisted manly genre films, and he does a decent job here, although it's fair to say that the heavy-lifting of this adaptation is largely done by the aforementioned sets and special effects -- it's the spectacle of size, not necessarily what happens within that space. fairbanks' thief is an atheist in a world of genies and flying carpets, a man who scoffs at islam but uses an invisible cloak for his own romantic wiles. one can imagine that walsh, a practical man of action, keeps even his fantasies at a secular drawl.

Fairbanks is an absolute joy to watch on screen, never knowingly underacting, his bouncing, jumping, acrobatic thief is brilliant throughout. His physical performance (the man was in incredible shape) is the best special effect in the film. Though, a special mention is deserved for the irresistible Anna May Wong.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: It’s apparent right from the beginning that this is not a conventional war film. Adapted from the 1962 James Jones novel of the same name, screenwriter and director Terrence Malick concentrates on the consequences of war; there are no dramatic acts of courage and no proclamations of patriotism, instead it explores the notion that war is an exceptionally personal and isolating experience in which each soldier undergoes the subjective atrocities of war by himself. Seldom are war movies this lyrical and introspective, and this continues to endure as one of Malick’s culminating accomplishments.

reviews.text: I really didn't expect this movie to be this good. Richard Lester brings his top Hard Days Night energy to George McDonald Fraser's Flashman-style immaculate historical detail and flair for comedy, brought to life by a cast that is absolutely on the same wavelength and having a great time. An historical adventure romp. The comedy is character driven and never breaks the dramatic narrative. I loved the fight choreography - there is humor, but more than that, it feels so much more true to life than the usual Hollywood (or Hong Kong) fare. A sword fight is a messy, dangerous thing. I don't think anyone will ever beat Oliver Reed as Athos - has to be the perfect casting, there.…

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Richard Lester’s spirited adaptation of Alexandre Dumas’s timeless novel immediately distinguished itself from previous film versions with its irresistible lightheartedness. It follows the brash, young wannabe musketeer d’Artagnan (Michael York) as he travels from the French countryside to Paris and befriends Athos (Oliver Reed), Porthos (Frank Finlay), and Aramis (Richard Chamberlain), famed swordsmen whom he must help to stop the conniving Cardinal Richelieu (Charlton Heston) and his plot to undermine the king. The Three Musketeers sweeps viewers away with its exquisite sets and costumes, chivalric romance, and breathless duels punctuated by the ingenious physical comedy that was Lester’s trademark.

If only those live action epics had this lightning fast 85-minute runtime. Even the editing rhythms are the same, a blistering speed-run of wreckage with the "camera" careening from one graphic panel to the next. This beloved geek totem features any number of nonsensical narrative wild cards and cringe-inducing "comedic" interludes, like an impromptu dance sequence set to a Weird Al song, stuff that would be roundly condemned today by nerds who insist that a 300 million dollar toy commercial take itself seriously.

reviews.author: JJ Gittes
reviews.text: The neo-noir genre wouldn’t be what it is today without 1974’s ‘Chinatown.’ It was a film that should’ve changed Hollywood, a film composed of the very best 70’s filmmaking techniques in every respect. Watching that film is watching the creative peak of everyone involved (and by extension Hollywood and its entire culture), due to their individual passion for the subject matter and the close knit community that the film’s production was made up of. Suffice to say, a sequel would not only be unnecessary but would also take away from the ‘they-don’t-end-movies-this-way’ ending, which is why ‘The Two Jakes’ is a film people dismiss far too quickly. For one, practically no one has actually seen it, and it certainly doesn’t…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: An abject failure as a thriller, let alone as a sequel to CHINATOWN, for lots of reasons but mostly that it's just not really very dramatic; the adultery, the violence, the supposed intrigue...it all feels very not-dangerous. Maybe the point is that it's passe? Because on the other hand the continued chronicle of L.A. land rights here is actually fascinating, as if someone tried to make a throwback noir out of a chapter of Mike Davis' City of Quartz; this ends primarily with litigation. Shame they couldn't find a real director for it. Parts even feel a bit Coppola but I may be imagining that.

reviews.author: Colin the dude
reviews.text: The year is 1990. Paramount Pictures is releasing two controversial sequels to all-time classics both sixteen long years after their predecessors. THE TWO JAKES and THE GODFATHER PART III. On a surface technical level, cast level, both films meet the desired criteria. But both films also share the fatal flaw of stories that do not justify existing and if you wanted to be a stickler you could say that these films devalue the legacies of the originals but in this case the mythology of CHINATOWN is so looming and singular that THE TWO JAKES feel like a total afterthought. Gone with the wind.

reviews.author: Chris Cabin
reviews.text: One of those instances where Ebert was right on the money, right out of the gate. If the undergirding of everything in Chinatown was land, oil, water, and money, there is only spectacle left to prop up the dream of California here. The so-called bad acting is, in effect, deeply moving portrayals of people - greedy and conniving, well-meaning and righteous in equal measure - unable to keep up the show, unable to forget all the death, furious manipulation, financial destruction, and pain that led to, well, a dreamland destined to be shook from its axis and thrown toward the bottom of the ocean. Fracking and earthquakes are amazingly front-and-center here, underlining a critical sense of instability and grounded knowledge…

reviews.text: Steven Soderbergh is a favorite filmmaker, one who sparks terrific performances from his actors byway of the vivid intimacy with his camera; he even has a way of finding momentous granular energy in the way he lights and shades his characters within an environment; when it's working, we can see the secrets and motives of the people he's dealing us. Soderbergh has done so many different types of movies, studio flight or indie, that it's easy to go back and find one that you haven't seen, one that might have been brushed under the rug just waiting to be plucked for discovery. I thought The Underneath, a time-sliding flashback-laden film noir, would be a mischievous, giddy little pleasure. It's not.…

reviews.author: Dizzle_Sizzle
reviews.text: The second to last Elliot Davis collaboration prior to Soderbergh predominantly maintaining his Peter Andrews pseudonym as DP, this is as visually seminal as anything from Traffic onward via split diopter, dynamic palette shifts and so on. Aims to be an out-and-out update of Criss Cross in a revisionary, obviously neo-noirish sense but with this comes something palpably slow to build and only as good as what transpires. Everything from the ne'er-do-well fuck-up trope to the love interest and corresponding backstories feels arbitrary and stale in comparison to the twisty turny climax despite the integral posturing strategy in place, however a technical showpiece it certainly remains in light of said shortcomings.

reviews.text: Desire and physical damnation. Mario Bava starts with Fisher's Horror of Dracula, shifts the perspective from the avengers to the victim and twists the puritan hysteria towards a form of catholic torture every bit as perverse and masochistic. To give away to desire is to seek a form of self-anihilation. No one has ever painted in variations of black with such vivid detail.

reviews.author: Ian West
reviews.text: There's more knife than whip but that's fine because Bava does his usual creating a stylish, deliberately paced, gothic feast for the eyes via wonderful set design, stellar cinematography, and an an almost monochromatic color scheme mixed with his ever present manipulations of shadow. A deviant ghost lover, a castle complete with crypt and secret passageways, ghostly muddy footprints, an ominous beach, The Whip and the Body is quite the captivating story of love, denial, and S&M with Christopher Lee ramping up levels of sadistic scumbaggery in ways we may never seen from him prior.

reviews.author: Angelica Jade Bastién🪼🌷
reviews.text: Shadows so rich and deep you get lost in them. I don’t think I’ve seen shadows painted in the frame like this in a minute. This is a film that exemplifies how this medium treats, embodies, and obsesses over beauty: The splendid use of wide shots taking in the breadth of a vibrant sky and a lone figure dotted upon the horizon; Daliah Lavi’s yearning eyes and sharp cheekbones; a bold use of colors like volcanic red and cobalt grazing against the skin of characters; Christopher Lee’s eye and taut smile communicating an overflow of lust — for violence; the violence of a whip to an open back chased away with a surprising caress. Love can really fuck you up. Love remakes you. This film understands that.

reviews.text: THE WORLD IS NOT ENOUGH is one of those “better than the sum of its parts” movies. I don’t think it’s as bad as its rep, there’s a lot that’s stupid and clunky with plenty of cheese, but it works as a whole. Some really good action set pieces. Brosnan is a great 007 and Sophie Marceau is a wickedly fun as Electra King. Robert Carlyle is a boring villian & Denise Richards' is miscast, but the issue was both characters for the most part aren't even fleshed out & are entirely just there as a plot device. It's kinda visual bland at times, Brosnan's first two films were shot better. This one is the last Bond movie to have Desmond Llewelyn play Q before his death and him disappearing into the floor hits me right in the feels.

As we all know, the man has a wild imagination and his worlds are often colorful and have some surrealistic designs. This one follows that trend for some time, but there comes a point when even this gets excessive and I felt like I was watching a spy kid movie. Bald Christopher Waltz sits on a bench outside with a hat leaning 45 degrees, like those rappers of the 90s and early 2000s.

reviews.text: A Pat Rushin/Terry Gilliam stream of consciousness that jumps from concept to concept without hesitation, posing a multitude of questions which it knows it cannot answer. Tonally inconsistent (though not necessarily in a bad way), oddly acted (but which Terry Gilliam film isn't?), sharply written, well directed, visually stunning, and existential yet (anti?)nihilistic... basically an awesome fucking mess of a film. Spectacular at times, meandering at others. I was going to wait to write up anything on this one until I had some time to digest it, but now I'm not quite certain that there is anything to digest. Some will hail this film as a grand statement on humanity, and others will find it to be unbearably meaningless. I think I land somewhere in the middle.

Instead let's pretend to deconstruct that with a naive romance between a couple of wistful rubes, with a vague bookending murmur, never explored, about capitalism reaping what it sows. reviews.author: Jon Peters
reviews.text: It's Black Power versus White Power in what was advertised as “the biggest black action picture ever made” in Gordon Parks Jr.’s wild science-fiction espionage thriller wearing the blaxploitation coat in THREE THE HARD WAY (1974), the first of the three ultimate team-ups with the biggest blaxploitation male leads in Jim Brown, Fred “The Hammer” Williamson, and Jim Kelly. Not only does Monroe Feather (Jay Robinson), a leader of a secret white supremacist organization create a serum that when placed in the water supply will only affect and kill all the black Americans, as he announces, “it took God seven days to create the universe, and now it'll only take 3 days to end it”, they kidnap the girlfriend of…

reviews.text: Considering the prestige of the big titular three and Parks Jr. in the director’s chair, I had some real high hopes for Three the Hard Way. It didn’t quite live up to expectations, but there is still a lot to like here. The first half is by far the best as we establish Jim, Jim and Fred’s characters and the plot, which sounds ridiculous, but sadly is not outside the realm of possibility (and is in fact, in some ways, based upon real-life efforts). The movie then proceeds to drag itself towards its conclusion, with tons of the generic action one comes to expect from a ‘70s shoot-em-up. By the time things finally begin pick back up in a literally explosive finale,…

Stabbing a guy in his leg, little Owl makes a run for it while Thunder gets a kicking. Chasing the poor lad to his camp site, they all start getting a bit carried away, egging each other on and end…

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: By the third movie, Thunder is clearly not a guy to fuck with but those rednecks just can't help themselves. This time the First Blood storyline is thrown out in favour of something more along the lines of Burt Reynolds in Navajo Joe. A right-wing militia made up of bearded, fat dudes get drunk and destroy an Indian village. Thunder survives and goes on a rampage, burning down the businesses in town. In order to pull this off, the special effects guys use small models of buildings (with hilariously obvious toy cars out front) and set them on fire. Thunder also gets hold of a motorbike (as opposed to the Trans Am in Part 2) and jumps through a lot of explosions. Good stuff but maybe just a notch below the first two.

reviews.author: Scrambled Face
reviews.text: Still determined to turn Mark Gregory into an action star, producer/director Fabrizio de Angelis delivered this third and final serving of Native American payback. Last seen about to get murdered by sheriff Bo Svenson, Gregory's broody rebel Thunder looks miraculously unscathed, peacefully teaching a little kid their tribe's bow hunting traditions when they're interrupted by a white trash desert militia. These proto-Proud Boy idiots naturally escalate the confrontation by blowing up the little trailer park where Thunder lives and dragging him behind a truck. The (new?) sheriff (John Phillip Law) says he sympathizes with Thunder, but because the trigger-happy yokels are also the podunk town's most prominent citizens (of course they are), he won't try too hard to get them…

reviews.author: Curtis
reviews.text: Thunder III flushes the majority of the previous cast, leaving only Mark Gregory in his role as the titular warrior, constantly finding himself at odds with the most troublesome crackers.

reviews.author: Marty McKee
reviews.text: Hard to believe three THUNDER WARRIOR films exist, all directed in Arizona by Italian Fabrizio de Angelis and all starring Mark Gregory, the shaggy-haired hero of 1990: THE BRONX WARRIORS. In this one, rednecks blow up trailers belonging to local Navajos and drag Thunder (Gregory) behind a truck. Thunder barges into the office of sheriff John Philip Law (the DANGER: DIABOLIK star basically replacing Bo Svenson) and demands $56,000 restitution. Law is ineffectual, leaving Thunder to take the law (not Law) into his own hands. Cue the exploding miniatures and impossible stunts while Thunder busts up cars, burns down the general store, and disables police vehicles.

reviews.text: Thunder started as a straight riff on First Blood, but at this point in the series it’s almost like the filmmakers forget what film they are trying to emulate in between scenes. Miffed, Thunder (Mark Gregory) turns to local sheriff (John Phillip Law) for justice, but when the sheriff offers little, he sets off on a destructive, violent rampage blowing and shooting up everything in sight.

reviews.author: Francesco Chello
reviews.text: Perde qualcosina rispetto ai primi due, ma conclude coerentemente una trilogia che riesce ad avere una sua dignità in un mondo come quello dei rip-off nostrani non sempre all’altezza. Calca la mano sul razzismo e sul tema dei nativi americani, argomento (al di là dell’etnia) più che mai attuale. Le razzie e la successiva vendetta sono la scusa per portare in scena un po’ di caos e movimento tra incendi, esplosioni, una manciata di inseguimenti e qualche sparatoria. Gregory conferma l’impressione di una maggiore disinvoltura, la malinconia (reale) del suo sguardo si sposa con l’animo ribelle e tormentato del suo personaggio. John Phillip Law è il nuovo sceriffo.

reviews.text: You can see the differing perspectives that Terry Gilliam and John Cleese, the two opposite poles of Monty Python, brought to the group, and also the areas where their sensibilities overlapped, if you watch this in close enough proximity to Cleese's A Fish Called Wanda or Fawlty Towers. Gilliam is interested in mood, atmosphere, and visual texture, and not concerned with narrative propulsion. This movie is a series of loosely-connected vignettes, all individually stimulating, but which do not crescendo. As with a lot of Gilliam movies, this is a garden of delights that feels a little exhausting by the two-thirds point. Cleese is obsessed with plot, assembling his complicated scripts like a watchmaker, everything in its place. A rigorous logician,…

reviews.text: I’m not saying this is perfect or great, but to me this is pure science fiction. Every frame looks like the cover of a paperback sci-fi novel from a used bookstore. It’s so magically strange and yet so confident; it knows exactly what it is and what it has to be. Nothing makes sense, but it works so perfectly. The Rene Laloux universe is enormous, vibrant, tumultuous, awe-inspiring, and all-around beautiful. Nothing about the story or the characters will blow you away, but it’s so aesthetically fantastic that it barely matters.

reviews.author: Sacha
reviews.text: This film is so unlike anything I've seen Hollywood churn out recently that I was genuinely staggered. You have to concentrate. Hard. For the entire film. Alfredson gives you no easy routes, and you find yourself crossing your eyes in frustration. Is this a flashback? Is this guy dead? What's happening here? And yet despite how much effort you have to put in, the atmospheric approach makes it seem worth it. A malevolent, dreary London; a secret service turned corrupt bureaucracy. There are no James Bonds here, no glamour. Just paranoia, creeping cynicism, overwhelming nostalgia. Oldman's turn as Smiley is note perfect. Betrayed personally and professionally, doggedly pursuing the truth.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: "It was an aesthetic choice as much as a moral one. The West has grown so very ugly, don’t you think?" Bureaucratic barbarism, an empire on its deathbed, a movie about how state espionage is as tedious and soul-sucking as it is impotent and grisly. There are no more morals left to be eroded, no more heroes, just a bunch of weary sociopaths looking for any kind of aesthetic pleasure in a labyrinth of confusion and carnage. I hope this will get the best of the decade consideration it deserves.

As a result of her Spiderman play disaster, Julie Taymor has become synonymous with creative genius, yet a lack of control, which, when well executed, can result in an opulent and wonderfully epic version of one of Shakespeare's least discussed plays. In contrast, when the director overdoes it, the result is a catastrophe that borders on incomprehensible. In this case, both sides are fighting for supremacy.

reviews.text: In my very humble opinion, this is the best Shakespeare adaptation of the last thirty or so years save for maybe Kenneth Branagh's 1996 Hamlet. The cast is excellent, the soundtrack is gloriously garish, bombastic and eclectic and quite possibly Goldenthal's best, and the story is at once ludicrous and sobering and remains highly relevant in today's active and tragic lifestyles. Not to mention that the visual aesthetic and production design are absolutely to die for here and Julie Taymor does an impeccable job of using an old story to push the conventional filmmaking narrative to its absolute limit in terms of execution and rationality (shame she never did anything this brilliant again when it comes to her cinematic career). All in all, a glorious adaptation and a beautifully fucked up little parable for humanity. It's a shame that Steve Bannon was involved with this, though. A real fucking shame.

reviews.text: Are you a dreamer, or a non-believer? Do you have hope, or do you live in despair? Are you an optimist, or a pessimist? Is the glass half full, or half empty? Do you like Coke, or Pepsi? What if you could travel to a world that was full of endless possibilities? Would you seize the moment? Would you make a difference? For Casey Newton, a teenage girl with a rebellious streak, nothing is impossible. She still sees the good, and doesn't focus on the bad. After getting arrested for some criminal mischief; Casey finds in her possession a magic wings pin, that if touched by her, takes her to a place called Tomorrowland. It's a Disney movie, directed by…

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: The best argument for TOMORROWLAND is its release date; one week after MAD MAX: FURY ROAD, a film about a world destroyed by an oil war, and a week before SAN ANDREAS, in which an apocalyptic earthquake destroys half of North America. Less a blockbuster action film than a stern but well-intentioned lecture accompanied by an elaborate audiovisual presentation, TOMORROWLAND argues that rampant cynicism is actively poisoning our future. People become so convinced by movies like MAD MAX and SAN ANDREAS that the world is doomed that they start to believe it really is. So they give up, and dystopia becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. TOMORROWLAND tries, through sheer force of will and a heaping helping of bright, shiny special effects,…

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: Orson Welles’s final feature film on Hollywood soil manifests itself as an exercise in both technical and spiritual transcendence, in which American cinematic machinery becomes the instrument for the expansion of a genius. Never again would his inventiveness be so opulent, nor his imagination so perversely extravagant as in this film (in some ways, even more than Citizen Kane). It's an expressionist delirium, saturated with shadows, oblique angles, and formal excesses, transforming the melancholic nightmare of film noir into something vaster.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: That slow pull into Charlton Heston's face as he watches Joseph Calleia discover the evidence Orson Welles planted, the evidence they both know must have been planted, instead of focusing the camera on the evidence itself. This shot, and the way it silently depicts the crucial shift in Heston's character—a shift which is never again noted or commented on, but which forms the entirely of his motivation—merely by pointing the camera away from the action, this is pure cinema.

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: Hyper-masculine sleaze fest, swinging from point to point with little concern in the world but to radiate pure, overly-silly patriotic sentiments. But it’s so damn fun. Knows its strengths and uses them to the utmost extent; Sam Witwicky a rage-fuelled, neurotic moron with hilarious one-liners and audacious machine-clashing vivid spectacles. Plus, this one clearly intended to highlight treachery and post-catastrophe-driven paranoia in a more cruel form than the previous entries. The final hour is genuinely Bay at his most insane (Bad Boys 2-esque)—a true demonstration of how to end a Hollywood blockbuster in the most explosive manner possible—total Bayhem, you might say. But god, these films are so fucking funny too; full of personality and unbelievably idiotic lines, there's plenty to chuckle about. runtime could be considered a little long, but the final hour more than makes up for it.

reviews.text: The United States’ fear of communism is one of those historical chapters that never stops echoing. The Cold War was also fought in living rooms, in workplaces, and most viciously, in the imagination. Fear became a weapon, wielded not only against foreign adversaries but against American citizens themselves. Hollywood, oddly enough, turned into one of the main battlefields. The blacklist era shows how politics seeped so deeply into everyday life that creativity itself was policed, careers destroyed, and lives dismantled under suspicion alone.

reviews.author: nomenclature
reviews.text: An action hero tasked with protecting Vanessa Williams from arms dealers? My friend, the movie I speak of is not Eraser, but rather Under the Gun, preceding the former by a good eight years. So what do we got here, whatcha got: starts with hookers, skronking sax and an intro worthy of Final Fight, 8-bit industrial music, striking closeups, screeching synths, a neon sleaze motel, nutso shootouts, a crazed death scene, hot guitar lickery, rocket launchers, 'splosions, techno funk, synthpop, Windham Hill mood music, plutonium hidden in a Robotech lunchbox, a condom slingshot, a sneak attack set to "My Boyfriend's Back".....yup, we are firmly within in the bounds of 1988. Ends in a 20-minute action setpiece and the bad guy has a pencil mustache and pomade hair......yes. Heavy Fair Game vibes. Only loses points for being a little too meandering. I wholeheartedly endorse the moral of the story which is to never go to law school.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A film about how the "West" as a concept was largely a series of intersecting male insecurities, from penis anxiety to the overwhelming fear of losing a fight. The hero is a man with a past of ruinous, pointless violence who bettered himself only when he separated himself from his old pack and settled down with a woman who showed him another kind of life, and his aged wisdom of the evil of his old ways constantly nags at him when he sinks into old habits. Honestly, more revolutionary a revisionist western than I think an actual liberal could produce today, or at least certainly one less interested in blaring these themes as opposed to teasing them out with subtle elegance.

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: In the Antigone section of Barton Byg's book on Jean-Marie Straub and Daniele Huillet, Byg cites a 1992 Cahiers du Cinema cover feature which discussed Unforgiven and Antigone together. In Byg's text, he writes, "Both Antigone and Unforgiven present a frontier where the laws of civilization have lost their credibility." While there is a cogent comparison to be made between the two films in their specific modes of deconstruction, what Byg is saying here is only partially true - because he is really describing Antigone only and not Unforgiven. With the Eastwood film, it would make more sense to write, "Unforgiven presents a frontier where the laws of a genre has lost its credibility."

reviews.text: This is one of those films that, due to some kind of modern injustice, lives forgotten in the shadows. A few talk about it when the subject is vampirism, and when they do, the tone is always one of curiosity, never reverence. Which is a mistake, especially for those who, like me, delight in atmospheres heavy with surrealism, with bizarre gothic, with images that seem to escape time and logic, like a half-woken dream or a memory of something never lived. This film demands a specific kind of gaze, a gaze willing to get lost and not rush. A gaze that accepts not understanding.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Resolute barnburner in which the valley of the morally gray is populated by the righteous and the sadistic alike. Adrenaline is the atmosphere, justice is the justification, and satisfaction is the means to an end that tells the tyranny of evil men exactly what time it is. Lustig appropriately casts everyman Robert Forster as audience surrogate, and this visceral revenge yarn enters the stratosphere by taking the time to have him engage with do-as-I-say-not-as-I-do deuteragonist Fred Williamson, both men illustrating the thoughtful viewer’s anxieties in detail before striking down upon their adversaries with great vengeance and furious anger. Jay Chattaway’s invigorating title theme quite purposefully calls Carpenter to mind: the politics here are in perfect step with Snake Plissken’s, and with great anarchy comes great responsibility.

reviews.text: A belated RIP to Bruce Glover. While I’ve only seen a small amount of his work, he should be known more for than just "He was Crispin Glover's father." Walking Tall is a movie I have known of since literally childhood yet it’s never been viewed before last night. Heck, I’ve had a copy of this film-nevermind how-for a little while. Now was finally the time to see Walking Tall and tip my cap to a late character actor who was talented no matter what poor schlock he was in. Even before hearing details about DIE HARD DRACULA, the presumption is that it is never something to be viewed seriously. No, I don’t plan on tracking down Die Hard Dracula…

reviews.author: Wesley Stenzel
reviews.text: This has gotta be the funniest legacy sequel ever made. It makes perfect sense that reactionary man-of-the-times Oliver Stone would be attracted to a project about the Great Recession, and it is absolutely preposterous that that project positioned itself as an in-name-only sequel to a 1987 drama that was not very good to begin with. Imagine if they made a Blind Side 2: Taking a Knee in 2032 and Sandra Bullock was the only returning cast member, except it’s a thousand times more ironic because it’s a cash-grab sequel to a movie that was primarily concerned with condemning greed.

reviews.author: Daryl
reviews.text: As a sequel, Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps doesn't hit the heights of its predecessor, a film I love, however as a standalone film, it's pretty solid, I found it engaging, and liked it more than others it seems. The story isn't quite as focused, and the narrative lacks a cold cutting edge which concludes in a somewhat sentimental ending. A stacked cast, and a fun cameo from Charlie Sheen.

reviews.text: I am genuinely dumbfounded by the negativity War Horse (2011) receives. Overly sentimental, unrealistic, not brutal enough and too manipulative, all seem to be the favoured opinions. For what it’s worth I think the cinematography and production design is incredible and the screenplay very effective, focusing on a cyclical structure that delivers both emotion and bags of heart. The war scenes are really impressive and respectfully done considering the demographic the book was written for. John Williams score is beautiful and Steven Spielberg’s direction graceful. A wonderful experience that would not have had the same impact had the sentimentality been toned down and the violence turned up.

reviews.text: “Warcraft” is a once-in-a-generation disaster, one of the most ill-advised and ill-conceived studio films of this modern blockbuster era, but you have to give Universal some credit for trying. At a time when films of this scale are defined by safety and defenestrated by compromise — at a time when blockbusters are rigorously engineered to appeal to the broadest possible audience — Universal went all-in on a summer movie so niche and nerdy that it makes “Willow” look like “Lord of the Rings,” and “Lord of the Rings” look like “Masterpiece Theatre.”

More power to you if you can get through more than twenty minutes of it and not check out entirely.

reviews.author: YI JIAN
reviews.text: It's fine, it's there, it happened. Never seen an adaptation of a video game that reaches this level of visual grandeur, but Warcraft is a film that requires a certain extent of dorkiness in order to be fully appreciated. (Wish I'm part of the horde.) All the establishing shots of unique Warcraft locations made the film a truly awesome sightseeing experience, so I'm gonna click that little like button over the corner there to show my respect to Duncan Jones for having the balls to direct this, and because to cover such a huge amount of source material in less than two hours is no easy feat. Thank you for trying.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Warriors of the Year 2072 is Lucio Fulci's Rollerball inspired contribution to the post-apocalyptic sub-genre. This one takes place in a dystopian future where two rival TV producers compete for ratings with violent gladiatorial combat inspired game shows, using convicts on motorcycles as contestants. It's all rather simple stuff - the convicts compete for their lives, Nazi inspired guards oversee the games and of course there's a deeper conspiracy going on in the background. It's cool how this film harks back to Italian history through the central plot, aswell as featuring the Colosseum and the Catacombs of Rome. The aesthetics are all bright lights, flashy visuals and cheap looking costumes. The effects budget stretched to plenty of exploding motorcycles and…

reviews.text: Fulci's entry in the Italian future-dystopia cycle is often-boring hackwork, but contains enough elements that prod my pleasure centres - flashing lights, lens flare, lasers, synth music, bleep bloop sounds, model cities - to keep me awake to the end. Fulci throws in a slit throat near the beginning and a bunch of beheadings near the end to let you know that he's still himself.

reviews.author: Daniel Shillito
reviews.text: Storming onto the 80s Italian Sci-Fi arena armed with full-throttle post-apocalyptic mayhem, hard chrome nihilism and mad blasts of il maestro's signature grisly gore, Lucio Fulci's Warriors of the Year 2072 takes great pleasure in delivering more than its fair share of gladiatorial combat in a future overrun by neon-lit decay and hyper-industrial landscapes. Despite working with a rather pitifully minuscule budget, even by Italian exploitation standards, it touches on ideas like spectacle as control, the commodification of violence and resistance within oppressive systems with Fulci valiantly attempting to make it work within what he's been given, delivering a wonderfully immersive film that feels like The Running Man by way of Mad Max. His direction is as stylish as always,…

reviews.text: Whale Rider is a humble film, a small story with a big heart. It shows Māori culture as part of contemporary New Zealand, specificially in regards to patriarchy and authority. Yet it goes beyond that too. It is a film of grief and resentment, centering on an almost unwanted child having to prove herself. Whale Rider is the sort of cinema worth showing to people of any age, because it presents simple themes and struggles in a very digestible and meaningful way. It has ideas around balancing tradition and modernity, as well as the personal and emotional growth that both adults and children need to learn in order to discover self-worth. Crucially the film's biggest arc belongs to a grandfather…

reviews.text: It is a very rare event to stumble upon a film that manages to be so pervasively universal and emotionally empathetic. The film sells itself in its covers and publicity as an allegorical film, maybe even a family/fantasy feature; opens as a metaphor through an ancient legend that pays respect to the tribal traditions of New Zealand; transcendently evolves into a parable about the power of love, family, perseverance, and respect; and closes with an unprecedented epic fashion that modern cinema is rarely afforded. What an impeccable film! What powerful revelations!

Who knows what the plot of the original Japanese film that they used was but the new plot is a villain named Wong tries to keep a small country off the globe by stealing their recipe for egg salad. That's right egg salad. Ands it's up to hero Phil Moskowitz(an Asian by the way)to save the day. The film does take a time out or two to catch up with Woody Allen or to watch a performance by the Lovin' Spoonful why? I don't know,it's that offbeat. You'll have a blast watching this one.

reviews.author: I.V.
reviews.text: Masochistically submitted myself to another Jack Gold movie. An American scientist returns from East Germany with a robot body, and it’s up to Elliott Gould and a team of prematurely middle-aged ‘70s TV actors to figure out whether he’s the real deal or a Commie impostor. Apart from the psychotronic premise, this is a plodding, indifferent piece of work, which is also the most bizarre thing about it; Gold’s direction of the camera and actors is sub-cop-show, but the mere presence of Joseph Bova’s sadsack, turtleneck-wearing robo-scientist in any given shot is surreal and sometimes kind of hilarious.

Saved from certain death by the Soviets, Martino is rebuilt into a silver faced cyborg. After months of rehabilitation (or possible re-education…), the metal man formerly known as Dr Lucas Martino is returned to the Americans. To those who knew him he sounds like Martino and knows what Martino knew, but obviously doesn’t look like Martino and there’s nothing left of him to biologically test. It’s up to abrasive spy catcher Sean Rogers (Elliott Gould) to investigate and trail the metal man from beyond the wall. That Martino is an essential component of an American military weapons…

reviews.author: DirkH
reviews.text: When a film starts with real footage from various wars in which we see children suffering and dying, you know it's not going to be an 'easy' watch. And it isn't, not by a long shot.What makes it stand out is not gore or easy scares, it's atmosphere. It evokes a feeling of 'wrongness', caused by the scariest antagonists possible, children. These kids do the most horrible things and therein lies the strength of this film. It's the disconnect between the rational expectations you have when you see a child and the sadistic things they eventually do. This slow realisation is acted out really well by the two leads. Even though I expected it, the inevitable conclusion still shocked me. There is a lot to admire in this film, it has something to say, the acting is very good, but what I liked most is that it doesn't try to give any easy explanations.

Although not an allegory for any specific scenario or event, decolonial/anti-imperial and youth revolts against existing systems are broadly evoked. There is always a calculus in the adult mind of how many children is it acceptable to kill to get the business deals, land grabs, tax cuts, ideological architecture, etc, desired at the moment,…

Una lista llena de maleantes y peligrosos púberes asesinos, liderada por la electrizante Quién puede matar a un niño, de Narciso Ibañez Serrador. reviews.text: Charlton Heston was one of those actors who divided opinion, mostly because of his political views away from the big screen. Heston was a complex individual, a man whose religious and political views changed over time, going from one extreme to the other. He was one of the first Hollywood actors to support the Civil Rights Movement in the late 1950's and 60's, he even accompanied fellow actors Harry Belafonte and Marlon Brando in the 1963 March on Washington. He supported various Liberal Presidential candidates too, but seemed to change tact as the years went on, especially on gun control which he spoke out on back in 1968. His Liberal views were replaced by a staunch support of numerous Republican…

Vincent Price is Matthew Hopkins - the Witchfinder General who will rid your village of witches through false accusation and forced torture, for a few pieces of silver. The film takes place in England in 1645 - it's a time of political upheaval, which has created a power vacuum perfect for a man like Hopkins to prosper. Enforcing the accepted orthodoxy and using his parliamentary approved powers for his own end. It's a brilliant performance from Price - unusually understated by his standards, but thoroughly malevolent all the same. The film is very well directed by Michael Reeves…

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: For a film that no longer gets a lot of attention, Peter Weir's "Witness" is an outstanding piece of work. A slow-rolling thriller as much about clashing cultures as it is about protecting its titular witness, Weir's film is grown up, exciting, and sure-handedly crafted. Combing peril, romance, and an observation about American cultural idiosyncracies, the film is an entertaining and engrossing heartland noir.

This isn't a film about a character who behaves badly, is punished for it, and is then redeemed. reviews.author: James
reviews.text: Yogi Bear is a subversive masterpiece. Through the depiction of these truly awe inspiringly animated bears, the audience is given a peak, a taster on their incredible ability to steal food. Yogi Bears relationship with his son is one for the ages. Through the subtle depiction of the forest, the audience is able to gather how tightly enclosed Yogi and has son are. The world is pushing them in. So when they finally leave the forest, the audience is mentally fulfilled. These subtle plot decisions truly lets the audience know what the film is about. Slaves. Being oppressed in the 1800s. The production design is also truly outstanding. Yogi Bears house tells you so much about his character, the quirky things on his walls give insight into his dark past. 10/10 would watch again.

Obviously, the circumstances in each film are completely different, with Linney’s scene played for comedy and Affleck’s for extreme drama, but this appears to be a particularly important type of scene for Lonergan. The guilt felt by both of these characters is shown to be excruciating to the point where they wish some form of authority would step in to administer the proper…

reviews.author: Marcissus
reviews.text: To get a stronger grasp on this films ideas and intent one must first comprehend this piece of trivia: Michelangelo Antonioni's original ending was a shot of an airplane sky-writing the phrase "Fuck You, America" Venomous though it may be—and it doesn't need that last shot to drive its message home—it's a markedly seductive and inviting rendition of American socio-political structures through the lens of youthful/foreign cynicism, however patent. If the man's language is guns, you talk to him with a gun, so says a miscellaneous hippie. Antonioni's language isn't the type to end with lingering gun smoke, though watching credits roll by isn't far from it. "The audiences won't like it" MGM insisted, well, "That's the same old jive…

Alternately wistful and cynical outsider view of America, a place where a hippie can just take a plane and get away with it, until he tries to repent. The callously arranged female models of BLOWUP give way to outright mannequins animated by ad companies who see people only as clotheshorse to prop up their products. reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: What Antonioni CAN'T do has always been as mind-blowing as what he can do. See Ingmar Bergman's infamous assessment that Antonioni is an amateur. In this film, Antonioni can't do anything; least of all, film two people talking to each other. Previously he never tried to film a conversation. He makes an honest attempt to do so here, and therein lies the problem: Antonioni doesn't have an honest bone in his body.

reviews.text: constantly draws your attention to its own overt artificiality. disguises everything: that woman is a man, those dice are fake, his cane hides a sword, this old guy is a mob boss, the blood is digital. eyes can't be trusted. Kitano trades his usual static deadpan for faster cuts and a moving camera, absolutely none of which his legendary protagonist -- who is totally in on the joke -- can see. and yet we're constantly sonically locked in to his perceptions, especially in the hidden music he hears everywhere.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Zatoichi is based on the Japanese cult character Zatoichi, who first saw the light of day in 1962 with "The Tale of Zatoichi" and subsequently starred in numerous films and TV series played by Shintaro Katsu. Kitano dared to tackle the material and obviously wanted to stray as far as possible from the familiar Zatoichi. Kitano, who wrote the screenplay himself, reworked Zatoichi completely and transformed the cult hero into a more passive, background figure. But when he gets going, he gets going. Gallons of blood spurt, limbs are severed, bodies are slashed open.

reviews.text: With all the Zatoichi I've enjoyed digesting in the greater collection Shintaro Katsu will always be the true Zatoichi to me. Yet that doesn't hinder any other attempts at impersonations, as Takeshi Kitano did here. It doesn't matter if he's not the real Zatoichi at all, his version of Ichi is as deadly as any other and vastly entertaining. It's faster, flashier, and bloodier than earlier entries. It's also a bit goofier with some modern cheesy comic moments thrown in. I personally wasn't a fan of all the arcs which is the only reason for the half star short rating here, but I was a big fan of the action. Also, while I think the musical number at the end…

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: When you're on muscle relaxers, this is a fifteen-star movie. After filming half of ZOMBI 3 in the Philippines, director Lucio Fulci left the production. So the producers asked co-writer Claudio Fragasso (TROLL 2) and assistant director Bruno Mattei (CRUEL JAWS) to complete it. That simultaneously explains everything and nothing about experiencing ZOMBI 3. This movie is an unholy mutation of DAY OF THE DEAD, THE CRAZIES, THE BIRDS, and RETURN OF THE LIVING DEAD. Plus surreal dubbing, outrageous gore, and righteous dad rock. There is no plot, but there are zombies with machetes. And lines like, “This place was buzzing with life, and now it's buzzing with flies!” Baffling and beautiful. (Joseph A. Ziemba)
